# Front Binding of the Manuscript

-> **Exterior Cover** <-

The manuscript is encased in a historical binding, likely constructed from <term>vellum<note>A durable, high-quality parchment made from animal skin, widely used for book covers during the early modern period.</note></term> or a similarly light-toned leather. The material shows the natural aging and texture of a well-preserved artifact.

The cover is framed by a double-ruled rectangular border. At each of the four corners of this inner frame, a decorative <term>fleuron<note>A stylized floral or leaf-like ornament used in bookbinding and typography.</note></term> has been impressed into the material, with each point directed toward the center of the volume.

-> **Central Ornamentation** <-

At the heart of the front cover is a large, symmetrical <term>cartouche<note>An ornate frame or medallion, typically featuring scrollwork, used to house a central image or title.</note></term>. This design was created using <term>blind-stamping<note>A decorative technique where a design is pressed into the leather or vellum without the use of ink or gold leaf, leaving a subtle, recessed impression.</note></term>. 

The cartouche consists of:
*   Intricate **scrollwork** patterns
*   Delicate **foliage** and leaf motifs
*   A blank central oval, which remains uninscribed.

The spine of the book exhibits several raised bands that provide structural integrity. The sections between these bands—known as compartments—are adorned with ornate **gold-tooled** patterns, suggesting that this was a significant or valuable work. While a dark leather label is affixed to the spine, the title or identification once written there is no longer legible.

<summary>This page presents the protective exterior of the manuscript, a vellum binding featuring blind-stamped decorative elements and a gold-tooled spine. Such craftsmanship indicates the volume was intended for a formal library or a person of means.</summary>

# The MICROCOSM
## A History

<note>The "Microcosm" (from the Greek for "little world") refers to the human being, who was viewed in Renaissance philosophy as a miniature reflection of the entire universe, or Macrocosm.</note>

->By the Author<-

### ROBERT FLUDD <note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was a famous English physician, mystic, and polymath whose works attempted to bridge the gap between science, music, and spirituality.</note>, etc.

<summary>This title page introduces Robert Fludd's influential study on the "History of the Microcosm," exploring the relationship between human existence and the greater universe.</summary>

<note>original image text: The circular diagram illustrating the "Microcosm" contains several labels that map the human mind and body to the cosmos. At the top, within the divine light, are Mind, Intellect, and Reason. The left side lists the Supreme, Middle, and Lowest Hierarchies. The right side contains Fludd's metaphysical divisions: Manifestation (Epiphania), Echo (Epiphonoma), and Essence (Ephiona). Inside the human figure, the bodily fluids or "humors" are listed: Phlegm, Blood, and Choler (Yellow Bile). # TO GOD, THE BEST
## AND GREATEST, THE INCOMPREHENSIBLE
### CREATOR OF MAN,
### FOR HIS VAST BENEVOLENCE AND
### MERCY TOWARD HIM.
### A PRAYER OF THANKSGIVING.

<margin>a Aristotle, Ethics, Book 2.</margin>
<margin>b Theological Resolutions, Vol. 2, part 2, page 3, question 1.</margin>
<margin>c Aristotle, Politics, Book 3.</margin>
<margin>d Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, 4.</margin>
<margin>e Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, 4.</margin>
<margin>f Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander, 4 & Asclepius, 3.</margin>
ALMIGHTY founder of all things, my incomparable creator, who out of your remarkable kindness toward man created him with such excellence and sublimity, <gloss>a</gloss> that you established him, in a certain way, as the end and purpose of all things: <note>The author is referencing the "Great Chain of Being," a historical concept where humans occupy a central position in the universe, linking the physical and spiritual worlds.</note> indeed, by granting him <gloss>b</gloss> reason, you made him compatible with the Angels; by attributing sensitive powers to him, you made him equal to the beasts; by providing natural forces, you made him like the plants; and by bestowing a body, you made him one with inanimate things. <note>original: "rebus inanimatis"</note> Truly, you wished to create him as <gloss>c</gloss> a creature <term>animal providum<note>A creature of foresight; this phrase was famously used by the Roman orator Cicero to describe the unique nature of humanity.</note></term> of foresight, wisdom, sharpness, and memory, full of reason and counsel, by a wondrous condition. <gloss>d</gloss> You so tempered his exalted nature that you made it known to the very dwellers of heaven and as close as possible to the Angels. <gloss>e</gloss> You shaped his whole being from the disposition of soul and body—that is, from the eternal and the mortal—so that the creature thus fashioned by your creation might satisfy both of his origins: both to marvel at heavenly things and adore you (eternal <term>Elohim<note>original: "Elohim"; A Hebrew name for God, often used in the Renaissance to evoke the mystical and powerful aspects of the Creator.</note></term>), and to inhabit and govern earthly things. Thus, he may love and care for the things that are below him, while he himself is loved and cared for by you and your superior ministers, namely the Angels. <gloss>f</gloss> Likewise, he himself may cultivate the earth, be mingled with the elements by his speed, descend into the depths of the sea by the sharpness of his mind, and all things may shine for him clearly and transparently. No gloom of the air can confound his mind’s intention, nor the density of the earth hinder his work, nor the deep altitude of the water take away his view. I, your man, your creature, glorified and exalted by the immense dignity and nobility of his creator, cry out through the fire, through the air, through the earth, through the heaven, through the universal spirit, through the abyss, and through the created things of the world:

<summary>This page contains a formal prayer of thanksgiving to God as the Creator, celebrating the unique "middle" position of humanity in the universe. It draws heavily on both Aristotelian philosophy and the mystical "Hermetic" traditions of Hermes Trismegistus.</summary>
<keywords>Theology, Great Chain of Being, Hermes Trismegistus, Aristotle, Creation, Elohim, Humanism, Elements, Nature of Man</keywords>

## You Alone, You Thrice Greatest, O Jehovah, Are God,
### whose unspeakable name be blessed forever.

Therefore, your human—your own creature, adorned by a ray of your unspeakable splendor—gives immortal and most just thanks to you (O Lord of highest eternal and infinite kindness), with sacrifices of soul and heart and the most humble adoration leading the way. These thanks are for your immense mercy and goodness toward him: <margin>g</margin> because you, the <term>skilful<note>original: "Dædalius," referring to Daedalus, the master craftsman of Greek myth.</note></term> builder of all things, prepared, arranged, fashioned, and brought him to a happy pinnacle or conclusion according to the <margin>h</margin> sacred image of yourself and the likeness of the most lively and noble "world-machine," both visible and intelligible. <margin>i</margin> Indeed, with your own hands, <margin>k</margin> you shaped him from clay at his creation <margin>l</margin> and so perfected him with your <term>supersubstantial wisdom<note>Wisdom that exists beyond the physical substance of the world.</note></term> that he might rule over the other creatures you brought into the world: <margin>m</margin> namely, the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the cattle of all the earth, and every creeping thing upon it. <margin>n</margin> Thus, by your irrevocable decree, all the beasts of the earth, all the winged creatures of the air, and all the aquatic animals of the sea were delivered into his hands, struck with fear of him; for you established him as a living being full of perfection, ruling over all, and far surpassing the other animals in virtue. <margin>o</margin> For your spirit, O strong GOD, made him, and your almighty breath gave him life, and at his creation, you adorned him with a divine mind above all other animals. <margin>p</margin> Indeed, you were so mindful and solicitous of him that you made him only a little lower than the Angels, crowning him with glory and honor; <margin>q</margin> you subjected the works of your hands to his dominion and put all things under his feet. <margin>r</margin> From his very origin, you did not disdain to be his guardian, <margin>r</margin> firmly establishing his steps (taking delight in his path) and ensuring that when he falls, he is not cast down, because you, Jehovah, support his hand. <margin>s</margin> Likewise, you number his steps, but mercifully spare him his sins; <margin>t</margin> you exercise kindness toward him throughout his life, and <margin>u</margin> your visitation preserves his spirit.

Since, therefore, you—who are the highest and first Lord of eternity—out of your infinite favor toward your creatures, established the world (or <term>Macrocosm<note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</note></term>) as the second Lord, and man (or <term>Microcosm<note>The "Little World"—the idea that a human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note></term>) as the third, and insofar as you, O admirable <term>Archetype<note>The original model or "blueprint" from which all things are made.</note></term>, sitting above the highest peaks of the whole world in inexplicable dignity and brightness, fashioned them according to your own pattern: let the Macrocosm first trumpet forth great and rightful sounds to your praise, famous proclamations, and symphonic voices. Let it declare the remarkable glory and dignity of its creator through living actions; let its thunders echo your holy will with a wondrous and trembling mouth (full of divine Majesty), and let it proclaim your honor and praise throughout the whole world like the raised trumpets of your omnipotence...

...let them proclaim and resound and announce your splendid glory to the living by the shining and flashing power of your breath; let them cry out with their own spirit—not without a great clatter and a mighty, awe-inspiring sound—as if to the whole world, the wondrous works of you, their King and Author; and let them explain the ineffable power of your arm to the creatures of the world. Let the seas, stirred by their secret spirit, give forth great murmurs and roars, so that your omnipotence as their founder and creator, and your command, may be perceived to be exalted with a heavy and stupendous thunder. Let the seas, drenched in no common joy by the presence of you, their King, be observed to surround the earth with a measured motion, an ordered ebb and flow, and with surging waves leaping in a <term>metric harmony<note>The idea that the tides and waves follow a musical or mathematical rhythm ordained by God.</note></term>. 

Let the living foundations of the earth tremble with the remembrance of their noble deeds, and let them seem to dance in your honor with a certain divinely inspired exultation. Let your glowing fires of the heavens persevere in dancing in a triumphant manner, with metric beauty and suitable proportions, in the <term>Elysian fields<note>original: "campis Elysiis," a reference to the blessed afterlife in Greek mythology, here used to describe the heavenly reaches.</note></term> and ethereal meadows before you, their fiery commander, and let them exult as if with remarkable joy. Let the universal spirit of the world (the true offspring of <term>hyla<note>original: "hylae," referring to the Greek "hyle" (ὕλη), the fundamental, primordial matter or substance of the universe.</note></term>) be carried here and there at your nod and be decorated; let it render itself subject to your fiery impressions and receive the mystic characters of the noble works of you, its creator. Let the shapeless darkness and the empty matter be driven by a new and unusual life by your word and your gaze alone, and let them be made into "something" out of "nothing." Finally, let the heaven, earth, matter, the abyss, the spirit (or the invisible waters), the sea, springs, rivers, rains, hail, snow, thunder, lightning, winds, and all other occurrences of the <term>Macrocosm<note>The "great world," or the universe as a whole.</note></term> rejoice to trumpet forth and make public to the whole spirit your praises and encomiums, O unspeakable **Elohim**.

What, then, can man—the <term>Microcosm<note>The "little world," or humanity, seen as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note></term>—perform any less than the Macrocosm itself in the celebration of your remarkable praises? You established man second only to the Lord of eternity, the Macrocosm, while you enclosed within him a portion of every mystery of that Macrocosm and imbued him with the sacred breath of life, breathed immediately from your own mouth.

### JOYFUL THANKSGIVING

I beseech you, allow my soul—carried on golden wings in its crystalline spirit <note>A "crystalline spirit" refers to a state of absolute purity and clarity, often associated in early modern philosophy with the highest heavens or the refined state of the soul.</note>, and filled with the fullness of healing grace in Christ and your true word—to die, so that at last, by the vitality of your Most Holy Spirit, I may rise again to you. You are the first and only unity of the created number—that is, the Beginning <note>The author uses Neoplatonic language here, where "Unity" or "The One" is the source from which all "multitude" (the material world) flows.</note> from which my soul was first infused, moving from simplicity into the multitude of matter, until it returns to the unspeakable unity and simplicity of your glory when the resurrection is complete. 

Be to me, O God, I pray, a rock, a shield, and a fortification through your power and strength, so that my enemies may feel that I am covered under the shadow of your wings, preserved, and breathing happily. Grant that I may be snatched up by a ray of your inexplicable majesty toward the true meditation of higher things, and let lower things be considered most vile by my soul. Grant, I say, that the memory of your glory may be perpetually retained by my spirit with deserved honor, just reverence, and fear, and that it may be inscribed upon it in living characters. 

Let your ineffable and most holy name be venerable and laudable to me forever. Be gracious and favorable to me through your justice. Let your providence direct and govern me in my ways, while I adore your counsel with admiration, preach eternity to the world, extol the incomprehensible riches of your glory, and declare the perfection of truth to the entire orb of the earth. Make me capable of your knowledge and doctrine, so that I, illuminated by your most holy light and well-acquainted with myself, may be able to revere you in a manner acceptable, pleasing, and decent. May I admire your loftiness, and with diligent meditation, search into the beauty of the nobility and sublimity of your dwelling place. 

Let me meditate in ecstasy <term>ecstasi: a state of being "outside oneself," a mystical trance where the soul communicates directly with the divine</term> on the mystery of infinity, and proclaim the unsearchable depth of wisdom to all people like the blast of a trumpet. Let me acknowledge the permanent will of your omnipotence, and finally, let me sing of your eternal praise and honor—which shall end in no age—with a voice in harmony with the whole world. May I relate it with the harmony of the lute, elevate it with triumphal glory, and confidently entrust it to the monuments of immortal fame and perpetual letters that no century can erase.

Nor shall I, a son of man <note>original: "hominis filius." While this is a title for Christ in the Gospels, here the author uses it to emphasize their own humble status as a mortal human being.</note>, ever cease to cry out with open mouth through the most holy rays of my mind, through the subtle and empyrean <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, fiery part of heaven in ancient cosmology.</note> spirits of intellect and reason, through the lucid substance of the vital soul and its heavenly liquid, and through the air which is the receptacle for every part of my internal man. Through fire, through water, and through earth—from which the composition of my muddy body is tempered—through my internal self, through my external self, and through my whole being, I cry out, and with a raised voice I proclaim:

**You Alone, You Thrice-Greatest, O Jehovah, Are God,**
who made the heaven and the earth, and the world; and you have benevolently formed man according to your own image. May your name be blessed forever.

# REJOICINGS

I beseech you to allow my soul—carried on golden wings in its crystalline spirit <note>original: "spiritu crystallino". In early modern mysticism, "crystalline" refers to a state of supreme purity and transparency, allowing the light of God to pass through without distortion.</note>, and in the fullness of balsamic grace <note>original: "gratiæ balsamicæ". "Balsamic" refers to the healing and preservative qualities of balsam, suggesting a grace that heals the soul and preserves it from spiritual decay.</note> in Christ and your true word—to die, so that finally, by the alacrity of your most holy spirit, I may rise again toward you, the first and only unity of the created number. That is, I seek the principle from which my soul was first infused—moving from simplicity into the multitude of matter <note>This reflects Neoplatonic philosophy: the soul begins in a "simple" (undivided) state with God but becomes fragmented or "multiplied" when it enters the physical world of matter.</note>—so that I may return to the ineffable unity and simplicity of your glory once the resurrection is complete.

Be to me, O **GOD**, I pray, a rock, a shield, and a fortification by your power and strength, so that my enemies may feel that I am covered, preserved, and happily breathing under the shadow of your wings. Grant that I may be snatched away by the ray of your inexplicable majesty toward the true meditation of higher things, and let lower things be held as most vile by my soul. Grant, I say, that the memory of your glory may be perpetually retained by my spirit with merited honor, just reverence, and fear, and let it be inscribed upon my spirit in living characters.

May your ineffable and most holy name be venerable and praiseworthy to me forever. Be gracious and favorable to me through your justice. Let your providence direct and govern me in my ways, while I adore your counsel with admiration, preach eternity to the world, extol the incomprehensible riches of glory, and declare the perfection of truth to the entire world. Make me capable of your knowledge and doctrine, so that I, illuminated by your most holy light and well-known to myself, may revere you in a manner acceptable and pleasing to you. May I admire your loftiness, most diligently search out the beauty of the nobility and sublimity of your seat through fitting meditation, contemplate the mystery of infinity in ecstasy, and proclaim the inscrutable depth of your wisdom to all people like the blast of a trumpet. Let me acknowledge the permanent will of your omnipotence, and finally, let me sing your eternal praise and honor—which shall end in no age—with a voice in unison with the whole earth. May I report it with the harmony of the lute <note>original: "citharæ". While often translated as lyre, the lute was the standard instrument for such metaphors in the Renaissance.</note>, elevate it with triumphal glory, and confidently entrust it to the monuments of immortal fame and perpetual letters that no century can erase.

Nor will I, a son of man, ever cease to cry out with open mouth through the most holy rays of my mind, through the subtle and empyrean <note>The "Empyrean" was the highest part of heaven, thought to be composed of pure light or fire.</note> spirits of my intellect and reason, through the lucid substance of the vital soul and its ethereal liquid, and through the airy receptacle of every part of my internal man. Through fire, through water, and through earth—from which the composition of my muddy body <note>original: "lutosi corporis". A reference to the biblical creation of man from the "mud" or clay of the earth.</note> is tempered—through my internal self, through my external self, and through my whole being, I cry out, and with a raised voice I proclaim:

**YOU ALONE, YOU THRICE-GREATEST O JEHOVAH ART GOD**, who created heaven and earth, and who benevolently fashioned the world and man according to your own image; may your name be blessed forever.

# Table of Contents
## TREATISE I.

This treatise concerning the **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmo". Literally "the little world," a Renaissance concept suggesting that a human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note> according to nature is divided into two sections, in which:

*   *In the **Former Section**, the Metaphysical and physical history of the Microcosm is narrated, in which three things are explained, namely its:*
    *   **Internal part, or the soul**, whose essence is of a three-fold disposition, insofar as it participates in the nature of the heavens:
        *   From the **Empyrean** <note>original: "Empyrei". The highest, most spiritual heaven, composed of pure light and fire.</note>, from which it is called:
            *   **Mind.**
            *   **Intellect.**
            *   **Reason.**
        *   From the **Ethereal** realm, from which it is called:
            *   **Vegetative** (the faculty of life and growth).
            *   **Vital** (the life force or breath).
        *   From the **Elemental** realm, and by this reasoning it is called:
            *   **Animal** (relating to movement and animal spirits).
            *   **Sensitive** (relating to the five senses).
            *   **Image-soul** <note>original: "Idolum". Not a physical idol, but the lowest "shadow" of the soul that mirrors the physical body and stores sensory images.</note>.
    *   **External part, or the body**, in which two things are explained, namely:
        *   The logic of its **constitution.**
        *   The **Harmony**, by which its rebellious parts are bound to one another in concordant peace.
    *   **The Internal within the External**, that is, the operation of the soul within the body, both in:
        *   **Creation.**
        *   **Generation.**
*   *In the **Latter Section**, the Technical history of the microcosm, concerning both its internal and external nature, is proposed and distributed into seven portions, namely:*
    *   **Divination or Prophecy**, *which is the science of the mind.*
    *   **Geometry**, *which is the clarification of the intentions of the intellectual and rational soul.*
    *   **The Art of Memory**, *which is the operation of the remembering and imaginative soul.*
    *   **Natal Astrology** <note>original: "Genethlialogiam". The study of birth charts to determine a person's destiny and guiding spirit (genius).</note>, or the inquiry into one's guiding spirit and birth, *which is the science pertaining to the vital soul.*
    *   **Physiognomy**, or the investigation of the vital and natural soul *through the inspection and observation of the face and other bodily features alone.*
    *   **Chiromancy** <note>original: "Chiromantiam". Palmistry; the practice of reading the lines and shapes of the hand.</note>, *by which we examine present, past, and future occurrences of both the mind and body through proper observation.*
    *   **Pyramidal Contemplation**, *by which the symmetry and musical proportions of the internal and external man are observed.*

# THE FIRST TREATISE,
## SECTION I.
### *B O O K  I.*
### Concerning divine numbers.

#### *C H A P T E R  O N E*
->or a prelude to this subject.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' set within an ornate square frame with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>Because we believe it is impossible to engage with the most noble disposition of man—the internal Microcosm <note>original: "Microcosmi"</note>—or to understand the wonderful harmony of the human soul without an exact knowledge of the world’s melody and symphony, we must look elsewhere first. Similarly, we cannot rightly judge or weigh "number, weight, and measure" <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Wisdom 11:20, implying that God created the world according to mathematical principles.</note> (from which the world and its soul are forged in a miraculous order and chain of agreements) without a proper mystical contemplation of the divine, formal, and hidden numbers, and a sincere inspection of simple harmony. Indeed, all musical compositions, the very essences of worldly things, life itself, and other effects of the living world-music are derived from these divine and original numbers, just as a number flows from unity, a point from a line, and a harmony from a single tone.

Therefore, we consider it necessary above all else—with an infinite effort of mind and talent, or rather with an untiring fervor of the divine itself, preceded by constant and faithful prayers—that we reach a complete knowledge of these things. This is achieved through deep meditation on these divine numbers and a sincere investigation of the simple harmony that flows ineffably from them. 

However, since it is deemed impossible for a mortal to reach this summit by starting from the very beginning (the "first cause"), because no mortal has ever been able to describe or reveal God according to His true essence (so hidden and obscured are the mysteries of Divine Majesty), the task falls to us. Although we labor in poverty and are wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, we possess the capacity for immortality through the enjoyment of the mind and the Divine Word. It is our duty to liberate ourselves from captivity through the power of the mind dwelling within us, to depart from the dim light, to embrace immortality, and to flee corruption. To do this with integrity and beauty, let us use the sharpness of our minds to penetrate the cracks of our bodily darkness. In this way, we may finally reach the goal of Unity by working backward from its effects <note>original: "à posteriori"; a logical term meaning to reason from observed effects back to their causes.</note>. Let us rise to the yoke of light (adorned with the highest beauty) and leap with a light bound into the super-substantial homeland of the mind, climbing Jacob’s ladder <note>A biblical reference to a ladder reaching between Earth and Heaven, used here as a metaphor for the soul's ascent through different levels of reality.</note> eagerly, but 

<meta>catchword: cautiously</meta>

<summary>This opening chapter argues that to understand human nature, one must first study the divine mathematical and musical principles that God used to create the universe. Since God's essence is unknowable, Fludd proposes an "ascent" where the mind studies physical effects to gradually understand their divine causes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book I, moving from the general necessity of studying divine numbers to the specific contemplation of the Monad, or Divine Unity. It bridges the previous page's discussion on the "Microcosm" by explaining the methodological path the author will take: ascending from human harmony to divine symphony.</meta>

...let us ascend cautiously, rising on the spiritual wings of St. Paul <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven."</note> (relying on the power of the Holy Spirit) to the life and immortal light of the third heaven. And if we cannot clearly see the secrets of the supersubstantial numbers according to the essence of the Deity with our intellectual eyes, let us at least behold in them the idea, icon, or example of the glory of the Trinity. Let us compare the Trinity's divine and formal numbers with material ones—with the highest reverence and adoration of the sacred divinity leading the way. Let us mix the divine with the worldly, and compare the worldly with the human; for thus the world was made, and thus man was propagated in creation. Therefore, let us ascend from the harmony of man to the symphony of the world, and finally—transcending that worldly symphony with the wings of reason—let us ascend to the divine. By this path, we can elicit through knowledge *a posteriori* <note>original: "à posteriore"; reasoning from effects back to their causes.</note> those things which would be impossible for the human grasp to comprehend through knowledge *a priori* <note>original: "à priori"; reasoning from causes to effects.</note>. We, however, following the order of knowledge *a priori* (as if moving from the beginning to that which is begun, having first understood these things *a posteriori*), will—for the sake of a more excellent method—begin from divine and simple numbers and the most simple harmony composed from them. Thus, by their guidance, we may arrive step by step and foot by foot at the composite or material numbers, both worldly and human, along with the symphony derived from them, and so finally immerse ourselves more deeply into material things.

## CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the <term>monad</term><note>A term from Pythagorean philosophy meaning "unity" or "the One," representing the source of all numbers and the divine origin of the universe.</note>, or the supreme and mystical unity.*<-

With the sharp edge of the divine mind’s eyes illuminated, let the **metaphysician** look all around with the clearest spyglass of nature. Let the **physicist** search the corners of the elements and the things composed of them with the deepest inspection of his intellect (occupied with concrete things). Let the **mathematician** look into Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, Optics, Astronomy, Astrology, and Geomancy with his prospective intuition (turned toward abstract things), leaning on the support of demonstration and standing as if on Atlantic shoulders <note>A reference to Atlas, the Titan who held up the celestial spheres; here implying the mathematician supports the weight of the heavens through his calculations.</note>. Let the **logician** speculate on the series and orders of predicables <note>Categories of relationship in logic, such as genus and species.</note>—subtle arguments of reason descending from the transcendent being to genera, from genera to their subordinate species, and from those to individuals. Likewise, let him watch the derivations, origins, predications, and relations of the categories, and especially the transition of the category of substance from the most general kind into a multitude of particulars. Finally, let the **grammarian** remember—with the trust of memory and a clear contemplation of the mind—the order and origin of the elementary letters, the propagation of syllables derived from them, the birth of words from the union of syllables, and afterwards the act of the sentence or the flow of speech emanating from the proper connection and concatenation of words to one another. 

Eventually, all these seekers will perceive and discern, with a manifest face and open eyes, that the origins and existences of all things sprout kindly from that one and only mystical root, and are derived in an ineffable but most certain way. This root is called the "monad of monads" <note>original: "monas monadum"</note>, the supreme and most divine monad, which is that one and thrice-great GOD <note>original: "DEUS solus & termaximus"; a reference to the Hermetic "Hermes Trismegistus" or "thrice-great," here applied to the Christian God.</note>, from whose fountain all things—both created and uncreated, though poured out into a multitude—are observed to flow and emanate by the sharp edge of the divine mind. For if we turn our contemplation to metaphysical things, in them this unity is found to exist as the root of roots, since it is the GOD of GODS, the summit of summits, the good of goods, the fountain of wisdom and the origin of all roots, the intelligence of intelligences, more powerful than omnipotence, unbegotten by any other, of infinite kindness and a mystical mind. Indeed, even in the trinity of persons...

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion on the method of "a posteriori" reasoning to a specific analysis of the Monad, or Divine Unity. # ON DIVINE NUMBERS

Of the supersubstantial essence <note>original: "essentiæ supersubstantialis"; a philosophical term referring to a reality that exists beyond or above the level of physical matter or "substance."</note>, it holds the first place, since it is that sacred unity from which divine number proceeds and into which it returns. Finally, looking out beyond its own essence into material and created things in a way that exceeds the imagination, it has produced from its shining root a chorus of Angels, a crowd of Demons, and a gathering of souls in immense multitude; and by its ineffable wisdom, it has disposed their ranks and company—each and every one—within the glowing and fire-shining spheres. Similarly, by considering the physical creatures of the world and regarding them in a proper manner, we will find that this mystical monad <note>term: "monad" from the Greek "monas," meaning "unity" or the "ultimate one."</note> holds the first place among them. This same unity is the root of the number ten no differently than it is the root of the hundred and the thousand; we shall declare further below that the fabric of the world was established from these numbers in the beginning and remains so now. Hence, among the physicists <note>In this context, "physicists" refers to natural philosophers who study the laws of the physical world.</note>, it is called the divine principle, infinite nature, and creative nature <note>original: "natura naturans"; literally "nature naturing," referring to God as the active, creative force behind the universe.</note>, the principle of principles, the star of stars, the light of lights (or the light of creatures shining everywhere), the spirit of spirits, and the maker and effector of spirits, the world of worlds, the leader, governor, and director of all things, the exalter and the humbler.

Even the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> will not deny that Time had its origin from this root, insofar as this monad exists in its eternal nature, not generated by another, as the beginning and end—the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "α & ω"</note>—of all created things. <margin>*</margin> Wherefore it also received its beginning, "The Now," <note>original: "Nunc"</note> from the said mystical root, without which no time would ever exist; since "The Now" is its boundary, from which time is drawn out and moved, no differently than a line is drawn from a point. Without this root, there would also be no logical relationship, since by no reason do we call someone a "son" unless it is in respect to a "Father"—neither in supersubstantial things, where the Father is called his own principle (or the principle rising from himself), nor in lower things. For there, this root is the hidden seed of beings, the parent of ages, and the life producing all things, filling and satisfying all things with the good and with its own goodness.

Furthermore, when this root is considered according to Mathematics in Geometry, it is the point of the primordial line and the center of the circle, from whose multiplication all lines, all surfaces, and all bodies—both mathematical and physical—proceed, and into which they finally return through a preceding resolution, as if to the principle from which they came. In Music, it is the origin of concord and harmony, namely that primordial unison, from whose supersubstantial tone the empyrean <note>term: "empyrean" refers to the highest heaven, characterized by pure light and fire.</note> melody (whether spiritual, worldly, human, or even instrumental) arises. This occurs insofar as the composite consonances of the Fourth, the Fifth, the Octave, the Octave-plus-Fifth, and the Double Octave <note>original: "Diateſſaron, Diapente, Diapaſon, Diapaſon cum Diapente & Diſdiapaſon"</note> are derived from the boundary of its voice or radical sound (which produces the Word). In Arithmetic, this monad also exists as the root from which digits, articles, numbers, hundreds, thousands, and so on are observed to arise and emanate into infinity. From this, it is manifest that this root—or monad and unity—is one and all things: one of all, one before all, and one in itself. It is the root and center of things present, past, and future. It is prior to material unity because it is the most simple: the number of numbers, unity and number, and a point-unity <note>original: "acunitas"; a specialized term for a unity that acts with the piercing simplicity of a single point.</note> which penetrates every number by its simplicity. For in the Trinity, the Father is ineffable; looking into the empyrean heaven, He is the Mind of mind and the Soul of souls; and looking further down into the material world, He is the Nature of natures. O, how admirable is the arrangement of the monad or unity! Though it is the cause and origin of the existence of things, what it actually is cannot be discerned by the sharpness of talent—no, not even by the sharpness of the mind (which flows immediately from it)—nor can it be expressed by any reason. Yet, the marvelous nature of this essence is clearly explained to our reason in the contemplation of arithmetic unity: for arithmetic unity is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers, containing within itself every number, however large, and yet it is innocent of all multitude, always the same, immutable, indivisible...

# TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK I.

...visible and without equal: And hence it is, that this unity multiplied by itself produces nothing except itself. For 1 multiplied by itself produces only 1 and an internal result; from that 1 multiplied by 1 nothing but unity alone will arise. From this it is clear that unity is its own root, square, cube, and so on, and yet it is always this same thing. For however much it is multiplied into units, none of the resulting units is greater or smaller than the radical <note>original: "radicali"; referring to the "root" or fundamental unit.</note> unit, nor is a part smaller than its whole, since it is not multiplied into parts but into itself. Finally, it is the beginning and end of all things, while yet it has neither beginning nor end by which it exists, since nothing is prior to one, and nothing is posterior to one. One, therefore, is the beginning of all things, and all things exist up to one, and beyond it nothing exists. Furthermore, all things that exist long for that One itself as their root, because they first proceeded from it, and by necessity they participate in that One. From this it follows that all things strive to return to that one, insofar as they flowed forth from it fundamentally; this regression and return to the first principle would never be completed unless plurality and multitude were gradually and step by step stripped away from them. 

Such, then, is that mystical <term>Monad of monads</term><note>The "Monad" (from the Greek *monas*) represents the absolute, indivisible One or God in Neoplatonic and Pythagorean philosophy.</note>, the unity of unities, the first summit of simplicity, the seed and center of all things, devoid of all substance, the beginning, root, and origin of all; the principle, I say, containing every number but contained by none, begetting every number, begotten by no number, father of all, father of himself, father of the only-begotten son. Indeed, such and beyond what the human mind can imagine is that unity, that one and monad, the holy of holies, the summit of highness, and the God of gods, who sits constantly joyful and filled upon his throne flashing with immortal glory above the peaks of heaven and outside all material existence. He sounds that most holy, mystical, ineffable, and original tone to the world; by its pulsation, act, and uniform breath, the world and its creatures are imbued with various concordances of forms by which they exist and live. The most elegant and distinct harmonies of things (soothing the thirsty ears of the mind) are heard and conceived and stored in the inner recesses of human reason. By this ineffable melody and effective voice and word (with the divine Spirit breathing from every side), the framework of the <term>macrocosm</term><note>The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, viewed as a giant living organism.</note> is observed to dance with a certain joy, to leap proportionally, and to live as if by springing forth. The stars, both fixed and wandering, are noticed to lead eternal dances as if they were drenched in supernatural gladness. The proportions and consonances of the <term>microcosm</term><note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>—in mind, intellect, reason, soul, motion, life, and the elementary construction of the body (completing beautiful and admirable functions)—are perceived to be propped up as if by a divine pillar. 

This unity, I say, is the player of the <term>Monochord</term><note>A single-stringed musical instrument used by ancient and Renaissance theorists to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of the universe.</note> and is the very form and soul of the whole macrocosmic and microcosmic harmony. Its string, or instrumental matter, is that universal spirit which it liberated by its ineffable act from the bowels of chaos, and made from nothing, so that something might exist in actuality and serve its astounding actions in a passive role. To Him, as King of Kings, all the things of all nature must be offered; as if a tribute due to him, the lives, essences, souls, and bodies of things must be attributed and conferred, insofar as they depend on Him. This, above all, every person of sound mind and adorned with even a modest gift of reason ought to acknowledge and confess with the greatest effort and the final endeavor of the soul.

# ON DIVINE NUMBERS.

->*Several examples, by which the Unity of the most holy Trinity (by comparing it to inferior things) is demonstrated according to human capacity.*<-

The super-substantial unity of essence is explained in Arithmetic by the number 1. For from this unity in Arithmetic, all numbers proceed to infinity—as if drawn from their font and fundamental origin—such as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so on. In Mathematics and the art of Geometry, it is demonstrated by the point, from which the line is derived, through which it is continued, and in which it is terminated (whence the line is most correctly defined as the flow of points bound together one after another). But because every surface is composed of lines and a body of surfaces, it follows of necessity that both lines and surfaces, and consequently the body itself, arise from a single point. 

In a similar way, from unity and its flow, the number ten is formed, in which unity joins itself to composition—namely, the super-excellently substantial nature with the matter to be created—just as 1 is joined with 0. Without the 1, the cipher <note>the zero</note> will be no more than primordial matter or <term>hyle</term><note>The ancient Greek term *hyle* refers to unformed, dark matter that lacks shape or spirit.</note> deprived of essential and lucid form. Hence, the simple unity stands to the number ten as the point stands to the line, and the number ten to the hundred as the line stands to the surface; in this arrangement, GOD (the unity) always precedes the "body" or manifested result, as we shall indicate more broadly below. From this it is clearly evident that unless God is placed before all things, things will no more exist in reality than Arithmetical ciphers, which, however great a multitude they might express by themselves, signify nothing at all without unity or some digit flowing from it; just as 0, 00, 000, 0000, 00000 denote nothing, but 10, 100, etc., denote something. 

Through the point, GOD is also wonderfully explained in the physical world, since the point is the movement in generation and corruption, the principle, and as it were this "now" <note>original: *nunc*</note> from which time proceeded as from its paternal foundation of origin, or the starting point <note>original: *termino à quo*</note>, and into which it returns again.

### CHAPTER III.
->*On the Dyad, or the mystical and super-substantial duality.*<-

The first <term>Monad</term><note>original: *monas*; from the Greek *monos*, meaning "one" or "alone." In this context, it represents the indivisible Unity of God.</note> of monads, and the holy Unity of unities, having poured out the simplicity of the heights in an inexpressible way through a super-substantial birth, brought forth and produced the <term>Dyad</term><note>The number two or the principle of duality.</note>. Indeed, this Dyad, springing forth through the first-born form, attained a threefold power: for where the depth of the Father is, there shines the luster of the illustrious Son and the reconciling brightness of the Holy Spirit. Thus is that super-substantial fountain crowned with the beauty of the offspring which flowed from its own center and revolves around that center. The Son was begotten, who is the renowned wisdom of the Father and the architect of all things. For through the pouring out of the One into the Son, an ineffable middle nature was born, which existed before all other natures—a sacred birth and the unspeakable fruit of the ineffable Father. No span of time has known his hidden and mystical origin, because he appeared together with the Father; he is always born, yet was always to be born, and remains within the Father even though begotten from Him, so that He might govern all things with a wise spirit. Springing forth, I say, the Son remains from the Father in the Father forever, and yet rules those things which are outside the Father. He is the Word of the Father, a crying-out and most prominent speech, the first-born from the first root. He is the root of all; for all things are established through his glorious birth, since he is the seed of all things.

Unity, therefore, is the source of the Duality of the same essence; and the Duality (or the Son) is the form and image of the Unity (or the Father). Unity (or the Father) is the power of the Duality; but the Duality (or the Son) is the beauty of the Father. And although the duality of *matter* is an ill-omened number—because it is the font and origin of strife, discord, impurity, and confusion (for this number, by taking matter unto itself, is separated from unity, enters the boundaries of conflict, and flows downward into the "many" by multiplying itself, fleeing the presence of unity and tending toward the center and depth of dark matter)—therefore this number in matter is said to be the most imperfect of all. It can never be resolved except through "resolution," being led back to the peak of essential and super-substantial unity. 

Nevertheless, this *divine* binary number of form, never retreating beyond the limits of the essence of unity, is the most formal and blessed number. This is because within that same essence, by the power of unity—with the Holy Spirit acting as a mediator and bond, proceeding from the center of the Father and the Son—it is reflected back to unity and reunited with it. This is according to the saying of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>original: *M. Trismeg.* An Egyptian-Greek legendary figure to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed.</note>: *The Monad generates a Monad, and reflected its ardor into itself.* And this God-like essence is uniform and yet triform, because although it is triple in respect to persons and numbers...

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the origin of the <term>super-substantial</term> Triad or ternary number.

For the Mind, who is GOD, most full of the fecundity of both sexes (I speak now by the mouth of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica," a body of texts on philosophy, magic, and alchemy.</note>), life and light, with his word brought forth a second creator-mind; who indeed is called GOD *fire* and *spirit divinity*, whom <term>Synesius</term><note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher and bishop known for blending Neoplatonism with Christian thought.</note> called the Holy Spirit, the mediating principle proceeding from the center of the father and from the center of the son, whose shining light is called the Reconciler, because his ternary number is the truest and most sincere love, which links the Father with the son by an unbreakable bond, seeing as duality (which is the multitude proceeding from unity) is reduced into a harmonious unity by the bond of the ternary number. Such then was the origin of the world—a progression, I say, from unity into multitude—and such is its cycle, namely, the reduction of multitude back to unity. 

According to the progress of these divine numbers always contained in unity, the order, harmony, proportion, measure, or intervals of the material duality—whether spiritual, or watery, or of a moist nature—are arranged. From this comes the division of the entire world into three regions, the second of which received its essences from the first and the third, and from both of them. From this come the three harmonies of every symphony: <term>Diapason</term><note>The octave.</note>, <term>Diapente</term><note>The musical interval of a fifth.</note>, and <term>Diatessaron</term><note>The musical interval of a fourth.</note>; of which the *Diapente* comes from the *Diapason* as if from unity, and the *Diatessaron* from both. From this comes the proportion of all things and of the world itself: double, <term>sesquialtera</term><note>A ratio of 3:2.</note>, and <term>sesquitertia</term><note>A ratio of 4:3.</note>, derived from the various arrangements of divine light in the universal spirit within <term>hyle</term><note>original: *hyla*; the Greek term for "prime matter" or the raw substance of the universe.</note>. From this come the intervals of things: namely, the line, the surface, and the body (or length, width, and depth); the line from the point, the surface from the line, and the body from both. From this come the three kinds of souls: intellectual, sensitive, and vegetative. From this comes the arrangement of the world from three: namely, number, measure, and weight. Finally, from this, three "Princes of the World" are proclaimed by the Philosophers: GOD, Mind, and Spirit. 

And this was the reason why the <term>Pythagoreans</term><note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> called unity *Apollo*, the dyad *matter*, but the triad *form and justice*, which is the highest perfection. The <term>Poet</term><note>Likely Virgil, who wrote in his Eclogues, "God delights in an odd number."</note> therefore says that GOD rejoices in an odd number, since the first and simplest odd number in the super-celestial essence is that love which joins the father with the son; whence <term>Synesius</term> says: *Hail, O purest Spirit, center of the son and the father.* And elsewhere: *He called him the companion of the son and the middle between the root and the sprout.* And elsewhere: *The reconciling light, because being derived from the two primary persons and united with them, it joined together the Trinity.* Therefore this ternary number is called the sacred number, the number of perfection, and the most powerful number, because it is uncomposed and the first odd number, by whose bond Duality becomes Trinity and Trinity is made Unity. And from this it is that the One has attained a threefold power, by which it happens that GOD is one and all things, one in himself and through all things, and that there is Unity although there is Trinity, and that there is Trinity although there is Unity; according to *Synesius's 2nd Hymn*: *I sing of you as Unity, I sing of you as Trinity: You are One, though you are Trinity; you are Trinity, though you are Unity.*

TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK I.

For Unity is an act alone in itself, while Trinity exists in its own perfection, flowing from Unity itself, by which all things are called created, perfect, and good. We conclude, therefore, that unity is the <term>starting point</term><note>original: *terminus à quo*; the point from which motion or an argument begins.</note> and duality is the firstborn of unity—appearing as a middle number between unity and the <term>ternary</term><note>The number three.</note>. By the perfection of this ternary, in the divine essence, duality (or the middle) is joined to the two extremes by an indissoluble bond; these, in turn, cling to one another in a circular progress in a wonderful way. From this it follows that all three persons, though distinct in their properties, are nothing but one in essence—namely, a single, supreme, and sole essence, which exists as nothing other than the three persons. That is to say, they are three properties, of which one is not the other, nor are any two the third, nor is any third the two; for they are two in the same way they are the third, and the third in the same way they are the two. What is this? One Deity, one essence, one thing finally. How so, if there are three? How three, if this is one? It is incomprehensible, and therefore wonderful. Faith alone knows it, yet the whole comes as if from the divine Spirit, with the formula for baptism establishing this relationship under this ternary number: *Baptize,* he says, *in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,*<note>original: "Baptizate... in nomine Patris, Filii, & Spiritus sancti."</note> which three relative terms indeed receive further explanation, as we will show more broadly below.

For the whiteness of the eye can be referred to the Father, insofar as from it the corneal sphere and the <term>uvea</term><note>The pigmented middle layer of the eyeball; Fludd uses this anatomical comparison to show how different parts of a single organ represent the Persons of the Trinity.</note> (compared to the Son and the Holy Spirit) proceed. For the Son (who follows most closely in his proceeding from the Father) is likened to the <term>corneal sphere</term>; and the Spirit (who is the power from both) is referred to the uvea, which is in the center of the cornea, just as that is in the center of the whiteness encompassing both orbs. ## CHAPTER V.

->*That each person of the holy and undivided Trinity has a distinct*<-
->*property in the construction of the world and the production of its creatures;*<-
->*And concerning the universal property of unity, and its*<-
->*agreement with the number ten.*<-

The admirable logic of the mystical creation of the world lies hidden in the secret arrangement of the Trinity and in the bosom of the Deity. Thus, there exists no member <note>original: "digitus," literally "finger," used here to mean a component or part of a mathematical/logical whole.</note> in the Trinity—whether it be one, or two, or three—which does not possess its own proper and peculiar mystery within itself, and which does not produce a varied effect in the world (according to the vast and admirable efficacy of its office). For in **unity** (insofar as it cannot be multiplied in itself, or be reduced or divided from its nature into a multitude) the likeness of the material world is sketched out in a hidden way, as if in a single, universal <term>ideal world</term> <note>The "ideal world" (mundus idealis) refers to the Neo-Platonic concept of a world of pure patterns or "ideas" in the mind of God, existing before physical matter.</note> that is purely formal. For without a doubt, there was one principal model of the things to be built in the mind of the Creator. Therefore, just as the <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Monad" (Monas) is a term for the number one, representing the source of all things, indivisible and absolute.</note> was first in the production of the Trinity (which is the first root of things both uncreated and created), so also second, after the birth of that simple square, **unity** occupied the first place in the <term>number ten</term> <note>original: "denarius." In Pythagorean thought, the number ten (the Decad) represents the completion of a cycle and the return to unity.</note> for the composition of the world, because it is bound to the number ten by a strong connection.

For unity is the father of the "supersubstantial" <note>Existing beyond or above physical substance.</note> birth, and the number ten is the father of the "substantial" birth. These two parents do not differ from each other, as both are one God, but they differ in the property of their action: because the former unity was simple and is occupied in the supersubstantial world in an inexplicable way, while the latter, in the number ten (that is, **joined with a cipher** <note>original: "cum cyphra conjuncto." The author refers to the number 10 as the digit 1 (Unity) joined to a 0 (the cipher), symbolizing God's entry into the material realm of numbers.</note>), acts upon the material world. Hence **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed.</note> says: *GOD is called the father of the cosmos, and the cosmos the son of God, etc.* Therefore, **GOD** is unity in the formal world and holds the place of the number ten in the material world. For just as the number ten is the end of the simple numbers, so it is also the beginning of the compound numbers, and the middle or center between unity and the number one hundred. Therefore, unity begins the number ten among the simple numbers, and again that same unity is observed to terminate any tens-based numbers.

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK I.

Or we can best illustrate this using a pair of compasses <note>original: *circinis*; the compass is a recurring symbol in Renaissance Hermeticism representing God as the "Great Architect" of the universe.</note>, the top of which is like a single point, or the **unity of essence**, which is divided into different properties. For one of its legs, fixed and standing immutably in the center, is always the same and does not move from its place. But the other leg is mobile and describes a regular circle at an equal distance from the center. 

To ensure the mobile leg is firmer and more obedient to the regular patterns of the leg that remains fixed and unvarying in the center, there is a certain bond of friendship and a "chain of love," as it were, passing regularly through the center of the mobile part. This is firmly attached to the fixed leg and governs the movement of the mobile leg so that it always agrees in number, measure, and proportion, maintaining a relationship to the fixed leg so that it acts according to the laws and justice of the fixed member. The following is an example of this.

->[Diagram of a pair of compasses drawing a circle. The hinge at the top is labeled **A**. A curved horizontal bar connects the two legs.]<-

**Labels within the diagram:**
- **A (at the hinge):** Unity of essence, One God <note>original: *Unitas essentia Vnus Deus*</note>
- **Fixed leg:** Fixed and unvarying leg or limb
- **Connecting bar:** Bond of love or the nexus of justice
- **Moving leg:** The leg sketching the circle—that is, the world
- **At the center point:** Center

From one essence, namely **A**, three distinct properties proceed, which in themselves are one and the same—namely, the super-substantial essence **A**. In the "fabrication" of the world, however, there are various and diverse properties of the Deity. For God, sitting constantly at the summit of the heavens, sent out from himself his Son (or his Wisdom) for the construction of the spherical world. This is no different than how the mobile leg of a compass proceeds by extending outward from the leg that remains fixed and firm in the center to produce a circle or circumference. By this operation the circle is sketched, and yet they agree in essence—specifically, in the unity or the point.

Therefore, the Unity (the Father), remaining constant and unvarying, ordained the Duality (the Son) to carry out his will. ->*That each person of the holy and indivisible Trinity has a*<-

**T**he admirable ratio <note>The word *ratio* here refers to both a mathematical proportion and the underlying "reason" or logic of creation.</note> of the mystical creation of the world lies hidden in the secret disposition of the Trinity and the bosom of the Deity. Thus, no "finger" exists in the Trinity—whether it be one, two, or three—that does not possess its own proper and peculiar mystery within itself, and does not produce a varied effect in the world (according to the immense and wonderful efficacy of its office). For in unity (insofar as it cannot be multiplied in itself, or reduced or divided from its nature into a multitude), as if in a single ideal and purely formal universal world, the material image of the world is sketched in a hidden manner. For without doubt, there was one principal exemplar in the mind of the Founder for the things to be founded. For unity is the father of super-substantial <note>Meaning "beyond physical substance" or existing in a higher, divine state.</note> birth, and the number ten is the father of substantial birth. Thus, unity begins the number ten among the simple numbers, and again that same unity is observed to terminate any ten-fold numbers.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mystical significance of numbers in the creation of the universe. Having established the role of the "bond of love" and the initial "Let it be" (Fiat), the author now brings in the authority of Hermes Trismegistus to explain how the number one (Unity) and the number ten (the Denary) relate to the World Soul and the structure of the cosmos.</meta>

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK I.

And Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: *Mercurius Trismegistus*; a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the *Hermetica*, texts which bridge Egyptian and Greek philosophy.</note> seems to support this opinion of ours, whose words are these: *The number ten is the parent of the soul; truly life and light are joined there, where the numbers of unity itself are born from the spirit; and so unity, according to reason, encompasses the number ten, and in turn the number ten encompasses unity.* With how much joy I am filled upon hearing these words of the wise man, so appropriately and fitly agreeing with this discovery of mine, I can scarcely express with my tongue or the sharpness of my pen. For what else would this divine priest have meant, than that in the creation of the world the number ten <term>the Denary<gloss>The number ten, which in mystical mathematics represents a return to unity and the completion of a cycle.</gloss></term> (which he later calls unity) is the parent of the world soul <note>original: *animæ mundanæ*; the "Anima Mundi" or spirit that animates all nature.</note>, and consequently the human soul? For, he says, *there life and light*, that is, the spirit and the divine splendor or form, are united. He says that the numbers of unity are born from the spirit—that is, from spiritual matter—being clearly articulated and composed. From these things he concludes thus, because of the composition of the Spirit with light: "And so unity, according to reason, encompasses the ten." That is, the unity which was the parent in the supersubstantial and simple birth, in the composite birth encompasses the number ten according to reason; and he says there is a reciprocal embrace between unity and the number ten. From these things he seems to argue that unity in the trinity is the same as the ten in composition. In another place he says *that by the presence of the number ten, the intellectual generation is composed—that is, the intellectual heaven with its choir of Angels, divided into nine spheres or places of the first composition of the ten-fold parts*, and so on.

Finally, we say that unity has a double relation to the world: either, namely, insofar as it is everything that exists; and thus the entire world is now compared to unity (which is whole and universal in itself). Hence the world, because of the integrity of its parts, is called by Hermes Trismegistus the **material and incorruptible GOD**. Elsewhere he says: *One GOD is the father of one world, one world is the progenitor of one sun, and the unique sun is the origin of one man*, etc. Or, it is viewed insofar as it claimed for itself the first craftsmanship of creation because of the property of its unity (embracing the number ten), and in its first disposition (insofar as it attributes to itself the reason of the first person of the upper machinery of the world: for its fiery spirit was first carried over the waters in that region). From these things it is therefore clear that the property and action of the first person of the Trinity in the structure of the world is concerned with universality, constituting one integrated world. For since everything that exists is established under his inestimable command and is encompassed in his power, it necessarily follows that he regards the entire nature of things and the universal spirit of the world, bringing it from potentiality into act, sustaining it with his fiery breath of life, and finally supporting the entire machine with his immense strength.

From these things, it seems clear that the property of the <term>Binary<gloss>The "Binarius" or the number two, representing duality and the second person of the Divine hierarchy.</gloss></term> among the super-celestial numbers concerns the ordering of the material world and its arrangement into regions, heavens, and orbs. It completes its operations by the power of Unity (or the Father), to whom it exists as a consubstantial co-helper in the arrangement of the universal machine. The Father and Unity, therefore, are concerned with the One and the Whole; and the Son, as if multiplied in the Father's goodness, distinguishes that universal One into different parts and distinct powers. Both are involved with material things, and the Spirit or holy splendor proceeding from both attributes to each portion of the world and each creature its own proper power. For according to the teaching of the Royal Prophet, just as the heavens were formed by the Word of the Lord, so were all their powers formed by the Spirit from his mouth. 

From these points it is evident that the first person operates chiefly in the ordering, determining in his secret counsel what is to be done in the creation of the world. The second person, most obedient to his Father and acting as the Father's sole counselor—or rather, as his very counsel and wisdom—executes the Father’s will with precision, mediated by the third person, who is always necessarily present in every operation.

For in the first uttering of the sacrosanct Word from the mouth of the Father, the rays of the Mind surrounded it, as if crowding around it, adorning it, and fortifying it with ineffable power against the invasions of strife or the passions of the moist nature hidden in the darkness. But the divine Mind immediately (at the command of the Word) fashioned the <term>World Soul<gloss>The "Anima Mundi," an intrinsic spirit believed by many ancient philosophers to animate all nature.</gloss></term>, making its composition from a portion of its own rays and the purest spirit, already uncovered and revealed by the splendor of the Mind and liberated from the darkness; this soul has already acquired the name of the "created and formed water," or rather, of the heavenly form itself. The Mind, indeed, the craftsman together with the Word, containing the circles and turning them with swift rapacity, bends its machine toward itself, and commanded it to revolve from beginning to end without end.* And elsewhere: *the craftsman fashioned the world with the word, not with hands.* And again: *God established all things by the word.* From these things it seems clear that the property of the **Binary** <note>The number two, representing the Second Person of the Trinity.</note> among the supercelestial numbers concerns the ordering of the material world and its disposition into regions, heavens, and orbs. He performs his operations by the power of Unity (that is, the Father), to whom he exists as a consubstantial coadjutor in the arrangement of the universal machine. The Father, therefore, as Unity, is concerned with the "One" and the "Whole," while the Son—as if multiplied in the Father's goodness—distinguishes that universal "One" into different parts and distinct virtues. Both are concerned with material things, and the Spirit (or the holy splendor) leaping forth from both, attributes to each portion of the world and to every creature a power proper to itself. For according to the teaching of the royal Prophet, *just as the heavens were formed by the word of the Lord, so by the spirit from his mouth were all their virtues.* <note>Psalm 33:6: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth."</note>

From this it is evident that the First Person works chiefly in the ordering, determining by his decree and counsel what is to be done in the creation of the world. The Second Person, most obedient to his Father and acting as the Father's sole counselor—indeed, truly being his very counsel and wisdom—executes the will of the Father with precision, by means of the Third Person, who is always necessarily present in every operation. Furthermore, **Hermes Trismegistus** clearly teaches us the mystical way in which the Word first descended from his immortal and <term>supersubstantial<gloss>Existing above all created substance; divine.</gloss></term> throne or palace into the formless mass of worldly matter for the creation of the world, in these words: *The soul is in the body, the mind in the soul, the word in the mind, and God truly is their father, etc.* Although in that passage he speaks of the dark human body, the same can be understood regarding the shadowy mass before the operation of the world. For at the first uttering of the sacrosanct Word from the mouth of the Father, the rays of the Mind surrounded it, as if crowding around it on all sides, adorning it and fortifying it with ineffable power against the invasions of strife or the passions of the moist nature hidden in the darkness. Then, the divine Mind (at the command of the Word) immediately fashioned the **world soul**, making its composition from a portion of its own rays and the purest spirit—now detected and revealed by the splendor of the Mind and freed from darkness—which then acquired the name of "created and informed water," or rather, the name of the celestial form itself: For the Spirit of the Lord was moved... <note>original: "Nam Spiritus Domini ferebatur..." A reference to Genesis 1:2.</note>

### CHAPTER VII.
### *On material numbers, namely the Binary, Quaternary, and Octonary, arising from the property of the God-formed Dyad.* <note>The "Dyad" refers to the number two, representing the first step from the absolute One toward the many things of the world.</note>

**F**ormal duality <note>The "Binary" or number two in its spiritual aspect.</note> is a most blessed number, because it is consubstantial with the formal unity from which it arose. It is also a most perfect number, insofar as it is the middle ground, or the center of the trinity; it has its beginning from the supersubstantial father of its nature, and its end in the number three, which is the infinite and incomprehensible spirit. Finally, it is the midpoint of itself and the center of the number three, proceeding from the center of the Father. For this reason, this number is the center of harmony, retaining within itself the image of the Father (Unity) and the radiance of the Holy Spirit (the number three). Therefore, this formal root is most blessed, life-giving, and preservative, producing the most fortunate formal square and a cube not unlike it. For this essential Binary (the germ of vital unity) does not proceed toward a mere multitude like the material version does; instead, as it flows from unity through the trinity, it returns again and is connected to the unity from which it was previously derived.

Hence, it is called the particular number of justice, and its proper act is justice itself, because it delights in two things weighed equally. It is also called the number of wisdom, knowledge, memory, and light—indeed, it is the very knot of humanity, charity, and mutual love. For just as two people are brought back into one flesh by matrimonial bonds, so in the mystical binary, two are united in the same essence through the third spirit. Similarly, this occurs in its square, which is 4. For the formal square is ascribed to God the Father; indeed, it encompasses the mystery of the entire Trinity. By its simple proportion—namely, the first ratio of one to one—the unity of the paternal substance is signified; from which the Son now proceeds as an equal. By a second procession, also simple (namely, two to two), the Holy Spirit is noted as proceeding from both. Thus, the Son is made equal to the Father by the first procession, and the Holy Spirit is equal to both by the second procession. 

From this, the most excellent name of God and the divine Trinity arose: the Tetragrammaton <note>The "four-letter" name of God in Hebrew: Yod, He, Vav, He (YHWH).</note>, namely *Jod, He, and Vau, He*, where the breathing of the letter *He* denotes the procession of the Spirit from both; for the letter *He* itself, being doubled, ends both syllables and the whole name. It is pronounced *Jova* or *Jehova*, as some prefer. This number is therefore the origin of all divinity; hence the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the ultimate reality of the universe.</note> called it the fountain of nature. It is also the number that fills all knowledge, for the Son is called the knowledge and wisdom of the Father. Furthermore, by the addition of this number with 1, 2, and 3 (1+2+3+4), there is a return to unity, namely to the number ten, from which the structure of the material world began. Finally, the cube rising from the number two, which is 8, the Pythagoreans call—
