...of the second or ethereal heaven, seeing that one portion of the pyramid found in the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual heaven, often associated with pure fire or light.</note> is found in a double proportion to that of the middle heaven, as we have more fully recounted in our treatment of worldly harmony. Next, because in the second place, 2 added to 3 produces 5, which number denotes the **diapente** <term>diapente</term><note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> consonance composed of five sounds or voices; similarly, because 2 stands to 3 in a <term>sesquialtera</term><note>A ratio of 3:2.</note> proportion (in which the diapente consonance is found), this proportion is therefore found twice between the second and third heaven; once, namely, by counting upward from the **Sun** toward the supreme heaven, and once by proceeding downward as far as the elementary heaven. Finally, since in the third place, proceeding circularly, the unity of the **Trinity** relates to its own number in a <term>sesquitertia</term><note>A ratio of 4:3.</note> proportion, the **diatessaron** <term>diatessaron</term><note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth.</note> consonance is therefore found in the third heaven, which is discovered in such a proportion, just as it is also found between the first person of the Trinity and the last. But in this place (contemplating it in passing) a great mystery <note>original: *magnum mysterium*</note> (as it seems to me) is to be drawn out; namely, that although bodies in the final and thicker proportion of the material pyramid are in the most imperfect consonance, and submerged in the abyss of imperfection and, as it were, darkness—namely, echoing in the material diatessaron—they nevertheless have a relation to unity in the *sesquitertia* proportion. Thus, there is hope for the resolution of bodies after death, through which that form and mind veiled in human bodies, which arose from unity, may return again to unity by a circular path.

From these things, therefore, it appears clearer than the sun to those looking diligently, that the diatessaron consonance of the empyrean heaven, joined with the upper diapente of the middle heaven, constitutes the supreme and spiritual **diapason** <term>diapason</term><note>The musical interval of an octave, representing a return to the same note at a higher or lower pitch.</note> consonance of the greater world <note>The macrocosm or the universe as a whole.</note>, beginning from **God** and ending in the **Sun**; and consequently it is indicated that the diatessaron of the first heaven and the upper diapente of the second heaven are the simplest and most spiritual consonances of the entire material mass of the world. Similarly, by joining the lower diapente of the middle heaven with the diatessaron of the lowest heaven, these consonances joined together produce the material diapason, beginning from the Sun and ending in the **Earth**. From this it is clear that the lower diapente and diatessaron consonances tend more toward matter than toward form; hence they are called "material," while conversely the upper ones are so called insofar as they regard form and fully informed spirits.

We see, therefore, that a triple harmony exists, composed of three symphonic consonances; the *former* of which is engaged in the uncreated essence where there is no discord—in the middle world, namely the formal world and the essence of the Trinity. The *last two* are included in created matter: namely, *one* in the material world, specifically in its subtler part, and the *other* in the denser part subject to opacity. But indeed, that uncreated symphony is united by an indissoluble bond to the created harmony—namely, to the supersubstantial, material, and substantial form—by this path: specifically, by the number three <note>original: *ternario numero*</note> of the **Trinity** (which contains the diapason within itself) being added to the number four <note>original: *quaternarium numerum*</note> of matter. (For according to the **Pythagoreans**, "two" in matter is not a number, but a confusion of unities, as has been said; wherefore they maintain that the number four is the first even number). This produces the number seven <note>original: *septenarius numerus*</note>, which brings forth the consonance of total perfection, namely the **diapason**, which is that bond by which **GOD** has both bound the music of life and light to His creatures, and liberally and assiduously pours it into the cosmos and the children of the cosmos.

# ON DIVINE HARMONY.

...depended; since it had acquired the principle of its perfection from an absolutely formal nature, namely from the unity of the divinity, which was the author of its existence. For how is it possible that perfection should exist of itself in a thing (speaking in an absolute manner) which cannot exist without the help of another? Since, therefore, duality multiplied within itself and divided into intervals produces nothing but even numbers; and since every symphony is perfected by consonances composed only of odd intervals, how is it possible that from duality (by producing only <note>In Pythagorean music theory, odd numbers were often associated with the divine and "limited" (perfect), while even numbers were associated with the material and "unlimited" (imperfect).</note> even numbers through multiplication) it could in any way propagate the consonances of melody and, consequently, harmony? On the contrary, it will instead bring forth discords and dissonances most opposed to harmony. 

From this it is clear that GOD and the most holy Trinity are the sole and unique origin of concord; whereas the Devil, conversely, is the parent of discord and antipathy, which is why he has also earned for himself the name of *Strife* <note>original: "Litigii"</note>. God, therefore, makes use of formal light for the birth of a proportional and most perfect symphony; but the Devil uses matter, darkness, and their veil for his dissensions and quarrels. From this arises the tireless conflict between concord and discord, between light and darkness, between the mind and the spirit that is prone downward, between the soul and the body. And this is why the most powerful Father of concord uses the sublime summit of the universal organ <note>The author views the entire universe as a giant musical instrument or "organ" played by God.</note> as His throne; while the father of discord, cast down to the center of the world-machine, holds his dwelling there and is forced to overshadow his envious face with the cover or veil of darkness, lest the Author of concord utterly exterminate him with His rays. 

By this kind of concord and symphony of the Trinity, the power of Strife and antipathy is broken and scattered; the hierarchies of the Angels are peacefully bounded and distinguished; the glowing fires are suspended more equally in the scales of justice; the four quarreling elements are arranged and established in their symphonic places by bonds of concord, with peace and wonderful harmony, through the proportions that are due and fitting to them; the bodies of both simple and composite things are moved and harmonize with the melody of their souls; and thus, by the power of this super-celestial symphony, all material things would strive from imperfection toward perfection and would suddenly become perfect from being imperfect, were it not that discord, with its deceptive darkness full of the world's errors, interjected itself at every hour into the actions of concord, and blinded the wills of living creatures—indeed, the very eyes of men, both physical and intellectual—with its illusions, fantasies, and tricks. By these, even good souls (inhabiting their various dwellings) are deceived by his errors and fallacies, and wrongly accept falsehoods or lies for truths, and iniquity for justice. Hence comes the fear of death and dissolution; hence all the daughters of darkness, or vices; hence the fall of Adam; hence evils are accepted as goods; hence the love of the world and its vanities; and, consequently, the hatred of God the Creator and of Truth itself. All these knots and bonds of the Devil, God—by the power of His symphony through His mercy—whenever it shall please Him, will most easily untie and dissolve,

Since we are urged to know ourselves <note>This refers to the famous Delphic maxim "Nosce te ipsum," a cornerstone of both ancient Greek philosophy and Renaissance self-examination.</note> both by the warning of sacred scripture and by the teaching of the ancient philosophers, we ought not to delay any longer in making ourselves—who have been unknown and hidden to ourselves—at last known and manifest to the best of our ability. For it is a sign of the greatest negligence to be ignorant of what that thing is, by whose profound power we contemplate celestial, indeed even divine things; by which we investigate and finally track down natural things with such subtle inquiry; or by which we desire such sublime things from our Creator himself. The mind <note>original: "animus"</note> by which we understand these things is not a foreign thing, nor is it to be sought far from us in distant places; rather, it is always with us, present, active, speaking, and born within. It has been granted to the mind to know the secrets of such great things, and yet can it not know itself? Indeed, it is permitted to a few to perceive the mind with the mind itself; that is, for the mind to see itself. However, by a certain divine providence, it is impossible for the faculty of discovery to be lacking in religious souls who piously, purely, and diligently seek themselves and their God. For souls of this kind are capable of receiving the rays of the divine mind, and, being removed from the fog of errors and darkness, Truth itself will be ready to serve them night and day. ...we consider it right to recognize our kind and to contemplate our immortal nature, the temple of GOD, and to gaze upon GOD fixed in the center of His temple with ineffable joy. And when we have beheld our internal immortal self with spiritual eyes, and have thereby known ourselves rightly, we shall pass into God Himself, the Founder of both worlds. Therefore, so that I might return myself to myself, or rather to my God, to whom I owe myself most of all, I have dedicated myself to the inquiry of my mind; and having now become a pilgrim to the world, and having consigned to oblivion the tracks of the body and the dense things of the visible world, I am carried by an aerial skiff through the spiritual waves of the invisible world. Emerging from the dark waves of the world and of opaque bodies, and climbing the ether of the heavens, I shall betake myself to the palaces of reason and intellect. There, with an enlightened mind, I shall begin to contemplate that Unity—residing in the highest peak of the heavens and of blessedness—with incomprehensible joy and gladness. 

I shall, therefore, first make myself invisible, and by leaving behind the sensible step <note>The "sensible" step refers to the level of the physical senses.</note> of the ladder of the internal man—which has been trodden many times—I shall lift my foot to the second step, which belongs to the imagination. Afterward, I shall rise with a light leap into the tracks of reason, and from its dominion, I shall elevate my internal self to the intellectual region. May the Founder of the heavens and the artisan of both body and soul be favorably and propitiously present to me; may He clarify my eyes with the benign spirit of His wisdom, illuminate my mind with the rays of His divinity, and make the middle part of my soul obedient to Him. Thus, by treading the right path directly, I may clearly discern in the revealed mirror of the Divine Majesty what, at last, I truly am.

## CAP. I.

### That GOD made man equal to the world in perfection in all things: Whence he is called the Microcosm.

That great Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to God as the original model or blueprint of the universe.</note>, whose immense power we celebrated in the first treatise of the first volume, wished to finish His universal work (namely, of creation) with no less wonder than He began it. He decorated the machine of the sixth day <note>This refers to the creation of Man on the sixth day of Genesis.</note> in its own creation with His Spirit, just as He had decorated that machine of all things—containing the empyrean spirit—on the first day of His workmanship. And as we see in the composition of a circle that the starting point is joined with the end point, so that there is no difference in the perfection of either end; so too, in the circuit of creation, the Artisan worked at the end with the same movement of divine action as He did in the beginning. For He sent His life-giving breath over the dark and muddy face of the body, so that He might illuminate that dark and immobile body, make it beautiful and mobile, and render this last work more divine. Thus, on this sixth and final day of creation, He produced something noble out of nothing, no less than He had done on the first day, when He willed His divine Spirit to be carried

...over the waters, to create the entire world out of nothing, and to illuminate its material spirit—which was overwhelmed by darkness—and to bestow upon it inexplicable virtues. By these, the world would not only become more noble but would also be regarded as a "universal animal," as the *Platonists* <note>Followers of Plato who believed the universe itself was a living, breathing entity with a soul (the Anima Mundi).</note> maintained. And this, therefore, primarily denotes to us that the same virtues and operations exist in man, according to the proportion and quantity of his body, as are contained in the universal world, both visible and invisible. 

This is also what *Trismegistus* <note>original: "Trismegistus." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with the Hermetic corpus, which emphasizes "as above, so below."</note> seems to affirm when he says that **GOD** *fixed two images according to His own exemplar: namely, the world and man.* And indeed, what can be found in the world that is not discovered proportionally in man? For if we consider the ideal or invisible world, we shall find a portion of each of its regions within the internal man. For that mind—a divine ray of uncreated light—is communicated to the internal man along with a composite portion of created light established in the spiritual heaven, through the pleasure and will of the divine Artisan. 

Similarly, just as in the visible world there are two parts, namely heaven and earth—the former raining down forms onto the earth, while the latter receives and preserves them—so also in man, that celestial ray, with its ethereal vehicle, bestows life and form upon that muddy body, which is called the "earth" of man. 

Furthermore, in both worlds, there are certain parts not subject to corruption—namely the supracelestial and celestial—while a certain portion of the visible world is corruptible, namely the elementary region. In the same way, the portions of the internal man are incorruptible, but the body and its visible parts are subject to corruption. The world is revolved and governed by the Divine Spirit, and by this same essential power, the human body is driven and revolved. Finally, He who is One created one world in His own image; and the same One also founded one living creature—namely, man—in His own image, in which He took great delight. 

Thus, man is not ineptly called "another world" and "another image of God"; for he has within himself everything contained in the greater world, to such an extent that nothing exists anywhere in it that is not truly and realistically found in man, performing the very same functions for him as it does in the greater world. For in him is the divine mind, angelic reason, celestial spirit, elementary harmony, the vegetation of the planets <note>The "vegetation of the planets" refers to the growth-giving or life-sustaining influence the planets were believed to exert on the natural world.</note>, and the senses of irrational animals. In short, he possesses the symbol of the world in all things, and maintains operation and conversation with all things. Why then should this final creature not be called by his proper name, the *Microcosm* <term>Microcosm: From the Greek 'mikros' (small) and 'kosmos' (world), meaning 'Little World.'</term>, since he is in all things so very similar to the *Macrocosm* <term>Macrocosm: From the Greek 'makros' (large) and 'kosmos' (world), meaning 'Great World' or the entire Universe.</term>? 

Moreover, since God the Artisan, being infinite, created the world round and perfectly proportional in its members; are not the measurements of all human members likewise proportioned and consonant with those of the world, matching its roundness? The center of the circular world is the earth; however, the central point of human roundness is, according to some, in the navel; but we believe it should rather be placed around the genitals. For just as the seeds of things are hidden away in the center of the world, so also the seminal power lies hidden near the testicles of man. Therefore, if a compass <note>original: "circinus." A tool used to draw circles, symbolizing divine geometry.</note> is drawn from this mark, we shall perceive the external man to be exactly round, following the example of the external world, as is clearly explained in the following illustration.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the internal or invisible Microcosm, and how it*<-
->*contains within itself all the ideal parts of the world.*<-

Moreover, we call the internal Microcosm that hidden, invisible, and immortal portion of man, fashioned from the invisible parts of the heavens of the invisible Macrocosm. By these parts, he not only carries out his natural functions but is also accustomed—by the power of those super-celestial portions—to occupy himself with divine contemplations. From this it follows that both theologians and philosophers have called the internal man a *living soul, enfolding within itself the intellectual, sensitive, and vegetative powers* <note>These represent the hierarchy of life: the ability to think (intellectual), to perceive through senses (sensitive), and to grow or reproduce (vegetative).</note>. Each of these is derived from a specific heaven of the greater world: namely, the intellect from the Empyrean heaven <note>original: "cœlo empyreo." In ancient cosmology, this was the highest heaven, composed of pure light or fire, and the home of the Divine.</note>, the vital power from the ethereal heaven, and the operations of the senses from the more "formal" or structural qualities of the elements. 

Thus, we say that the internal man is fashioned from invisible matter and a most pure and spiritual form. He possesses his material part from the substance of the ethereal heaven—just as the visible body takes its own from the physical elements—but his spiritual part resides within that ethereal body in the same way that the ethereal spirit resides within the composite elementary body. For the rays of the superior region are like life and soul to the lower heaven nearest to them. From this it is manifest that the intellectual part of man is like a soul to his own ethereal spirit; and because of its preeminence over the lower parts of the internal man, it gives man his very name and being. And this is what *Trismegistus* intended in the first book of the *Pymander* <note>original: "Pim. 1." The *Poimandres*, the most famous text of the Hermetic tradition, which discusses the creation of the world and the nature of the human soul.</note> by affirming: *that the internal man consists of life and light, which [God] himself...*

### CHAPTER III.

->*On the infinite and ineffable property of light, and how man possesses within himself a portion of every luminous species.*<-

In the first volume, Treatise 1, we proved both by reason and authority that every thing is more noble the more <term>essential light</term> <note>original: "lucis essentificæ"; light that gives a thing its very being</note> it contains. We showed that greater or lesser imperfection arises from a greater or lesser quantity of body and matter, while greater or lesser perfection comes from the exuberance or diminution of the luminous form. For we said that God is sheer and purest uncreated light without any addition of matter—that is, purely formal and simply fiery. Hence, He is called the true, proper, and first light by Saint *John in chapter 1*. We also said that the substance of the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the universe, associated with fire and light</note> itself is the fiery dwelling of the light created on the first day, which is called empyrean because fire holds dominion within it. And this heaven—neither in time (since it is created) nor in perfection (since the composition of this place consists of only one-quarter spiritual matter and three-quarters of the simplest light)—is in any way comparable to the uncreated intellectual light and splendor. Furthermore, we proved that the substance of the middle heaven drew its form from that empyrean origin; but, because it is the midpoint between the material heaven and the formal heaven, it therefore seems to participate equally in both extremes. From this, it is certain that the substance of this heaven is more imperfect and less formal than that supreme one; for it has more matter, but less form, than the other. Indeed, it consists of two parts of thicker spirit and two equal parts of light infused into it from its source on the second day of creation through the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>A dividing boundary or membrane in the cosmos</note> of the empyrean heaven. And hence it is called <term>ether</term>, as if *ath-aer* <note>original: "athäer"; Fludd uses a pseudo-etymology suggesting "fiery air"</note>, that is, fiery spirit, or composed equally of spirit and fire. Similarly, in the last place, we declared that light is weakest in the lowest heaven, while the substance of matter or the waters is most rebellious; for it consists of three-quarters matter and only one-quarter light. Thus, it stands at this extreme in the quantity of matter just as the other, namely the Empyrean, stands in the abundance of form. We also demonstrated that light is the simplest act of all things, insofar as it is the simple act of intelligence and of the uncreated intellect, first diffused from the divine mind into all things—yet in a different manner, according to whether the nature of the body is more rebellious or more obedient. We say, therefore, that uncreated light is totally and originally in God the Father Himself: for He is the Father of lights, indeed He is the first and true light itself, whose rays exist as the first acts, as <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many ancient mystical and scientific texts were attributed</note> testifies. Whence that saying: *I am the light of the world, etc.* We also affirm with *Trismegistus* and the Holy Scriptures that in the *Son* there is an illustrating and exuberant splendor, in whom is the light and life of men, as Saint...

<margin>John, chapter 1.</margin> In the Holy Spirit, there is finally a brightness surpassing all understanding, as *Dionysius* <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian philosopher who wrote extensively on celestial hierarchies</note> says. Furthermore, after the creation of light, the most simple portion of it concurred in the composition of the Angels, along with the splendor of the <term>uncreated intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus increati"</note> or the divine mind. For this reason, *Dionysius* calls them *Agallmata* <note>original: "Algamata"; from the Greek 'agalmata', meaning cult images or statues, but here interpreted as mirrors</note>, which is to say, the clearest mirrors reflecting the light of God, in which God himself is also seen. After this, a portion of this composite light descended to the formation of the celestial bodies, giving them an abundance of life and effective propagation; and this light is visible splendor. Finally, the furthest portion of light is infused into the elements themselves, granting them a fiery vigor by which the bodies live—those lower bodies which they constitute through distinct and harmonious proportions. 

In man, ultimately, there is a due portion of all these species of light, both uncreated and created. For by the <term>breath of life</term> <note>original: "spiraculum vitæ"</note> is meant not the vital soul (for this is granted even to beasts and plants, by which they live), but the divine mind and uncreated light, which is infused into him immediately by God, whereby he first puts on the image of God. Next, he is adorned with angelic and rational splendor; he holds this portion from the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most spiritual level of the heavens</note>, by which he is called "rational." Through these two gifts, he is seen to excel the other animals and all other creatures of the world. Afterwards, he receives the life-giving, vegetative, and multiplicative light from the Sun and the splendor of the ethereal creatures; by these, he is led bodily here and there, he is increased, and he possesses the growth of his species through propagation. From the light of the elements, he possesses the <term>symbolization</term> <note>The correspondence or shared qualities between the elements and the body</note> of the parts of his body and the nature and harmonious proportion of the elementary humors, according to that saying of *Trismegistus* in the *Pimander*: *Female air and water, being capable of joining, took maturity from fire and spirit from the ether, and nature joined them together to shape the form of man.* <note>original: "Fœmina aër & aqua coëundi compos ex igne maturitatem, ex æthere sumpsit spiritum conglutinavitque natura ad hominis speciem effigiandam."</note> 

Who, then, will doubt that all these species of light are in man, when *Saint John, in chapter 1*, testifies that the origin of them all—namely the divine mind and the portion of uncreated light—is in men? For from that uncreated source, all other species of created light are derived. As it says in the words of the *Royal Psalmist*: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power.* <note>Psalm 33:6; original: "Verbo Domini firmati sunt cœli & Spiritu ab ore ejus omnes virtutes eorum."</note> We conclude, therefore, that there are three species of rays, which are called "acts": namely, **supercelestial rays** or **acts of God**, from which the nobler portion of the human soul is derived; next, **world rays** or **celestial rays**, which are acts of nature, and the soul proceeding from them, from which the sensitive and vegetative life of man is derived; and in the last place are the **elementary rays**, which do not prepare life itself, but rather the dwelling-place of life, and these are the qualities properly hidden within the elements. Regarding these rays of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "Little World," a common Renaissance term for a human being as a reflection of the entire universe</note>, we shall discourse more widely below.

## CHAPTER IV.
### On the supercelestial rays, which are acts of GOD.

Regarding supernatural rays, since we have indicated that some are in God himself (as the Holy Scriptures also testify) and others are, as it were, the substance of the Empyrean heaven and its creatures, we call those existing in God **uncreated**, but these of the Empyrean heaven **created**. We call the divine ray, along with *Scotus* <note>John Duns Scotus, a major medieval Franciscan theologian and philosopher</note>, the **uncreated intellect**; but that other ray, proceeding immediately from the divine, we call the **created intellect**. Hence *Scotus* affirms that "intelligible objects" are produced into "intelligible being" through the act of the divine intellect, and that all truths concerning them necessarily shine back within them; so that the created intellect, understanding objects of this kind and, by their power, also understanding the necessary truths about them, sees within them truths of this sort. And so, that created intellect, seeing infallible truths in such objects, appropriately...

...it can be said that [the soul] sees them in the eternal light, or by eternal rules. This also seems to be confirmed by the *Theological Resolutions, treatise 2, part 2, question 2*, where it asserts that *it can be fittingly said that the created intellect sees these types of infallible truths in the light of the <term>uncreated intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus increati"; refers to the divine mind of God rather than the human capacity for reason</note> because, namely, by the power of that uncreated intellect, objects are produced in their <term>intelligible being</term> <note>The state of existing as an idea or concept that can be understood</note>, and having been so produced, they move the created intellect itself, not by their own power, but by the power of the divine intellect.* From these points it is established that there is a light of both the created and the uncreated intellect; and the created intellect can understand nothing unless it sees it, as it were, in the light and splendor of the divine intellect, which they call the Mind. Consequently, it is certain that the divine Mind concurs with the created intellect in the constitution of the human soul, so that through the former, the latter is accustomed to see the aforementioned infallible truths, as we shall declare below. However, since this divine portion could not come to man—on account of the immense unworthiness of his body—without the divine grace of the Creator, God therefore granted him that same gift on the very day of his creation which He had previously communicated to the <term>Empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, fiery heaven in ancient cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God</note> and consequently to the entire world on the first day of His workmanship. For just as on the first day of creation His Spirit was borne over the face of the Empyrean heaven, illuminating it spiritually, so also on the last day of creation the Spirit of that same Archetype was borne over the face of man; for *He breathed into the face of man the <term>breath of life</term> <note>original: "spiraculum vitæ"</note>, which, because it was uncreated, was immortal life and light,* as testified by John 1 and <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> in his *Pimander*, book 1. Such, therefore, are these supercelestial rays, which are truly the proper acts of God; the former of these proceeded immediately from God and are, as it were, rays emitted by God Himself, and just like His Spirit, they are a divine act and eternal splendor—indeed, they are God Himself, present everywhere according to His divine will. Thus, supported by the *Theological Resolution*, it is not ineptly said that *in every creature there is a <term>trace of the Trinity</term>* <note>original: "vestigium Trinitatis"</note>, in no other way, for example, than we say the sun is in this house or that part of the earth when its rays strike those places. But the secondary supercelestial rays are those which were created immediately by God on the first day to bring the matter of darkness from potentiality into act and to forge the actual and visible world; by their actions, the darkness was driven down to the center of the world-globe, and all power was given to the heavens and all parts and creatures of the heaven. Whence these can also be truly called the secondary acts of God, insofar as they flow immediately from the Spirit of the Lord. Yet truly, these are not simple like those uncreated rays (since they are entirely formal and fiery), but they are joined with a little bit of the spirit of <term>hyle</term> <note>Ancient Greek term for "prime matter" or the raw substance of the universe</note>—the thinnest matter—as has been said; in which composition that passive spirit exists along with the essential active light and the true emitted ray of God. Moreover, the whole substance of that heaven is called *created* because something was produced into act from nothing—that is, from a non-pre-existing matter; specifically, the formless and potential spirit of darkness (or most subtle water) was <term>informed</term> <note>In philosophy, "to inform" means to give shape, essence, or character to raw matter</note> by the presence of divine light. Whence also this heaven is called "intellectual" and "rational," and this simple composition is called "light." In this way, "created light" is understood as the mixing of divine light with the spirit which it informed—that is, the composition of spirit with light. In this composition, because the proportion of light is triple to that of the matter, light gave it its name and its being, and in this way light was created on the first day. Since, therefore, this formal light acts upon its passive subject, and the passive spirit suffers while receiving the form, and [receives] those actions just as matter receives form—is it not likely from this that the light of this substance (composed simply of two things) is that which the Philosophers called the **Agent Intellect** <note>original: "intellectum agentem"; the active part of the mind that transforms sensory data into abstract thoughts</note>? For it makes all things that are potentially intelligible into things that are actually intelligible, in the same way that it reduced that matter—which existed only in potentiality due to its formless disposition—into a visible act. Whence also *Franciscus de Maronis* called this intellect the *light and reason of knowing*, and according to *Proclus* in...

<margin>Treatise on the Soul</margin> He provides us with understanding, namely the light of intelligence; but the Spirit, which is the other part of the composition, if I am not mistaken, is that intellect which the Philosophers called "passive" <term>passive intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus patientem"; the capacity of the mind to receive and store sensory information and thoughts, acting like a blank slate or mirror</note>, whose role is to receive the understanding of all things within itself. Thus, it provides the immediate subject for the appearance, which—though only potentially visible before the action of light—now actually appears and is seen in a mirror. And this is what **Trismegistus** seems to assert in **Pimander, Book 1**, saying that *the mind is in reason, namely understanding the substance of the intellectual heaven through reason; since it is in reason, it is both action and passion.* And **Aristotle** in **On the Soul, Book 3**: *In the intellectual soul, because of the passive intellect, an active intellect must be placed; that is, an active form must be imposed upon its passive matter.* From this, therefore, it follows that some, according to **Basil** in **Hexameron, Books 1 and 2**, have rightly called this heaven "intellectual," and others have also called it "rational." And **Augustine** in **On Genesis, Book 1**, understands "angelic nature" through the concept of primary light. However, according to **Boethius** in **On the Trinity, Book 3**, angelic nature differs from the pure, luminous form, which is uncreated; this is because it is subject to accidents <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, these are non-essential qualities of a thing (like specific thoughts or feelings) that can change without changing the thing's basic nature</note>, namely acts of understanding and willing, which is why he says there is "matter" within them. But we have explained this clearly in **Treatise 1, Volume 1, Book: On the Creatures of the Empyrean Heaven**. These, however, are properly called "acts of God," since they proceed immediately from Him; by their brightness, man is inwardly illuminated and is said to possess the image of God Himself, as we shall explain more extensively below. This is true even though we also maintain that all lower rays are derived from God in a secondary or tertiary way, which **Trismegistus** also seems to assert in **Pimander, Book 3**: *GOD is divine nature, the beginning of the universe; GOD is mind, nature, act, necessity, end, and renewal;* and consequently, he seems to assert that all worldly rays or acts are divine and proceed from God Himself.

### CHAPTER V.
#### *Why is man called the image of God? And concerning the nobility which he receives from the supernatural rays—both uncreated and created—that are within him.*

When that uncreated Craftsman breathed the breath of life into the muddy body of man, that body, though thick and opaque, received the divine mind. Through its inexplicable and most luminous beauty, that mind gave the most polished splendor of a well-tended mirror to the muddy and rough bulk of man; so that first, the form and image of the Archetype <term>Archetype</term> <note>The original divine model or "blueprint" in the mind of God from which the world was created</note> could be seen spiritually within it. Thus, **Trismegistus** says that man, made in the image of God, represents the Trinity in a certain passage; likewise, the Holy Scriptures in many places say that man was made in the likeness of God himself. **Trismegistus**, in **Pimander, Book 1**, also called man’s mind the "proper form of God." And elsewhere, he calls the mind of human reason "God," which is "intellect, life, and brightness." And according to **Saint John, Chapter 1**: *In the Word of God is the life of men, which is the light shining in the darkness*—that is, in the dark human body—and this is the true light or divine form. In the same way, **Trismegistus** in **Pimander, Book 1**, says that the internal man consists of *life and light*; and he calls *life and light* "God and mind," and in that same place speaks these words: *The Father of all, being intellect, life, and brightness, brought forth a man similar to himself, and rejoiced in him as in his own son.* In the same way, **Paul** called man, and **Xystus the Pythagorean** called his soul, the "temple of God." That polished matter, receiving these rays of uncreated light, is the spiritual and intellectual substance of the first heaven, created in the image of the Word (the first exemplar and cause of causes), which according to the **Platonists**, is derived immediately from God. Therefore, through a more perfect soul—an intellect proceeding immediately from the supreme Architect <term>Opifex</term> <note>original: "Opifice"; refers to God as the master craftsman or demiurge of the universe</note>—he understands this world-soul through another less perfect one, which he willed to proceed from the lower gods, namely the ethereal ones. For he asserts that some souls are derived from the Solar sphere, others from the Mercurial sphere, and several from the Lunar sphere; through these, he seems to denote a diverse nature of rays following the different dispositions of places and spheres. And these lower Gods, called the "seven governors" by **Trismegistus**, **Proclus** named "the younger ones," as if to say that although they proceed from the supreme God, insofar as they are younger and lower, they create imperfect and irrational souls. Thus, he speaks in these words:

> *The rational soul is more noble than the irrational soul, because the first Architect of the world, namely the super-celestial God, procreated the former; while the younger Gods—that is, the ethereal ones—produced the latter.*

This soul, though vital in itself, is irrational, yet it becomes rational through the acquisition of a super-celestial portion. And then **Augustine**, in his book *On the Soul and Spirit*, defines it *as being a certain substance participating in reason.* Hence this middle soul, insofar as it looks toward higher things, possesses the power of understanding; and insofar as it looks toward lower things, it possesses the power of sensing. Similarly, because this soul is composed of light and spirit, and because it contains within itself the divine mind along with a portion of the substance of the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most "fiery" or "light-filled" heaven in ancient cosmology</note>, it is rightly defined by **Aristotle** in his book *On the Spirit* as *being an intellectual and rational spirit always in motion, etc.*

But the reason why this soul, consequently, cannot provide reason to lower things by itself is, if I am not mistaken, this: First, because it is certain that the very substance of the middle heaven consists of an equal portion of the primary created light and an equal quantity of the spirit of the middle heaven; this spirit is liberated and purified from its own lack <note>original: "privatione"; a philosophical term for the absence of a quality that should naturally be present</note> by the presence of this light. Now, we have said that the primary light is fashioned from three parts of purely formal light and one part of spirit; it is therefore called "intellectual" in respect to its divine and most simple form, but "rational" insofar as the spiritual substance (which is its material act) resists it in a way by undergoing its influence. Consequently, it renders this matter "rational," which is a lower level of rationality than pure intellect. 

For in *Theological Resolutions* it is held that, *insofar as the soul looks toward higher things, it is called "intellect"; insofar as it looks toward lower things, it is called "reason."* Now, it is beyond doubt that a thing is more "intellectual" the more it approaches the true light, splendor, and understanding; and it is more "rational" the closer it is to the true seat of the intellect. For the created intellect proceeds immediately from the uncreated Intellect, just as worldly rays proceed from the Sun. 

But because a thing participates less in the action of its rays the further it is removed from the source of light—as we see that an animal body receives less benefit from fire or feels less of its heat the further it stands from it—therefore, the middle region of the world is less suited for intellect and reason. This is both because it is a place very remote from the intellectual source, and also because its spirit is somewhat coarser. Although by its creation it is sufficiently effective and fit for life, it is less apt for intellect and reason due to the thickness of its substance and its great resistance against the most simple acts of the uncreated light; for the thicker the matter, the more disobedient it is to formal action. 

Accordingly, it is certain that the rational faculty operates very weakly there, and as a consequence, that middle soul was made irrational in its own creation. However, through that familiarity which the spirit of the empyrean heaven has with that of the ether, and by the divine will of God, intellect and reason descended through the "diaphragm" <note>A metaphorical barrier or dividing layer between the highest heaven and the lower heavens</note> of the empyrean heaven on the sixth day for the creation of man, into the soul of this heaven. Thus, when this vital middle soul was infused into him, it simultaneously brought him both intellect and reason along with life. And because the species of this middle heaven was founded as irrational in its creation, it cannot possess reason by its own nature, no more than vegetables created before the rising of the Sun can possess sensation in the manner of animals; although, without doubt, celestial creatures are no less...

...are refreshed, and rejoice in the presence of this intellectual splendor, just as plants do at the approach and sight of the Sun. But to prove the irrationality of this "heaven of the soul" <note>original: "coeli animae"; referring to the vital or world-soul as a celestial sphere</note> in a more familiar way, we see in the light of the intellect guiding the sense of sight that the further an object is from it, the weaker are the visible rays of that same type directed toward it. Indeed, it is such that truth itself sometimes does not shine back upon them. This is exactly how the matter stands in our proposal regarding this soul; for its medium is different from that of the intellect, and it is distant from the intellectual seat by the length of the world's semi-diameter. Hence, because of the diversity of the medium, the rays of the intellectual heaven are, as it were, refracted in the middle heaven, and they do not operate according to reason. Furthermore, if this soul were rational in itself, why is it not also perceived to impart reason at the same time to all things to which it is accustomed to give life? For the substance of this heaven exists in metals as much as in plants and animals of every species; for the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the fifth element or "quintessence," thought to be the pure material of the heavens</note>, which is the sensible nature of all things, exists only as such, and is not intellectual, as witnessed by **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a polymath and philosopher famous for his works on alchemy and logic</note> in his *Book on the Fifth Essence*. We conclude, therefore, that the <term>empyrean heaven</term> <note>original: "coelum empyreum"; the highest, fiery heaven in medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God</note> has its soul from the uncreated rays of God, and its substance is entirely lucid; yet it is not the "simplest light," as that is proper only to the Trinity, since it is uncreated. However, the spiritual appetite of this heaven's substance is so fulfilled that it is entirely converted into a lucid and formal nature. Whence that composition is called "empyrean," that is, "fiery," by whose formal substance the dark spirit of the middle region is given form. And thus the entire substance of the celestial region is made from a portion of this empyrean substance, which is its form, and from its own spirit, which is its matter; this composition is called **ether**, that is, **igneous air**. And just as the entire substance of the empyrean heaven is the form or "essentializing soul" of the ethereal heaven, so again the whole substance of the latter—which they call the fifth essence—is the soul and nature of all creatures of the lower world, except for man, who draws his greater perfection from a higher region. In this way, the previously mentioned words of **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential Christian theologian and Neoplatonist</note> in his *Book on Divine Names* are verified: *Those things which are in lower realms exist more perfectly in the higher ones*; that is, the higher one ascends, the greater the perfection found. For as the same author says in his *Book on the Angelic Hierarchy*: *A higher Angel, by common law, illuminates a lower one*; and so it is with the regions of the world. For the interior or "ideal" world is the exemplar of God himself, while the external and visible world is the image of that invisible one.

## CHAPTER VII.
### On elementary rays and the sensitive soul.

**Timaeus** <note>The speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name</note> says that the essence of our soul was not constituted from the "first" types of all things, as the superior souls were, but was composed from the "second or third" types. By the "first" types, he denotes the natures and substances of the empyrean heaven; by the "second," those of the ethereal heaven (which we discussed above); and by the "third," those of the lowest and elementary heaven, which we shall discuss here. The **Pythagoreans**, as we explained above, wishing the soul to be composed from the simple, double, triple, and quadruple proportions, understood by the "quadruple proportion" the <term>sensitive power</term> of the soul. This is what **Plotinus** and the other Platonists called the **idol** <note>original: "idolum"; here meaning a phantom, image, or reflection rather than a false god</note>, because it is, as it were, an image and "idol" of that quality which is sensed. And **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings</note> says in *Pimander 6*: *Whatever things move the senses are idols and certain vain wonders; for it is not possible to find "The Good" in the world or its parts; for just as the sharpest eye does not discern God, so it does not recognize the beautiful and the good.* Saint **Paul** calls this the "animal man," and we call it the "carnal spirit"; for these bodies only...

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK III. ###

...only perceives, since incorporeal things are not at all presented to the senses. From these things it is clear that the **sensitive soul** <note>original: "animam sensitivam"; the part of the soul responsible for sensory perception and basic movement, shared by humans and animals</note> participates in the body, since without the body's organs it can accomplish or complete nothing; indeed, unless it exists within some animated body, this function or power of the soul is nothing. It is established, therefore, that it consists rather of the elements and their virtues and mixtures than being derived from the virtues of the higher heavens. 

Hence *Porphyry* <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who sought to reconcile Aristotle and Plato</note>, in his *Book on Occasions*, seems to distinguish it from the higher powers of the soul with these words: *“The soul is indeed the middle between the indivisible essence, which is the intellect, and the essence divisible into true bodies; for qualities and material forms are divisible according to bodies.”* 

Where by "soul" he understands that life-giving soul of the ethereal heaven; by "indivisible essence," the intellectual and rational substance of the Empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most spiritual part of the heavens</note>; and by "essence divisible into bodies," the sensitive power. He denotes that this sensitive power is concerned with elementary qualities and material forms, which are divisible according to bodies, and that it arises and is derived from their actions. 

Hence, among the *Philosophers*, it is defined thus: *“The sensitive soul of this kind is the act of a natural organic substantial body, by which it lives, feels, desires, breathes, and moves from place to place, whose apprehensive power captures and perceives the sensory forms of visible things, both present and absent.”* For the sense is as suited to receive the abstracted impressions of natural things as wax receives the image or mark of a seal from a ring, abstracted without the gold or silver of the ring sticking to it. 

And this power is prepared both in the **exterior sense**, to which five forms are subjected—namely **sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell**—and in the **interior sense**, of which there are three distinctions: namely **common sense, phantasy <note>imagination</note>, and memory**. 

By its **motive power**, the animated body is moved, either externally by changing location, or internally by spirit and pulse. If this power is commanding, it is the ***concupiscible virtue*** <note>original: "virtus concupiscibilis"; the faculty of desire and attraction</note>, containing within itself hope and joy, or the ***irascible force*** <note>original: "vis irascibilis"; the faculty of anger and defense</note>, under which are included fury, rage, madness, fear, sadness, pain, and other things of this kind. 

Therefore, this sensitive faculty is the daughter of the earth and of darkness itself, the mother of all evils, the instigator of the flesh toward all wicked things, constantly exciting the appetite for sinning within it and repeatedly offering objects of sin to man. For by the sense of the apprehensive power, the present "species" <note>sensory appearances or forms</note> inciting one toward evil are perceived. 

Whence ***Eva*** <note>Eve</note> was first enticed to sin by **hearing** the persuasions of the serpent; then by **seeing** that the fruit was beautiful and delightful to the eyes and sight, she **touched** that fruit, and at the last she **tasted** and **ate** it. Thus it was that for the completion of this sin, all those five sensory forms concurred, especially since **smell** is also a familiar companion to taste. 

But the forms of the motive power also concurred in this action; for she immediately coveted and desired the fruit, and to fulfill that appetite, she went to the tree and took of the fruit; afterward, struck by fear and sadness, she fled from the face of God. From these things it appears that there were three incitements for *Eve* to commit that sin of disobedience against her Creator: namely, ***the Devil, the flesh, and the world itself***. 

The Devil tempted the flesh with some object. The flesh, through the operation of the apprehensive sense, grasped and saw the worldly object, and having been conquered by diabolical persuasions, it desired that sensible form. By its motive power, the flesh led her to fulfill her appetite, and she took wondrous delight in that worldly subject she had seen—which finally is subjected to her as a reward, or rather a punishment, for her disobedience toward her Creator. 

Hence, therefore, is the origin of all the evils of the entire human race, which, swelling immediately from its birth, straightway defiled the universal human condition. For the woman herself also gave of the fruit to the man, who ate, and through that sin he was reduced from an immortal state to mortality with all his posterity; so that ***Trismegistus*** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed</note> now rightly described him as an ***earthly God, but a mortal one; for he lost his privilege of immortality through his disobedience; and***

For the Lord God said in *Genesis 2: Of the tree of knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die.* Hence, therefore, Adam was expelled from Paradise, lest he taste of the tree of life and live forever; and so even on account of his sin, all his posterity and succession is rendered mortal: for God says in *Genesis 6: My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; for flesh has corrupted its life upon the earth, wherefore I will destroy all flesh in which is the spirit of life under heaven.* 

This, I say, the beginning of the sensitive or carnal soul's malice, was an evident omen of future calamities. For it steadily drew the "natural man" <note>original: "hominem animalem"; refers to man living by basic instincts rather than spiritual reason</note>, to use St. Paul’s words, toward the worst of everything; and God saw the malice of man so coalescing on the earth, and every thought of his heart so intent on evil at all times, that it even repented Him that He had made him. (*Genesis 9* <note>likely referring to the narrative in Genesis 6</note>). For it happened that after the fall of Adam, the senses and thoughts of the human heart were prone to evil from his youth. (*Genesis 8*). From this comes the love of bodily beauty and the lustful gaze upon women, and the contempt for super-celestial beauty and sincere, truly fiery love. Whence *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and alchemical texts are attributed</note> in the first book of the *Pymander* claims that *the love of the body is the cause of death.* And elsewhere: *He who embraces the body through the error of love shall wander in darkness, perceiving the evils of death through his senses; for unless one hates his own body, he cannot love himself.* 

But what finally must be said regarding that unspeakable tribulation which this carnal faculty introduced to the human race, by which good is discerned from evil? Man in his innocence did not know this distinction, and by the benefit of that same ignorance he was free from hardships; he was not passive, in no way afflicted by cares and anxieties, immune from the disturbances of the soul, of a most enduring spirit and inexperienced in evil, inasmuch as he was occupied only with the goodness of the Creator, the only good. Oh, the highest good of man! Oh, his inexplicable happiness! But now, truly, by his error arising from disobedience, he is able to distinguish good from evil, light from darkness, a tranquil soul from one that is tumultuous and oppressed by vexations and passions. Now the fire of conscience is perceived to burn, the madness of hell <note>original: "gehennæ"</note> is feared, diabolical invasions are constantly noticed, and human damnation is dreaded; besides which, he is also afflicted by infinite worldly tortures, even the safest of all men, and those fortified with the strongest security. The arrival of death is mournful, the misfortunes of friends are deplorable, and our own are to be constantly dreaded; no one in this world is secure, everyone is suspicious of his neighbor, no one is ever fortunate enough or content with his status, because he is a knower of good and evil. Oh, therefore, the supreme misfortune of the human race! Oh, its inexplicable unhappiness, drawing the origin of its miseries from the treacherous disposition of the sensitive power and the rebellious and lewd intemperance of human flesh. 

We conclude, therefore, that this lower portion of the soul, or its sensitive function, is like a more essential elementary form or quality, wonderfully delighting in the changes and disturbances of the body; concerning which *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) known for his work on theurgy and the soul</note> in *On the Mysteries* seems to argue in these words: *Whatever passions are in the animal are not in the soul of any kind, but in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul, through which it may both suffer and be disturbed.* Where he seems to understand by this "quality under the soul" the lower portion of the soul, which it received from the elementary form; which indeed we have said in the chapter on the element of fire is the occasion of every change. Occasionally, once peace is made, there is a friendly communication between this soul and its dark flesh; because of this, it occupies itself with empty and vicious pleasures, and is ready to observe all the commands of the devil alongside the flesh. At such times, deprived of the royal light of the mind due to its dark association with the flesh, it produces the worst of all things. Of this, **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a syncretism of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with the Hermetic writings</note> also speaks when he says: *the plague of ignorance subverts the entire earth, corrupts the soul enclosed in the bonds of the body, and does not allow it to choose the path of salvation; rather, it causes the soul to be submerged in the pit of corruption and death, and does not permit it to return to the fountain of life.* <note>original: "ignorantia pestis omnem terram subvertat, animam corporis vinculis inclusam corrumpat..."</note> We shall declare more broadly below how its disposition is utterly opposed to the mind because of the malice of the flesh and the devil.

---

### C H A P T E R VIII. ###

->*By what vehicles, or through which means the lights of each heaven, which constitute the human soul, are joined to the body.*<-

Among the Philosophers who noticed that divine powers are diffused into all things, **Democritus** and **Orpheus the Pythagoreans** called those powers "Gods," saying that all things were full of them. **Zoroaster**, however, called them "divine lures" <term>illices; forces that draw the soul toward the divine</term>. **Synesius** called them "symbolic charms." **Trismegistus** and others called them "lives"; and all generally called them "souls" and "essences," attributing both a name and existence to things. The Platonists, diligently investigating the descent of these souls into bodies and the manner of their conjunction (for they perceived that the soul is primarily and spontaneously mobile, while the body is by itself ineffective at motion, and consequently these two extremes are entirely opposite in nature and therefore not easily joined), noticed that this union happens through some spiritual medium. They saw that through this intervening medium, those two extremes and "strangers" might have some commerce between them, and be coupled to each other by its bonds. This medium they further called the **ethereal vehicle of life** or the **chariot of the soul**. 

They affirmed that this is that ethereal spirit which has familiarity with both extremes; not unlike how the substance of air shares qualities with its opposites, fire and water. Whence also that ethereal spirit, involving the soul in the middle region of the world—situated between the spiritual and corporal extreme—is defined as being neither soul nor body, but as if it were already soul (insofar as it touches the superior region) and as if it were not soul, but already body (insofar as it is joined to the elementary region). This spirit, I say, the Platonists noticed is that **vehicle** in which and through which those wonderful gifts of forms are conferred upon lower things, and all hidden power in herbs, stones, minerals, and animals is propagated by the power of the sun, moon, planets, and fixed stars. 

But **Trismegistus**, looking somewhat more deeply into human nature than those Platonists, discovered that *the ethereal spirit is the vehicle of the divine mind.* And although **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist who wrote on the "garments" or "vehicles" of the soul</note> in his book *On the Soul* makes mention of the garments of the human soul in these words: *The soul descending is variously clothed and finally purified*, he speaks of them more confusedly. For in the first book of the **Pimander** <note>The *Poimandres*, the first and most famous book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note>, it is held that *the garment of the mind is the soul, and the garment of the soul is the spirit itself.* <note>original: "mentis indumentum esse animam, animæ vero indumentum ipsum spiritum"</note> Here, the Author understands "soul" to mean the rational substance of the empyrean heaven, and "spirit" to mean the informed substance of the ether. From this, in the 10th sermon of the *Pimander*, he seems to explain that same passage of the first sermon with these words:

...through which he <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage associated with the Hermetic texts</note> most effectively declares the true movement of the mind from its uncreated starting point to its created destination: *The soul of man is carried in this manner; the Mind in reason, reason in the soul, the soul in the spirit, and the spirit in the body.* <note>original: "Anima hominis in hunc vehitur modum; Mens in ratione..."</note> With these words, he clearly suggests that the divine and uncreated mind—a ray of uncreated light—puts on the substance of the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven in ancient cosmology, believed to be composed of pure fire or light</note> as a garment. By this vehicle, it descends further down into the formal substance of the middle heaven; for the form of the middle heaven is of the true nature of the Empyrean substance, and like naturally rejoices in its like. Furthermore, that ethereal form, embracing a twofold supercelestial nature, is wrapped in the coverings of the ethereal spirit, in which, as in its own proper vehicle, it is transported into the muddy body. The fountain of the Mind, therefore, is that uncreated **Monad** <note>The 'One' or the ultimate source of all being</note> which Trismegistus calls *the proper form of God, similar to Himself*, and which Holy Scripture calls the *God-formed breath*. And Trismegistus proves in Discourse 10 of the *Pimander* that this Mind cannot exist in an earthy mass, nor can earthy dregs receive so divine a mind or sustain such a great divinity. *Hence it is,* (he says) *that the mind assumes the soul as if it were a cloak, because the soul, being divine, uses the spirit as its vehicle.* Certainly, this divine mind cannot be carried into the middle region without its Empyrean vehicle, any more than the nature of the middle soul can be carried into the lowest region without the mediation of the middle spirit. For the same relationship exists between the heaven of the Trinity and the Empyrean as exists between the Empyrean and the middle heaven; and the same between that middle and the lowest, as between the Empyrean and the middle. For the soul of any higher heaven is more noble than that of the heaven immediately below it, according to that saying of **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul's descent</note> concerning the soul: *The rational soul is more noble than the irrational, because the first Creator of the world produced the former, while the junior gods* <note>In Neoplatonism, "junior gods" are lesser celestial beings who fashion the material world</note> *or ethereal beings produced the latter.* That is, the fiery spirit of the intellectual heaven, which they also call "rational," proceeding immediately from God the first Creator of the world, is more noble than the spirit of the ethereal heaven, to which is given only the power of infusing life and growth into lower things, but by no means the power of infusing complete reason. And hence it is that Proclus himself asserts in the same place that *some souls descend from the Solar sphere, others from the Mercurial, and some from the Lunar.* From these things it clearly appears that the first garment of the mind is far more noble than that ethereal one, since it serves as a form to that middle spirit which receives it during its descent. The Mind, therefore, is first enclosed in the rational spirit; then the rational spirit, with its most divine contents, is received by the spirit that is vital in itself. This then, from being an irrational spirit, becomes rational and intellectual through the presence of the Mind and its vehicle, according to that saying of **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher known for his work on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine</note> in his book *On the Mysteries*: *The soul is illuminated by the beneficent divine will.* And **Aristotle** now rightly defined it in his book *On the Spirit*: *it is an intellectual, rational spirit, always in motion*—namely, insofar as those supercelestial gifts are joined with its nature. Finally, this ethereal spirit, exalted by both supercelestial and worldly rays, because of its constant communication and familiarity with lower things, is infused into bodies which were appropriately prepared and proportioned by God at creation to receive it. Running through the entire human body, it first introduces into them a **sensitive** power from its own nature—which it also grants to other animals, namely the irrational ones, just as it does to humans—and then afterwards it also grants the **rational** and **intellectual** power, which it confers on man alone by the virtue of supercelestial lights. And in this way

->that internal man is forged, folding together the intellectual,<-
->vegetative, and sensitive faculties all at once.<-

TREATISE I. SECTION I, BOOK III.

# CHAPTER IX.

## *On the opinion of Theologians regarding the creation of the soul.*

In the preceding chapter, we clearly explained what the more divine philosophers established regarding the creation of the human soul and its descent into the muddy <note>original: *lutuosum* — literally "miry" or "clay-like," referring to the physical body as terrestrial dregs</note> body. Here, however, we will briefly deal with the differing opinions of the theologians themselves. The greater chorus of theologians concludes that the soul is infused into the body and, in the act of being infused, is created, citing for this that passage from *Genesis 2: He breathed into him the breath of life*, <note>original: "Inspiravit in eum spiraculum vitæ"</note> that is, He created the soul in the body. But Origen, along with several Greek theologians following the opinion of the *Platonists* in this matter, openly contradicts this assertion; they all move toward the opinion that *all souls were created equally with the Angels in the beginning*. Certain others also wish for this, as is found in the *Clangor Buccinae*, <note>A title meaning "The Clang of the Trumpet," a 15th-century alchemical/mystical text</note> where it is expressly written in these words: *The souls which today, and every day hereafter, are newly infused into the mother's womb, are not created anew, but were created from fire alone in the primordial beginning of the universe, and are nurtured in the mind and power of the Creator until the predetermined time when they must be infused into the body; and they do not depart from the body unless the spirit has first departed and vanished, upon whose departure the soul also vanishes.* And Augustine also seems to wish to agree with these, as is held in Book 7 of his commentary *On Genesis*, unless he should find the Holy Scriptures stating otherwise; hence he speaks thus doubtfully about the soul of Adam: *If no Scripture is found which contradicts it, it seems it should be said that the soul of Adam was created from the beginning with the Angels, and afterwards came voluntarily to the body to administer it.*

But this doubt of Augustine’s will, in my judgment, be most easily removed if we consider that the eternal Spirit of God, borne upon fiery wings over the waters, assiduously infuses all powers into the parts of any Macrocosm <term>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or the universe as a whole, which Fludd believes mirrors the human "Microcosm"</term>, according to that never-sufficiently repeated sentiment of the Royal Psalmist: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of His mouth.* <note>Psalm 33:6</note> Since these things are so, why should not that same spirit, which the Architect <note>original: *Opifex* — referring to God as the Divine Builder or Craftsman</note> once breathed into the face of the Microcosm <term>Microcosm: "Little World," a term for Man, seen as a miniature version of the universe</term>, suffice for all propagation of men, since it seems to be reserved in the mind and power of the Creator until the predetermined time when it must be infused into the body? It is so, clearly, that—preserving that passage in *Genesis*—that intellectual soul, which, insofar as it is the image of God itself, can be called infinite for the informing <note>In scholastic philosophy, "informing" means giving life and specific form to matter</note> of men, extends itself infinitely. This is no different from that spirit which GOD gave to the Macrocosm at the beginning of creation, by whose presence the Macrocosm itself is daily adorned with infinite gifts without a repeated creation of that spirit.

Is it not also said according to Saint John, chapter 1: *that in the Word of the Lord is the life of man, and that life is the light, etc.*? And *Trismegistus* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Hermetic texts are attributed</note>, by calling light and life God Himself, says that man is created from them, by which he proves that God Himself is the life of man, through which he tastes supercelestial things. He suggests that the mind of man—as it were, the divine uncreated essence of God Himself or the true image of God—is always reserved with God Himself for the creatures whom He intended to form in His image. Furthermore, it does not seem likely that the soul is created anew—that is, from nothing or from non-pre-existing matter—since the matter of its composition is spirit, and its form is light, as the theologians themselves testify. But the sacred Scriptures testify that the general spirit and likewise that universal light, from which every form and matter of things is derived, were created in the beginning only by divine power from non-pre-existing matter. To these things is added that the Father, the Architect of all, said before the existence of the world: and immediately by His Word the heavens were confirmed and the Spirit proceeding from His mouth [confirmed] the power of the heavens...

...powers produced. Who indeed does not see that light is the primary virtue and life of the heavens and of all creatures, and that it proceeds immediately from the divine Spirit moving over the waters? Since that general light was the first of all created things, and is the brilliance or image of that most holy Spirit, it is the universal gift from which all other specific gifts proceed. Among these is the soul of every individual thing, which Heraclitus called a "spark of essence" <note>original: *scintillam essentiae*</note> and, as it were, the "only single ray of the shining fountain." And therefore, what need will there be for any new creation of light, or for a new spirit, when the light and spirit of every heaven—indeed, the very breath of God <note>original: *spiraculum*</note> from which all life and light of men proceeds—is spiritually and invisibly present everywhere? It exists to provide a continuous succession to all things, according to the order and nature implanted in them by God during the first creation.

Consequently, since God—among all His creatures—breathed as if twice into man alone (namely, a portion of the universal spirit and that particular spirit of life), this divine gift is uniquely suited to man. Among all other things, the human body alone was ordered and disposed by God at its creation to receive the spirit of life, or that divine image. It is therefore a traditional teaching <note>original: *tralatitium*</note> that this spirit, sent forth on the last day of creation, is sufficient on its own to continue the succession of human forms without any further "new" creation, just as that first spirit is sufficient for the constant propagation of all other things.

We conclude, therefore, that the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual level of the universe, traditionally associated with fire and the dwelling place of God</note>, although made from no pre-existing matter, was nevertheless made from a pre-existing and previously created form. This form, in relation to the middle and lowest heavens, is entirely formal <note>Meaning it consists of the "blueprint" or soul-essence rather than physical substance</note>. But in relation to itself, it is composed of spiritual matter and a greater portion of "form," and is thus forged from uncreated light and non-pre-existing matter. We have already explained this uncreated light to be like a "ray of God" <note>original: *radium Dei*</note> present in all created things; thus, God Himself is said to be present everywhere, and this light is properly called "light" because it is totally and simply formal.

Just as we have asserted that the creation of the Empyrean heaven consists of uncreated matter and a portion of God’s ray, so we also establish that man is formed both from "informed" matter and from that same uncreated ray of God. This ray gives man his form and his very being <note>original: *esse*</note> while floating in the super-celestial spirit. For these divine rays, although they are within the human body, are nevertheless also said to be in God Himself. In this respect, God is said to be present everywhere, much like a solar ray is said to be "in" the sun, and in this way the Sun is everywhere. But this ray existing in man descended immediately from God into this dark mass on the sixth day; this is no different from how the light of God entered the dark part of the superior heaven on the first day to illuminate the world.

Man is therefore worthier than the bodies of the ethereal heaven <note>The planets and stars</note>, because the stars are composed secondarily from created rays, while man is formed from uncreated rays. Furthermore, these celestial bodies are more excellent than lower, earthly things, because their light proceeds secondarily from that created substance (the matter of the ethereal heaven), since the substance of any superior heaven acts as the "soul" for the heaven immediately below it.

Accordingly:
* The substance of the uncreated forms (or the "Heaven of the Trinity"), which is pure form in itself, exists as the spirit or soul of the **Empyrean heaven**.
* The composition of the Empyrean heaven is the "form" of the **ethereal spirit**.
* Finally, the substance of the ethereal heaven is the "form" of the creatures and parts of the **lower [elemental] heaven**.

And truly, it was necessary for the rays of uncreated light to be joined with the substance of the Empyrean spirit. Without that most pure and subtle medium, that exalted form could not descend to the middle region; similarly, this "middle soul" could not have been carried to the lowest region without the medium of the ethereal heaven’s spirit, which acts as its vehicle.

Therefore, this created soul is proper to the Empyrean heaven, which we called the light created on the first day; it is the fount and origin of souls, which, since it was created on the first day, thereafter...
