### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK III.

Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian theologian who famously proposed that souls existed before their bodies, a view that was later deemed controversial.</note> did not believe that creations happen **anew every day** <note>original: *quotidie de novo*</note>, but rather that all substances of souls—which we previously called "rays"—flow forth from this one fountain. This happens in different ways: either primarily, such as the soul of man which proceeds immediately from God himself; or secondarily, from that multitude of rays which informed the ethereal region at the time of creation. From these latter rays, plants <note>original: *vegetabilia*</note> were produced before the creation of the Sun, and sentient but irrational beings <note>original: *sensibilia, irrationalia*</note> were produced after the Sun’s rising. It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that the human soul is forged from a **purely formal ray**, which we call the **Mind** <note>original: *mentem*</note>, and its receptacle, which is that rational spirit of the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean was considered the highest, most refined part of the heavens, composed of pure light or fire.</note>. It is also formed from the vehicle of this spirit, which is the ethereal form or soul. This is ultimately enclosed in its "chariot" <note>An ancient Platonic concept where the soul travels through the spheres in a subtle body or vehicle.</note>, namely the ethereal spirit. Once this is done, that entire composition—by which the **inner man** is made similar both to God and to the world itself—descends into the **outer man**. Hence, it is likely that just as the aforementioned substances of the heavens are not created anew, so too the soul (which is a composition of those parts) is not created daily by infusion.

But where am I being carried away, or by what divine fury am I led? I beg pardon from you, O most sacred choir of theologians, if perhaps I have stepped beyond my limits; I most willingly submit myself to your authorities. However, I believed my intention to be good: to reconcile the holy theologians with these philosophers—who are profound in their wondrous divinity—by a bond of peace, and to bring their differing opinions into harmony.

TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK IV.

...the <term>composition<note>original: "complexio." In early modern medicine and philosophy, this refers to the specific "temperament" or balance of the four humors and elements within a person.</note></term> in any composite thing, just as those skilled in natural things have proven through experience in the binding, joining, and mixing of the four elements, which resist one another with contrary qualities; indeed, the said elements could not yield to this resistance in such a way as to be joined into one, unless there were this honorable medium, which moves confusedly through all elements, participates with each of their natures, and makes peace between enemies. What, then, is this love? It is this benevolent nature, this bond of things in harmonious peace, beyond the power of <term>active nature<note>original: "natura naturans." A philosophical term meaning "nature naturing," referring to the creative power of God or the active principle behind the universe, as opposed to "natura naturata," or created matter.</note></term> or the Idea of the Divine Spirit immersing itself into this moist nature. This is called the "Image of Divinity," the "Universal Form," or the <term>World Soul<note>original: "anima mundi." The belief that the universe itself has a soul that connects all living things.</note></term> by the Platonists and all other wise men. By its living and bright presence, an exact <term>trinity<note>The author uses the "trinity" here as a mathematical principle of perfection that resolves the conflict between the "duality" of spirit and matter.</note></term> is made in the composition out of a discordant and imperfect duality—that is, out of formless matter. From the perfection of this trinity, every perfect number and every harmony arises, whether it be divine, mundane, or human. For form, taken absolutely and considered without any matter, is a unity, insofar as it is a single ray leaping into the world from the identity of the <term>supersubstantial<note>Existing above or beyond the nature of physical substance; divine.</note></term> form so that it may be involved in the informing of the world, and yet it is in no way separated from the unity and essence of its source. In this same way, we see the ray of the Sun in the air, water, and earth, which nonetheless is not separated from the Sun, which is in the heart of the heavens. Therefore, by the mixing of the bright power of God with matter, matter itself is led back from the degree of imperfection to the goal of perfection. Yet, such perfection is not immediately absolute, but relative, insofar as created matter participates in the goodness and perfection of the Creator; for thus every creature is called "good" through participation. From this it happens that where nothing but discord had been found, there divine music, symphony, and harmony is now perceived and heard. But this harmony differs from the excellence of that divine harmony in this: no discord or <term>antipathy<note>A natural repulsion or opposition between things.</note></term> at all is found in the divine; whereas in the worldly, there are as many—indeed more—dissonances than concords. Thus, unison is the beginning of concord, and duality the beginning of discord. The Trinity, therefore, is the first degree of concord; the <term>quaternary<note>The number four, associated with the four elements and the material world.</note></term> is the first appearance of discord; and so on with the rest. Since, therefore, in the composition of the world, the peaceful form is joined with litigious matter, it follows that the composition of the world is a mixture of concords and discords at once. Having noted these things with diligent intuition, we shall first gird ourselves for the investigation of the numbers proper to the internal man, so that we may thereafter approach his harmony by an easier method.

## CHAPTER II.
### On the numbers of the soul.

When we deal with number in this place, we do not speak of that Arithmetic kind (called the <term>Algorithm<note>In this period, "Algorithm" referred to basic Hindu-Arabic numeral arithmetic used for trade and calculation.</note></term>) which merchants use in their business, or Geometry and Astrology use in their calculations; but we understand such numbers as are called Metaphysical, Physical or natural, and proportional. For by "unity," we do not understand a common "one," but rather an essence or unique form; nor by "duality" do we mean "two" in the abstract, but we denote something material in the concrete and found in the nature of things. Therefore, a **metaphysical** number is a distinction of the property of the supersubstantial essence, flowing forth from one and the same source or spring. But a **physical** and natural number consists in various proportions, by which the higher part of the world differs from the middle, and likewise the middle from the lowest and third part. And that first part indeed is found in the ratio of the **denary** <note>original: "denarii," referring to the scale of 10.</note> number, the ethereal part in the **centenary** <note>The scale of 100.</note> proportion, and the elemental in the **millenary** <note>The scale of 1,000.</note>. By considering these parts of the world through *Geometry*, the higher numbers correspond to lines, the middle to surfaces, and the lower to bodies; by the reasoning of *Music*, the simple numbers or divine digits correspond to the super-excellent voices, the <term>empyrean heaven<note>The highest, most "fiery" part of the heavens in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God and the angels.</note></term> to the excellent voices, the <term>ethereal<note>original: "aetherei." The middle region of the heavens, often associated with the stars and planets.</note></term> or middle heaven to the sharp <note>high-pitched</note> voices, and the elemental heaven to the deep <note>low-pitched</note> voices; furthermore, by the reasoning of *Arithmetic*, the <term>supersubstantial<note>Existing above or beyond the nature of physical substance; purely spiritual or divine.</note></term> correspond to unities, the empyrean to roots, the ethereal to squares, and the elemental to cubes. Therefore, what is intended here is not a "natural" number, but the <term>formal ratio<note>The underlying logic or "form" that gives a number its spiritual and philosophical meaning, rather than its use for counting physical objects.</note></term> which exists within number. For the form of the world, flowing from the essence of unity into the nature of duality or the <term>quaternary<note>The number four, which for Renaissance philosophers represented the material world and the four elements.</note></term>, produces proportional numbers, weights, and measures in this world through its greater or lesser presence. 

Hence it happens that the portion of matter or "moist nature" deprived of this formal presence is heavier, coarser, cruder, and more opaque, and tends more downward; whereas on the contrary, the portion of it that is rich and full of formal presence is subtler, thinner, lighter, more beautiful, more lifelike, nobler, more mature, and more elevated upward; and indeed this occurs through many proportions. Thus, the orbs of the substances of the four elements are suspended higher or lower according to the merits of their form, by the scales of justice. Thus the stars and every sphere of the ethereal heaven, decorated with glowing fires, are sustained and suspended with admirable artifice and order according to the nobility of their form. 

And in their center, the beauty of the Sun is placed so that, like the **eye of the world**, it may gaze upon all things, or like a **heart**, it may everywhere disperse and dispense the life of its light, flashing in a circular fashion. The empyrean heaven is also distinguished by the virtue of this form into its <term>hierarchies<note>The traditional nine-fold ordering of angels (Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.) or celestial powers.</note></term> (one of which is more sublime and excellent than the other in virtue), and so it is in the rest. These divisions of the material world are again subdivided by other infinite steps, which we have not defined. And these portions of the world, differing in their portions of matter or form, we call our "physical numbers"; from their union and various mixing, various things—distinct in nature, species, appearance, and quality—are produced in the world. 

From these, therefore, the world and the parts of the world are constituted; from these, its soul acts in different ways here or there in its spirit or its watery and moist matter; from these, the single soul, expanded into the multitude of matter, enters into the name of "multitude" according to the species of creatures, and even the individuals of those species; so that any ray of the universal world, entering into the matter or body of a creature, is called its "soul." 

But yet man, a divine animal, enjoys this honor above all other creatures of the world: he received a special breath from God beyond that general gift of world-life. Hence, besides the world’s gift, he enjoys the **divine mind**, the divine act and ray of God, by which alone among all other animals is he called intellectual and rational. Therefore, having considered these things in the proper way, let us approach the "numbers" of the human soul; for the soul indeed retains in itself a portion of every region or heaven of the world. Thus, man is called the **image of the world**, just as the world is the **image of God**. 

From the highest heaven, therefore, man has his intellect and reason; from the middle, his vital soul and ethereal spirit (the vehicle of that same soul); from the lowest, he receives the more "formal" part of the elements, which serves the organs of the other more excellent portions of the human soul. Above all these portions is carried the **Mind** (<term>Mens</term>), an offspring of the eternal essence, a ray of God and an uncreated gift, breathed forth from the supersubstantial mouth. The Mind, therefore, easily joins itself with the seeds of its own nature, namely with the <term>active intellect<note>original: "intellectu agente." In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought, the part of the mind that actively creates thought or perceives universal truths.</note></term>, or the fiery portion of the empyrean heaven; similarly with the soul, which is the fiery or bright nature of the middle heaven, and these three local portions join with the more formal portion of the element of fire; this indeed happens more easily because they all arose from the same bright source. 

So also there is a single and easy mixing among the material parts. For the rational spirit or <term>passive intellect<note>original: "intellectus patiens." The part of the mind that receives sensory information and is acted upon, rather than the part that actively theorizes.</note></term> unites itself with the ethereal spirit, and that with the air; for they are of the same nature, since they are derived from the same abyss and <term>hyle<note>original: "hyla." A Greek term for primordial, unformed matter.</note></term>. But yet, the portions of light...

### CHAPTER III.
->*By what power of worldly harmony the Mind is drawn toward its dark body.*<-

It is a very difficult matter, and one scarcely accessible to human reason, how the divine and immortal <term>Mind|Mens; the highest, most divine part of the human soul</term> is introduced from its highest tabernacle and most holy seat into the lowest, dark, filthy, and mortal mansion of man, which is so opposite to its own nature. We see this happen, however, by the divine will; and that movement of the soul toward the lower realms is undoubtedly induced by the allurements and flatteries of the <term>worldly spirit|spiritus mundanus; a mediating vapor or force that connects the physical world to the soul</term>, which possesses a significant love for the mass of darkness, as if for its own parent. Yet, this is only perfected by the movement and will of the Creator, so that even on earth and in the lowest heaven, a certain noble creature might be found made in the image of the Creator; one who, imbued with reason, may know its Creator, contemplate and admire His works, and extol, praise, and honor God the Creator with divine worship.

And this is indeed proven by the fact that it would be impossible for that Mind to descend into this place, so contrary to its nature, without that excellent and admirable symphony of the Creator, from which all worldly concord and harmony arises. Therefore, the Mind first descends with the intellect into the sphere of the "middle soul," carried on the wings of the rational spirit. But since 1 (the peak of the material pyramid) stands in a <term>double proportion|the ratio of 2:1, which creates the musical interval of an octave</term> to 2 (where the intersection of the pyramids occurs at the "place of equality"), it follows from this that the Mind is carried downward from its connatural seat to that station by the power of the <term>Diapason|the Octave</term> harmony.

It is then moved further downward through the <term>Diatessaron|the interval of a Fourth</term>, leaping all the way to the base of the <term>empyrean heaven|the highest, fiery heaven where God dwells</term> or the firmament; from there it is carried again through the <term>Diapente|the interval of a Fifth</term> to the sphere of the Sun or the "soul of the world," always penetrating deeper. Thus, the Diatessaron joined with the Diapente produces the Diapason: and this is its worldly harmony, forged from the spiritual Octave. This is the Mind’s middle station in its worldly journey, in which the <term>World Soul|anima mundi</term> with its spirit receives the Mind and the "active intellect" along with its rational vehicle.

From this station, the Mind slips down even further into its double lodging through the material or corporeal Diapente harmony; by this harmony, it is carried down to the curved surface of the element of fire, where the elemental region in its airy embrace receives it—along with its double vehicle and its governors—not without adoration and respect for the divine. And so the Mind, with its three governors—namely the intellectual, vital, and sensitive (or elemental) light—tends downward in its triple chariot, reaches the earth, and is enclosed in its dark prison by the power of the elemental or physical Diatessaron. In this way, by the power of the material Diapason harmony, the Mind descends with its subjects and puts on its corporeal veil. For from the material Diatessaron and Diapente, the Diapason leaps forth; which is also proven because the 1 of the formal pyramid's peak (found at the center of the material pyramid's base) is found to be in a double proportion compared to the 2 of the intersection. ### C A P. IV.
->*How the mind and intellect, penetrating from above through the entire world to its lower parts, even to its very center, observe the mysteries of each heaven, participate in the nature and disposition of each heaven, and introduce their virtues within the worldly man.*<-

Just as the human soul migrated into its dark dwelling <note>the physical body</note> through the harmony of the world, so too, while inhabiting the worldly man, it not only retains within itself the action of that worldly symphony but also carries with it the Idea <note>the perfect divine pattern</note> of divine concord. This is why man is so wonderfully affected by the sounds of common music. Hence, *Iamblichus* <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> put forth these arguments: *The soul,* he says, *heard divine harmony in the intelligible world; it remembers this harmony here whenever it hears a trace of divine melody. In remembering, it is vehemently moved toward it—if it is among those souls who once chiefly contemplated that very Idea of harmony in their true homeland <note>original: "patria," referring to the celestial realms before the soul's descent into a body</note>. Having become familiar with God through such an affection, the soul is now moved by a singular presence of God, through which it performs wonders.* Therefore, the cause of this inspiration and miracle is not a mere passion brought on by sounds, nor is it that the soul's nature is composed of harmony, but rather its likeness to God and God's presence. There are, therefore, primarily traces of divine music and melody in the mind, by whose sweet pulsing we are drawn toward the highest good and the contemplation of divine things.

From the perspective of the intellectual soul, man (when endowed with bliss) tastes the properties of the nine orders of Intelligences <note>the traditional Christian celestial hierarchy of angels</note>: namely, the fiery intellect of the *Seraphim* and the gift of their charity; the most excellent gift of the *Cherubim*, dwelling in the fullness of wisdom and knowledge; the sincerity of the *Thrones* in judgment and justice; the excellence of the *Dominions* in power; the character and reverence of the *Principalities*; the strength of the *Powers* to defeat malignant demons in spiritual warfare; the illumination and miracles of the *Virtues*, whom the power of God enlightens; and the secrets of the *Archangels* and *Angels* in their duties, announcements, and obedience. I say that man participates in all these endowments by virtue of the excellence of his own intellect, which grants such thoughts to men. By the power of this intellect, the soul (with the mind leading the way to its aid) could undoubtedly achieve as much as the Intelligences themselves, were it not confined within its thick and dark prison and led astray by the deceptive illusions of the same.

Furthermore, the virtues contained in the ethereal heaven are not lacking in man, due to the portions of the soul’s middle nature and its spirit. For from the *Primum Mobile* <note>the "First Moved" sphere, the outermost sphere of the physical universe</note>, which is contiguous with the intellectual heaven, the soul possesses such power that it has its will—derived from it—joined with the intellect, always tending toward the good of the mind. This intellect marks out the ways and paths for the will, just as light does for the eye. However, it does not move the will against its own appetite; the will remains the master of its own operation. For this reason, this will is called *Free Will* <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity of the mind and will to choose between different courses of action</term>. Although this will tends toward the good as its proper object, it is sometimes blinded by error and the deceptions of its dark veil, and under the impulse of animal force, it chooses evil, believing it to be good. Hence, free will is defined as a faculty of the intellect and the will by which good is chosen when grace assists, and evil is chosen when grace departs. Thus, Grace itself—which theologians also call charity or love—is in the will like a prime mover; when it is absent, the entire consensus falls into dissonance. In these things, therefore, the ethereal part of the soul participates in the nature of the *Primum Mobile*. The properties...

# ON THE NUMBER AND HARMONY OF THE INTERNAL MAN

[The soul] also seized three properties from the starry heaven, corresponding to each of the three triplicities <note>groups of three signs belonging to the same element</note> of the Zodiac, which it joined to itself for the perfection of its duties within the human body. For it drew its **attractive** faculty from *Aries*, *Leo*, and *Sagittarius*, which compose the fiery triplicity; it claimed the **retentive** faculty from *Taurus*, *Virgo*, and *Capricorn*; the **digestive** <note>original: "concoctricem," referring to the internal "cooking" or processing of nutrients</note> from *Gemini*, *Libra*, and *Aquarius*; and the **expulsive** faculty from *Cancer*, *Scorpio*, and *Pisces*. 

Next, passing through the sphere of *Saturn*, it received its receptive power from him, as well as gravity, constancy in its purpose, and deep prudence. From the orbit of *Jupiter*, it snatched its portion of justice, love of virtue, honesty, gentleness, and the governance of its natural faculty. From the region of *Mars*, it gained impulsive and spirited force, audacity, power, and strength. From the *Solar* circuit, it drew its vital faculty <note>the fundamental "life-force"</note>. From the path of *Venus*, it took the virtue of desire, cheerfulness, and delight in Music. From the orbit of *Mercury*, it acquired its imaginative power and sharp wit, a love of the sciences, and the perfection of memory. And from the sphere of the *Moon*, it attracted its power of growing and diminishing. 

Finally, its lower portion—which we call the sensitive and animal soul—introduces into its dark dwelling <note>the physical body</note> the complexions, humors, and other properties suitable for the sense organs, bringing them along for the perfection and completion of the elemental composition. From these things, it appears most evidently that the soul, on its journey—wandering from unity toward multitude—allures to itself infinite properties of the macrocosm <note>the "Great World" or universe</note> flowing from its divine harmony. 

And here it must be carefully observed that discords do not strike the human soul from the empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most spiritual heaven</note>, because that realm, due to its purity, divinity, and simplicity, is always occupied with the good; but discordant sounds are very often perceived to come from the starry heaven. For example: *Saturn* sometimes pours seeds of envy into the soul in a jarring and discordant manner; similarly hatred, a shameful life, melancholy, and other such things. *Mars* also sometimes sends down anger, sedition, strife, mockery, adultery, incest, inconstancy, and other such things into the lower parts because of its incongruous "pulsing" with certain lower natures. For this reason, these are called **unfortunate planets**; the reason for this we have recounted in our *Mundane Music*. 

The regions of the elements, however, found because of the vast amount of matter existing within them, are completely full of discord; for their "binary number" <note>the number two, representing duality and separation from the "One"</note> is the origin of discord and strife. And from this it happens that there are so many disputes in this region, so much corruption of things, and so many changes of things from one form into another. Indeed, the elements themselves would struggle and wage perpetual war against each other, were it not for that honorable "medium" <note>the soul or a balancing force</note> whose virtue binds and connects the warring things in the bonds of peace and concord. 

But the mind (*mens*) is free from every passion and from the malevolent disposition of matter; it is always found constant and immovable in its own state. It is not bent by the influences of the stars or the impulse of the [celestial] Intelligences, but exists immune to every operation and action of the things subjected to its natural seat. From this it is manifest that the stars cannot impose necessity upon the bodies over which the mind predominates. For the wise man, sprinkled with and imbued by the blessed rays of the divine mind, **will rule over the stars themselves**. Certainly, the influences of the stars and planets have no power over that intellectual part of the soul, insofar as the rational spirit is the mind’s closest vehicle and is naturally exalted above the power of the constellations. 

But there are those men who, refusing the gifts of the intellect and the benefits of the mind, are content only with the vital soul in the manner of beasts. Putting irrationality before rationality, and in no way gazing upon divine things with spiritual eyes, they look down only toward earthly things with a downward-cast face, [clinging to] the animal...

This is because the plant possesses its specific property from a spirit enclosed in the darkness of the "second shadows"—namely, the darkness of the middle heaven <note>Fludd divides the universe into three heavens: the highest (Empyrean), the middle (Ethereal), and the lowest (Elemental). This is demonstrated both by their position in the earth and by their nature and disposition. Conversely, vegetables or plants penetrate the surface of the earth, and are sublimated and raised every year toward their natural place in the region of air and water; they are perceived to live sensibly and to move from state to state <note>This refers to the observable growth and seasonal changes of plants compared to the "static" nature of rocks.</note>. This allows some to swim in the waters upon the earth, others to fly in the air above the waters, and others to run here and there upon the surface of the earth and the face of the water in the air. 

There is therefore undoubtedly a still greater mystery to be investigated here, from which we must ascend from the effects to the causes, higher toward the point of unity. In our *Treatise on the Macrocosm*, we deduced the origin of the Sun and the reason for its creation immediately from the foundation of the earth and its gathering around the center. Likewise, because air is adjacent in its nature to the element of fire, it does not allow the fire to depart without its company. The element of water has this same privilege with air, and the element of earth with water.

For this spirit has such communication with the ethereal heaven as the vegetable spirit has with the earth; indeed, its roots are fixed in the center and heart of the ethereal heaven just as the roots of plants are fixed in the earth. It is for this reason that this golden, vital, and incorruptible "plant of the world" <note>This "plant of the world" is a metaphor for the Sun or the solar spirit, which Fludd views as the source of all vitality.</note> is not hindered in its ascent by the elements: because its matter is not contiguous with them, but is instead the substance of the middle region interposed between the fire and the empyrean or intellectual heaven. Thus, neither fire, nor air, nor water, nor earth could retain this spirit as it flew upward from the earth, but only the aether, which is contiguous to it in its natural position, just as fire is to the aether. 

From these things, therefore, it will be clear to those who look closely that the nature of the Sun—since it originates from the empyrean or rational heaven—produced those animals of every kind which were created on the fifth and at the beginning of the sixth day. This occurred both because of the supreme vitality of its actions and because of its miraculous power and virtue in the life of animate things. For before the Sun’s appearance in the heart of heaven, no animal was created in the expanse of the lower region or upon the earth. But truly, after the fourth day, in which the Sun appeared in heaven—namely from the beginning of the fifth day until the end of the sixth—animate creatures were produced step by step. 

From this it is right to consider why an animal requires a greater quantity of heat and light for its composition and existence than a mineral or a plant, and that various kinds of animals are procreated according to a greater or lesser effect of heat and light. For at the first appearance of the Sun from heaven, the vapors of a moist nature—the clouds and material spirits leaping forth from the rebellious mass of darkness—were still crude and less "cooked" <note>Fludd uses the term "concoction," a concept from ancient medicine and alchemy where heat "ripens" or "digests" raw matter into more perfect forms.</note>. These were subsequently subdued more and more each day by the solar rays and actions, and having been made more obedient in this way, they then brought forth more perfect and mature things. 

Hence, at the beginning of the fifth day, because the humors were still very crude and undigested, the more "crude" animals were brought into the light by the Sun's life-giving operation. For thus we read: on the first day [of animal creation], fish and aquatic creatures were created immediately after the revelation of the Sun. Then, the cloudy spirit of darkness having been made more obedient, the more aerial and volatile animals obtained life and saw the light in the second place. Afterward, when the fifth day of creation had finally passed, the warmer and more fiery animals began to live and draw breath—namely, the four-footed animals and reptiles. 

It is clearly evident, therefore, that the dominion of the Sun, increasingly attacking the moist nature and the terrestrial mass, was the cause (the divine and immortal nature so willing it) that various and diverse kinds of animals were found in the lower world; some of which were colder, others warmer, some terrestrial, some aquatic, some aerial, and some more fiery. Indeed, the bodies of all these were selected from that portion of the earth which was more obedient to the solar and formal rays, and more corresponding to their actions. For this earth is the mother of all elements, because they proceed from her and return to her. Indeed, the earth is the mother and nurse of all things, which she conceived in her womb from the fire—that is, from the heaven, or from celestial action. For the heaven, of which the Sun is the commander, is the father of all composite things; but the earth is their mother. 

She carries these things in her bowels just as a mother carries her fetus. For into the depths of the earth flow all celestial and especially solar influences, which are enclosed there like the "seeds" <term>spermata: Fludd uses this biological term to describe the celestial influences that fertilize the material earth.</term> of things, as if in a common matrix or womb. From this, because of the variety of proportions of those descending influences, the diverse generations of different things occur in the earth, and various impressions arise, all of which are made in the substance of the muddy earth. In truth, the earth itself is the palace of the solar rays carried in the ethereal spirit, in which they are enclosed like captives and are called "vital spirits" <note>original: "spiritus vitales"</note>; namely, those by whose benefit even these houses and tabernacles of theirs live, feel, and ra[tionalize]...

From these things it follows that, since the mind is the most divine ray and act of the Creator, proceeding immediately from his mouth, it is necessary that it also requires a most excellent palace similar to itself, in which it may reign and perform its wonderful operations. Therefore, from the most excellent and refined slime and mud of the earth, that external Adam <note>The "external Adam" refers to the physical body of the first human, as opposed to the internal, spiritual man.</note> was forged. From this it is clear that his earthly portion was not entirely dry, as "gross earth" <term>Gross earth: the heavy, physical element of earth in its unrefined state.</term> is in its own nature, but that it had in itself the substance of water, by which its dryness was reduced and tempered into a certain muddy and slimy disposition. And yet, the naming of this entire body is taken from "earth" for the reason that thick water is nothing other than subtle earth, and earth nothing other than thick water. But just as the element of fire, in its relation, is contiguous to gross earth regarding its dryness, and therefore also exists potentially within the earth, so also in subtle earth (or thick water) there is potentially found that "subtle water" or air, from which water acquired its mobility; for these two elements are continuous in the nature of moisture. And yet, because nothing in the image of the external Adam was seen or touched except earth alone, for that reason it is called "earth," "mud," and "dust" in many places of the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, this mass was prepared into the softness of mud or wax, which is suitable for receiving any figure and image of any likeness; and finally God, the Best and Greatest, formed it with his own hands into the icon and appearance of the external man, according to that passage:

### CHAPTER IV.
### *On the correct position of the Microcosmic body according to the four regions of the Macrocosm.*

Although finding the fitting position of the Microcosm <note>Man as a "little world"</note> that corresponds to the four regions of the Macrocosm <note>The universe as the "great world"</note> is a very arduous and difficult task, we nonetheless draw from the fountain of Holy Scripture that there is a certain suitable relationship between these two worlds. For in many places we read that in prayers and the manner of supplication, the face of the petitioner should be turned toward the East. Similarly, in *Matthew 24:27*, we find that the lightning comes from the East and flashes even to the West. And in *Numbers 35:5* it is read: *You shall measure the eastern region, etc., and the southern region, and the western region, and the northern region, etc.* Furthermore, it is written in *Job 23:8 and 9* according to the translation of *Pagninus* <note>Santes Pagnino (1470–1541), a Dominican philologist and Hebraist</note>, where the search for the place and seat of *Jehovah* is discussed: *Behold, I shall go to the East and he will not be there; and to the West, and I shall not perceive him; or to the North, while he works there, and I shall not see him; he hides himself in the South, and I shall not see him, etc.* Indeed, *Jerome* <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> interprets this passage of Job thus: *If I go to the East, he does not appear; if to the West, I shall not understand him; if to the left, what shall I do? I shall not grasp him; if I turn myself to the right, I shall not see him.* *Tremellius* <note>Immanuel Tremellius (1510–1580), a Jewish convert and leading Hebraist of the Reformation</note> also translates that passage of Job into these words: *If I go forward, he will not be present; but if backward, I will not notice him; when he acts to the left, I will not see him; he will cover the right region, and I will not behold him.*

Therefore, from these passages, we can most clearly perceive the proper position of man according to his nature in the world. For from that passage in *Numbers*, we gather that man, above all, ought to look toward the East in every operation, and then in a circular regard toward the South, the West, and the North. Moreover, from the words of Job, we discover that the Eastern region—according to the translations of both *Jerome* and *Pagninus*—must be referred to the face of man; that is, as *Tremellius* interprets it, to the "forward" or his anterior part, and the Western part to his back. From this, it necessarily follows that his left side turns toward the North, just as his opposite side, namely the right, looks toward the South. The Holy Bible teaches us, therefore, that this arrangement of the Microcosm toward the regions of the Macrocosm is more congruent for him according to the laws of nature.

Now, looking diligently into the nature of the matter, let us inquire whether this position of the Microcosm relative to the site of the Macrocosm, according to its physical constitution, agrees with the nature of the world or Macrocosm, or not. Upon accurate inspection, we find that every region of the lesser world <note>Man</note> agrees by nature, temperament, and disposition with every quadrant of the greater world <note>The Universe</note>. For we attribute the light of the eyes to the solar splendor; the intellect and reason to the Prime Mover <term>Primum Mobile; in traditional astronomy, the outermost sphere that moves all others from East to West</term>, which whirls its orbs from the East toward the Setting; and we rightly compare the human heart to the Sun, as its prince—inasmuch as it is written that Jehovah placed his tabernacle in the Sun. Thus, all things of man, both interior and exterior, rejoice to greet the Sun as the bright tabernacle of the Creator, preceded by devout prayers and thanksgivings to their Creator and Lord; for the Sun is the driver-away of sadness and darkness, and the author of gladness, joy, and light. Conversely, the posterior parts of man are referred, not without merit, to the West. For just as the East is accustomed to bring day, light, and joy, so on the contrary the West brings night, darkness, and sorrow. ## CHAPTER V.
### *A brief anatomy of each region of the Microcosm.*

The head of the human body, which we previously compared to the empyrean heaven <note>the highest, most spiritual part of the universe</note>, has been called by some the "highest belly" or "uppermost cavity." It is bounded by the neck and contains the spark of the mind in its rational vehicle. Physicians distinguish the exterior of this head into the forehead, the top of the head <note>original: "sinciput"</note>, the back of the head <note>original: "occiput"</note>, the crown, the temples, and the face. They further observe its hair, with its manifold uses, and the skin—dense, hard, dry, and thick—to which the roots of the hair adhere. Its interior, however, they distinguish into the skull <note>original: "cranium"</note>, its attachments, and the brain with its various parts. 

The skull they divide into five sutures <note>the joints where the bones of the skull meet</note>, of which one is at the back, called the *Lambdoid* <note>shaped like the Greek letter Lambda (Λ)</note>; another is at the front, called the *coronal* <note>crown-like</note>; a third is straight and is named the *sagittal* <note>arrow-like</note>. The two remaining ones are called *false*, *squamous* <note>scale-like</note>, and *temporal*. A certain membrane, arising from the "thick meninx" <note>the dura mater</note> through the sutures, surrounds the convex surface of the skull; this is therefore called the *pericranium* and *periostium* <note>the connective tissue surrounding the bone</note>. Beneath these, two other membranes meet to cover the brain in a circle. The one that is thicker and harder, adhering to the concave surface of the skull, is called the *dura mater* <note>literally "tough mother"</note>; the other, however, joined deep within the brain, is thin and soft,

In this region, the heart has its primary station; its building is its capsule <note>the pericardium</note>. Furthermore, the larger parts of the heart are its two chambers; namely the right, into which are fixed two veins, the cava and the arterial <note>the pulmonary artery, which early anatomists often classified by its structure as a vein-like artery</note>, and the left, to which the arteries, the ***Aorta and the venous*** <note>the pulmonary vein</note>, are connected. The third and lowest region of the human body, extending from the Diaphragm downward to the pubic bone, encompasses the liver, the spleen, the gallbladder, the kidneys, the bladder, the seminal vessels, and other such things. The substance of the **Liver** is flesh and nerves, from which originate the veins—the portal or branching vein and the cava—and the arteries. The **Spleen**, however, the gallbladder, the kidneys, and the bladder are members prepared for the use of the liver, namely for carrying away the superfluities from the liver. Similarly, this region contains the stomach, the mesentery, and the upper and thinner intestines—namely the duodenum, the jejunum, and the ileum—and the lower and thicker ones—namely the cecum, the colon, and the rectum. Finally, we could fill entire volumes of this anatomy with observations, and thus affect the eyes of the readers with weariness in matters common to the world, rather than soothing them with delight or the whisper of a pleasing novelty; for this reason, it has pleased us to pass over the anatomy of the human body at least lightly in this place, so that

->we may prepare our mind for things more new,<-
->and not so commonly known, and yet<-
->true and demonstrable.<-

# TREATISE THE FIRST,
## SECTION I.
### *B O O K VI.*

## On the harmony of the external Microcosm. <note>original: *Microcosmi*; the "little world" or human being as a reflection of the universe</note>

### *C H A P T E R I.*

->*On the harmonic comparison of the constitution of the regions of the Microcosm with those of the heavens of the Macrocosm.* <note>original: *Macrocosmi*; the "great world" or the universe</note><-

The human body, which we have called the "external man" above, is forged from the same matter as the world. And although the spirit of the world—because of that subtlety which it received from the property and presence of light—is recognized to be transparent, clear, and easy to see through; nevertheless, that clarity and transparency of its spirit often becomes black, dark, and obscure through thickening and condensation <note>original: *inspissatione & incrassatione*</note> (which occurs more or less according to the greater or lesser absence of light, or the dominance of thickening cold). This is seen, for example, in the transformation of air into a dense cloud; and again, by the freezing power of cold, that cloud or condensed aerial spirit is changed into the appearance of "white earth," as seen in hail, ice, and snow. Indeed, it can even turn into the thickest earth itself, as is demonstrated by considering the thunderstone <note>original: *lapide fulminis*; prehistoric stone tools or fossils once believed to be solid bolts fallen from the sky during storms</note>.

For it is certain that the types of "earth" <note>In this context, "earth" refers to any solid or semi-solid physical matter</note> are of diverse natures: that is, participating more in the purity of fire, the disposition of air, or the quality of water. And yet all these types of earth are for the most part opaque and in no way transparent. Thus, the brain is observed to participate in the fiery element, the heart and lungs in the aerial, the stomach, liver, and humors in the aqueous, and finally the spleen and intestines in the coarse earthly element. This is because these body parts became the receptacles of those elemental natures after the soul was placed into them, as we shall teach below. 

But indeed, all these portions of "earth," though differing in their disposition, are observed to have nearly the same dimension of length within the geometric symmetry of the body, nor is one part more opaque than another. This happens because God fashioned this external dwelling-place of the soul or "breath of life" before He breathed the soul into it. For this reason it happens that, although the element of water is greater in dimension than earth, and air than water, and so on for the others (which occurs because the same substance, when expanded, requires more space for its existence; if—

...and similarly, just as that which is opaque is made transparent by expansion) the human body, however, since it was completed before the infusion of the soul into it, remained such after the imposition of the soul upon it as it was before. <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg."; a legendary Hellenistic figure credited with foundational texts on alchemy, magic, and philosophy.</note> seems to give the reason for this matter in these words: *When **GOD** noticed that the form of the divine likeness could not be attentive to all things unless He covered it with a worldly covering, He wove it with a corporeal house, and perceived that all such beings were so; blending them into one from both natures, and mixing them as much as was necessary. Thus He fashioned man from mind and body—that is, from an eternal and a mortal nature—so that the living being thus fashioned could satisfy both its origins: both to marvel at and pray to the celestial and eternal things, and to inhabit and govern earthly things.* Nor indeed shall we find the words of *Mercury* to be empty, if we consider the matter rightly. For since the nature of the free mind and the disposition of the intermediary soul—indeed, the very property of the thicker fire itself—is to neglect lower things and look back at higher things by natural instinct when they are free and released from dense bonds, it is necessary that they be enclosed in an opaque body and possess material organs, by whose direction they may be occupied with corporeal, dense, and lower things. For the nature of the soul, and much more that of the mind, is so conversant with spiritual and invisible things that it would not be able to notice visible and corporeal things unless it were enclosed in an opaque body, so that it might look upon them through material, earthly, and lower organs. This, therefore, is the reason that the rays of both the mind and nature work around opaque things. For if they were freed from the corporeal prison, leaving the earth empty and void, they would leap into the heavens with a light bound.

**Mind** therefore is given only to man, to distinguish his vital soul from the souls of other living beings, and to exalt it in dignity above others.

And although the **vital soul** was granted by itself to both plants and other animals in the creation, yet the soul of the bestial animal—immediately fortified and increased by the power of the **Sun**—is more excellent in both reason and motion than the soul of vegetables, inasmuch as the latter was infused into them before the positioning of the Sun in the heaven.

From the aforesaid things, therefore, we see that the regions of the <term>Microcosmic</term> <note>The "little world," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note> body do not differ in thinness and thickness after the example of the regions existing in the <term>Macrocosmic</term> <note>The "great world," or the universe at large.</note> body, because the former [the human body] was prepared before the inspiration of the soul, and consequently remains after the infusion of the soul just as it was before; the latter [the universe], however, received its preparation and disposition in thickness, thinness, location, expansion and constriction, transparency and opacity, immediately from that divine soul which was carried over the waters.

Finally, from this disposition of the simple terrestrial mass (divided and prepared by the **Creator** into more noble and less worthy regions according to the dignity of the parts of the heavens, which the **Architect** <note>original: "Opifex"; the divine craftsman or demiurge.</note> decided by His divine counsel to arrange and prepare before the ages), a material harmony is observed, suited to both the celestial bodies and the elements themselves, and to the symmetrical proportion of the terrestrial parts,

### CHAPTER II.

->The relation of the Microcosmic Harmony to the Macrocosmic: that is, concerning the correspondence of the external man or body with the shape of the world, and concerning the relation of the Planets to its members.<-

That the diameter of man is very similar to the diameter of the world, and that from the center—namely the place of the genitals and reproductive organs—a circle can be drawn that corresponds to each extremity of that diameter, being not unlike the periphery of the world, we have clearly explained in *Volume 2, Treatise 1, Section 1, Book 3*. From a proper contemplation of this fact, we perceive that the structure of man is conformable to that of the world in every respect of geometric figure; except that the metric proportion of the human body is more hidden, while that of the world is more manifest. For if the contracted members of man were expanded according to their proper natural proportion, we would see clearly that his arrangement or geometric figure is perfectly round.

His hidden figure is therefore of this kind, as is demonstrated below; which specifically denotes, first, that the structure of man is round like the machine of the world, and second, that every <term>wandering star</term> <note>original: "stella erratica"; a classical term for the planets.</note> corresponds to his members, either by natural harmony or by some unnatural discord. Specifically:

*   **Saturn** corresponds to the right ear, spleen, bladder, teeth, and bones.
*   **Jupiter** to the lungs, liver, arteries, pulses, and seed.
*   **Mars** to the left ear, gallbladder, kidneys, veins, and genitals.
*   **The Sun** <note>original: "Sol"</note> to the brain, nerves, heart, and right eye.
*   **Venus** to the womb, kidneys, genitals, breasts, throat, loins, liver, and sperm.
*   **Mercury** to the brain, the spirits, imagination, memory, tongue, hands, and fingers.
*   **The Moon** <note>original: "Luna"</note> to the brain, the left eye of a man and the right of a woman, the stomach, intestines, bladder, and the sense of taste.

Indeed, by the unlucky radiations or unhappy <term>aspects</term> <note>The geometric angles between planets that astrologers believe influence human health.</note> of these Planets, discord or diseases of these members are induced. These may either infect the man totally—as in the unfortunate position of **Saturn**, which causes leprosy of the whole body, universal paralysis, wasting, black jaundice, or quartan fever; or a bad disposition of **Jupiter** which causes apoplexy, convulsions, etc.; or **Mars**, which brings plague, acute fevers, tertian or daily fevers, and yellow jaundice; or the **Sun**, causing <term>syncope</term> <note>Fainting or sudden loss of consciousness.</note> and universal failing; or **Venus**, the <term>French disease</term> <note>original: "morbus gallicus"; an early term for syphilis.</note>, weakness and impotence of the entire stomach, and liver failure; or **Mercury**, causing mania, lethargy, epilepsy, etc.; or the **Moon**, causing epilepsy, and so on.

Alternatively, they may infest certain specific parts which they oversee. Thus **Saturn**, when ill-disposed, induces paralysis in the tongue, arms, or bladder; cancer in the breasts; or <term>iliac passion</term> <note>original: "iliacam passionem"; a painful intestinal obstruction.</note> in the bowels. **Jupiter** brings <term>peripneumonia</term> <note>Inflammation of the lungs.</note> to the lungs, pleurisy to the ribs, cardiac distress to the heart, <term>angina</term> <note>In this context, a severe sore throat or quinsy.</note> to the throat, and spasm or numbness to a particular limb. **Mars** brings burning <term>apostemes</term> <note>Large inflammatory swellings or abscesses.</note> to a site (such as <term>carbuncles</term> and <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: "erysipelas"; a skin infection known as St. Anthony's Fire.</note>), dysentery in the intestines, or wounds to the face. The **Sun** brings syncope and cardiac distress to the heart, and <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>Severe eye inflammation.</note> or watery discharge to the eyes. **Venus** brings "suffocation of the womb," <term>gonorrhea</term> and <term>priapism</term> to the testicles and penis, diabetes to the bladder, weakness to the liver and stomach, <term>pustules</term> of the French disease to the face, and <term>lientery</term> <note>A form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested.</note> to the intestines. **Mercury** brings deprivation of the senses to the brain, stammering to the tongue, cough to the lungs, and an abundance of spit to the mouth. The **Moon** brings colic to the intestines, <term>oppilations</term> <note>Blockages or obstructions.</note> in the liver and <term>mesentery</term> <note>original: "miseraicis"; refers to the mesenteric veins.</note>, and phlegmatic abscesses in particular places or members. Here, therefore, we have delineated the directions and sympathy of these Planets in their spheres to each member of the body in the following way.

There are also several others who establish the navel of the belly as the center of the <term>Microcosmic<note>Literally "little world"; the Renaissance idea that the human body is a miniature map of the entire universe.</note></term> circumference. This particular invention of theirs does not please me, for the reasons we have alleged above. The composition of the external <term>Microcosm<note>The Renaissance belief that the human body is a "little world" that perfectly mirrors the "Macrocosm" or the great universe.</note></term> is also adapted and shaped to match any other regular figure; for, depending on the different positions of the protruding limbs, it is arranged in different ways. ...mistress of the [wise], it behaves otherwise than human ingenuity can devise; since it is tender and covered with a most thin and chaste spirit and ordained within itself in an ineffable way. From this it is clear that the constitution of the brain is to be referred to the excellence of the uncreated nature <note>The divine soul or "uncreated nature" of God reflected in man.</note>, for which it is the tabernacle. And therefore it is clear that its hidden nature is most fitting to the super-celestial fire, its moisture to spiritual moisture, and its color to the complex of both; and finally, the loftiness of its place or position is most suitable to the highest element, namely fire. 

Yet the reason why the brain is neither thinner nor more transparent than the other members is drawn from the creation of man, in which it is evident that man's body was created and prepared by the Creator before his soul was infused into it. The cause for this was so that the soul, darkened by shadows, might perceive, distinguish, and look upon bodies through material organs; which indeed it could not have accomplished unless it were veiled in dark flesh, since by itself it understands nothing except invisible things—that is, things such as itself—while nevertheless with the aid of the body it sees visible things and gazes with corporeal eyes. In this way, therefore, God made the dark mass subject to Himself and subdued both the earth and the heavens to His will, and stirred up dark bodies in respect to their condition. 

The middle region of the body, however, insofar as it relates to moisture and heat, can be compared to Air; for it relates to the brain as air relates to fire, which is why we consider the entire chest of the Microcosm <note>Microcosm: literally "Little World," a term for a human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the whole universe.</note> to be referred to the element of Air. As for the opacity and thickness of the heart and lungs, the same reasoning applies as was cited above. 

The watery region in the Microcosm is the origin of the manifold humors found in its lowest division. For the chyle <term>chylus: a milky fluid of emulsified fat and lymph formed in the small intestine during digestion</term> of the stomach, the thick blood of the liver, and urine or the serum of the blood constitute the watery sphere. For this reason, the stomach, the liver, the kidneys, and the other parts of this region are far grosser in their hidden nature than the upper members. This is proven by their effects, namely, in that the upper members produce spirits that are purer and more invisible. 

For example: the brain contains "animal spirits" <note>original: *spiritus animales* — from *anima* (soul). In Renaissance medicine, these were the refined fluids in the nerves that enabled sensation and movement.</note> which are invisible, and the heart contains vital or arterial spirits, which are almost invisible. But the earthy dregs themselves are terminated and stored in the intestines and the spleen, which are found near the center of the Microcosm just as the element of Earth is found near the center of the Macrocosm <note>Macrocosm: The "Great World" or the universe as a whole.</note>. From these things, therefore, we see that the regions of the external Microcosm are distinguished by symphonic differences in no other way than it is known that the entire disposition of the elements of the Macrocosm differs in quality and position; whose harmony we have clearly enough depicted in our treatise on the Macrocosm. 

And indeed, that composition of this harmony in the elementary region was nothing other than a likeness of the universal worldly harmony, derived from the mutual action and resistance between the source of all light and the abyss of darkness. For the element of fire relates to the element of earth as light to darkness; similarly, the region of moisture between fire and earth relates as the intermediate universal spirit to the two extremes, namely light and darkness. From these things we can diligently consider how great the similarity is between the proportions of the human body and the worldly elements, and by what metric dimensions these two might be reduced to music, so that they may agree with one another in harmony. 

That human harmony agrees with the sympathy of all things is demonstrated in this way: God is light; light is concord, and concord is the origin of creation and existence, a sounding word making things beautiful and moving the spheres from their starting point to their goal, and back again to their principle, as if to a unison from which all concordances have flowed. Whence...

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VI. ###

It came to pass through a process of revolving that the elements—and shortly thereafter, the further elements—were produced. In this same way, the divine mind—which is the light and supreme harmony of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," a term used by Renaissance philosophers to describe the human being as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>, and the very origin of human creation and existence—produced a beautiful image of the Microcosm. It leads the spheres of the human being through their motions—both the voluntary or natural ones, and those involuntary or "ravished" <note>original: *rapto*; referring to motions driven by an external spiritual force</note> by the spirit—skillfully completing his elemental composition. 

Hence, man is called a God, but a mortal one; just as the Creator himself alone is called GOD, but immortal. Similarly, the Devil is darkness and discord, the author of destruction or deprivation, and the discordant strife that was the first-born son of chaos. He is the adversary of the Word of God and of light, rendering the sphere of the earth immobile by his own nature and causing the elements to clash through his discordant character. In this same way, the body of man is dark, the author of discord and disease, the obscure son of chaos, most opposed to the mind, soul, and light, and immobile by its own nature.

All of this occurs because there is a duality <note>The number two, representing division, conflict, and the separation of matter from spirit.</note>. Consequently, if the unity of the soul is joined to that duality—or if the trinity of form <note>The spiritual "three" (mind, soul, spirit).</note> is joined to the quaternary of matter <note>The physical "four" (the four elements: earth, water, air, fire).</note>—then the body will be led back from discord into an exquisite harmony. By this reasoning, the darkness shall be illuminated, discords shall be driven away, life shall be preserved, and death shall be cast into exile. A peace shall be established between God and the darkness—or between the body and the soul—through the illumination provided by the divine presence of the mind. The body, which is immobile by itself, will then receive action and motion from an internal moving principle. 

From these things it is clear that these two extremes, which are contrary to one another, produce various effects by their own natures: namely light and darkness, or soul and body. For the former gives birth to harmony, under whose dominion small things grow; while the latter is accustomed to induce discord, by whose presence even great things fall apart. The contrariety of these extremes is denoted by the opposing positions of their triangles in the composition of the world. The apex <note>original: *conus*</note> of the **formal pyramid** <note>The pyramid representing spiritual or "forming" energy.</note> is in the earth, while its base is in the first heaven. Conversely, the position of the **material pyramid** <note>The pyramid representing physical matter.</note> is the opposite: its apex is contiguous with the center of the formal base, while its own base is firmly set in the center of the earth, as it were.

In the middle point, where life alone is found, they meet: specifically in the **sphere of equality**, or the place where the two pyramids intersect. Here, a portion of the one is weighed against a portion of the other on the scales of justice. And just as these two pyramids differ in their position, so too the natures that spring from their bases are perceived to be opposite in their disposition. For we see that the soul, proceeding from the center of the formal pyramid, becomes more perfect and lively the longer it stays in the body; it is observed to "grow young" in its faculty, wisdom, and prudence. On the contrary, the body—the older it grows in age—is recognized to decrease and fall into ruin, as if through a certain senility. Furthermore, the stronger the soul is, the weaker the body is, and vice-versa.

We conclude, therefore, that the human body consists of four elements:
1.  **Earth** appears most clearly in the flesh and bones because of their fixed and solid earthly substance.
2.  Similarly, the element of **Water** has its power and existence in the humors <note>The bodily fluids, such as phlegm or bile.</note>.
3.  **Air**, besides being found abundantly in the blood of the lowest region, is perceived to dwell in the lungs as its most proper place.

From this it was established from the beginning that this member of the body (the lungs) is always in motion, serving in the place of a fan or bellows to cool the heart. This prevents the heart—which is the chief seat of the **fiery virtue** <note>The vital heat or spiritual fire that drives life.</note>—from being consumed and dissolved by excessive heat.

The shape of the heart is therefore pyramidal, and in this shape it is adapted to the flame of fire. For in the upward-rising flame of fire, we see its base is like the base of a pyramid, while its summit is sharp like the apex of a pyramid. However, in the body, the situation with the heart is the same as with the **Sun** in the world. For the base of the solar pyramid is in the body of the sun, but its apex points downward, contrary to the nature of common fire. This occurs by a singular divine will. For otherwise, if the power of light always tended upward, the lower things would be deprived of the efficacy of the life-giving light—

Furthermore, through even more marvelous virtues, it ineffably leads the stupendous power of its rational and intellectual spirit to a peak and a happy conclusion.

## BOOK VII.

->On the internal aspect of the Microcosm within the external, or on the act of the mind within the body.<-

### CHAPTER I.
->*On the creation of man.*<-

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'A' featuring architectural elements, scrolls, and floral decorations within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
The human soul—according to the manner and reason alleged in the first book of this work—glides down from the higher regions to the lowest heaven by means of musical proportion and spiritual vehicles <note>The author refers to the Neo-Platonic idea of the *ochēma* or "soul-vehicle," a subtle substance that allows the immaterial soul to attach to the material body.</note>. Prepared at last for entry into its home, it is infused and breathed by the breath of the Artificer <note>original: *opificis afflatu*; a reference to God as the Great Architect or Craftsman.</note> into that dwelling. This dwelling, fashioned from earth, dust, and mud by the hands of the Creator himself, was adapted to receive such a God-like breath <note>original: *spiraculum Deiforme*</note>, as was stated above. By the life-giving power of its presence, the soul moves, vivifies, and animates the external man. In this way, man was created as a double being within a single individual, and was made a living animal, endowed with reason and intellect. He is (I say) an admirable animal, an earthly God <note>original: *Deus terrenus*; a common Renaissance Hermetic concept suggesting man's semi-divine status and dominion over nature.</note>, created immortal in himself, but made mortal on account of sin—in short, the image of his ineffable Maker. 

However, we have already dealt elsewhere—specifically in our *Theological-philosophical Treatise on life, death, and resurrection*—extensively with the breath of his life and the purity, cleanliness, transparency, clarity, and perfection of his body in the state of innocence, as well as his placement in Paradise along with the description and explanation of the delights of Paradise itself. Therefore, we shall pass over those matters lightly in this place, so that we may concern ourselves only with the opinions of the ancient Philosophers as we debate the actions of the internal man within his external part. In the first part of this book, therefore, we shall treat the operation, dominion, and power of the human soul, considering its supernatural aspects as well as its celestial and elementary parts, insofar as the soul is considered alongside the body in the context of creation or generation alone. We perceive, then, that creation differs from generation in many ways; yet we do not [wish] this word "creation" to be considered so strictly...

HEADER: ON THE INTERNAL MICROCOSM WITHIN THE EXTERNAL

we wish [to define creation] as those do who define it as the production of a thing and its origin from non-pre-existing matter, that is, from nothing. For in this way we do not correctly say that man was created, insofar as in his beginning his external part was made from pre-existing matter that stood ready for the work—namely, from the mud and earth that were the suitable material for his composition. Rather, we more correctly define creation as that process by which the species of things, which did not exist before, now begin to be. Thus, the first species of man took its beginning in the creation of Adam, the Lion in the first production of land animals, and so on.

In this, therefore, creation and generation differ: creation is concerned with the origin and production of non-pre-existing species, while generation is concerned with the propagation, multiplication, and conservation of pre-existing things or creatures—species already created through the first **LET THERE BE** <note>original: *FIAT*; the divine command from Genesis 1:3</note> and continuing until the final **LET IT PERISH** <note>original: *PEREAT*; referring to the end of the temporal world</note>. In the former (creation), God the Creator works immediately; in the latter (generation), the "second image of the first mind" works—which is created Nature herself, or the daughter of God, proceeding and derived from Him before the creation of all things.

### CHAPTER II.

->*On the free disposition of the middle spirit, by which it is accustomed to participate in one or the other extreme, and on the cause of the internal man's happiness, and the reason for his dejection and misfortune.*<-

Saint Paul, agreeing with Sextus the Philosopher <note>likely referring to the *Sentences of Sextus*, a collection of moral aphorisms popular in the early Church</note>, constantly asserted that the human soul is the temple of God. Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure said to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus, blending Greek and Egyptian wisdom</note> also demonstrates the reason for this in the 12th book of the *Pimander* <note>The *Poimandres*, a key text of Hermetic philosophy</note> with these words: *The Good Spirit,* he says, *pronounced the soul to be in the body, the mind in the soul, the Word <note>original: *Verbum*; the divine Logos or Reason</note> in the mind, and God to be their Father. The Word, therefore, is the image and mind of God; the purest portion of matter is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the mind; and finally, of the mind, GOD. Truly, GOD is around all things, the mind is around the soul, the soul is around the air, and the air is around matter.*

Hence it is that others, seeking to constrain human nature more tightly, have joined it from three parts: namely from the soul, the intermediary spirit, and the body—signifying the mind and soul through the term "soul." But these, it seems to me, have not distinguished the internal man so exactly. That is, they have not distinctly described the portions of the internal man which he acquired from each of the three heavens, and consequently, they left the description imperfect, since all perfection consists of a beginning, a middle, and an end. 

We shall instead listen to the opinion of the Platonists <note>followers of Plato’s philosophy, particularly those in the Renaissance who sought to harmonize him with Christianity</note> which here does not differ from Hermes Trismegistus. They ascribed three parts to the internal man: namely the highest, the lowest, and the middle. By the **highest**, they understood that divine thing which they call the mind, the illuminated intellect, a portion of uncreated light, and the act or "Ray of God." This is the superior portion of man. In this portion of the soul, Hermes Trismegistus—ascending higher by the counsel of the good and never-lying Spirit—asserted that the Word dwells. Saint John also seems to agree with this, calling the Word the life of men and the light of the darkness; and likewise Hermes calls it the "life and light" from which man is composed. And elsewhere he says: *The Word in you sees and hears* (*Pimander, 1*). So Moses calls it the "breath of life" <note>original: *spiraculum vitae*; from Genesis 2:7</note>, breathed immediately by God Himself into the external man. And this superior portion of man, embracing the illuminated intellect, is that by which man, excelling all other animals, approaches the nature of the Deity itself. For this reason, he is called the "Image of God" and the "Son of God," not only by philosophers but also by the Scriptures themselves. By the **mind**, therefore, the Platonists understand the intellect and reason—

they wished. Furthermore, through the lowest part—the airy and lowest portion of the internal man—they seemed to signify the "act of the elements." As *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: *Mercurius Trismegistus*; the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic writings</note> testifies in the passage cited above, this part belongs to the entire elemental region. It gathers to itself the formal dispensations of the elements in proportion to the subtlety and thinness of the matter existing there. With the assistance and guidance of the leaders—the higher portions of the soul—it acts upon the body according to the corrupt disposition of the flesh and of darkness, as these are more familiar to it by its very nature and position. Thus, this portion of the soul is more inclined toward the passions of the body and lower things than it is suited by its nature to the mind and divine matters.

And so, this lowest portion of the soul is called the <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>original: *anima sensitiva*; the part of the soul responsible for processing physical sensations and movement</note>, which the *Apostle Paul* called the "natural man" <note>original: *hominem animalem*; referring to 1 Corinthians 2:14</note>. It is an idol produced from the bosom of corporeal matter which, when the body is dissolved, perishes along with it; or at least its shadow does not survive long in the vapors of its dissolved body, participating in nothing of immortality but returning into the formlessness of matter <note>original: *hylæ deformitatem*; 'hyle' is the Greek term for primordial matter</note>, unless it is also united to a more sublime power, by whose virtue alone it can claim immortality. This portion of the soul is the motive power, the life-giver, the ruler of the body, and the material origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of perception within the body. For it perceives bodily things through the body, moves the body through space, rules it in that place, and nourishes the body with physical substance. In this portion of the soul, therefore, there are two most powerful virtues: one is **Phantasia** <note>the faculty of imagination or mental representation</note>, whether we call it imagination or thought; and the other is the nature of sense.

Finally, by the **Middle Spirit**, they understood a middle or ethereal and vital act and ray of nature, connecting both extremes—namely, the mind with the animal soul. From this it follows that this middle nature participates in both extremes. Thus, from the virtue of the Sun (because of the relation of its light to the empyrean heaven), it possesses a spark of reason, which is subsequently increased by the presence of the mind and the intellectual spirit. It also possesses a sensitive faculty derived from the lowest extreme and the subtlety of the elements. Consequently, this middle nature—uniting the extremes equally and joining the intellectual portion with the animal or sensitive soul (that is, carrying the mind with its rational spirit and vehicle toward lower things)—is by its nature essentially free. Thus, it is permitted to adhere more to one or the other: namely, to be occupied more with lower and sensible things than with super-celestial and divine things, or vice versa. It is exactly as if GOD said to this intermediate spirit dwelling within, by its own free will:

> Take whichever of these you prefer,

or according to the words of the *Leader Moses*:

> You have before your eyes life and death, choose whichever you wish,

or according to the choice of the *Apostle*:

> either be children of the world, or of the heavenly kingdom.

And similarly, it is said in this way: that Adam tasted of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he who in the beginning contemplated nothing but the secrets of the unmanifest <note>original: *ineptis arcana*; likely referring to the hidden mysteries of God</note>, and consequently was a participant in goodness alone. But as to how this matter stands, I pray you, listen. This intermediate spirit, full of vital breath and moreover imbued with reason—both solar and especially empyrean and mental—gives the body the power of living in a general sense from these sources; that is, it grants all functions of life to the body through the mediation of the sensory organs adapted for the faculties of life. 

But truly, since every action of life is occupied either with good or with evil (as there is nothing in this world besides these two extremes, the first being the gift of light and the last of darkness), it is necessary that this motion of the spirit in life tends either toward goodness—that is, toward the nature of God and the Father of Light—or toward the malice of the Devil, the prince of darkness. For it is impossible for both points of the spear to lean toward both extremes at once. Hence, as *Christ* says:

> You cannot serve God and man <note>original: *homini*; while the Vulgate uses 'Mammon,' the author here emphasizes the conflict between the divine and the worldly human condition</note> at the same time.

And *Saint John in his first epistle*:

> The children of God cannot be children of the world, nor vice versa.

From these things, therefore, it is clear that this spirit, like a Prince Elector, tends either toward higher things or toward the nature of lower things (the animal soul); that is, toward either the world's depravity and
