the nature of darkness and vices, or whether it looks toward the arrangement of the super-celestial goodness and virtue of heaven. If, therefore, this <term>intermediate spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus hic intermedius*; the "middle" part of the soul that acts as a bridge between the physical and the divine</note> clings constantly to the mind with its light, it is blessed. For this supreme portion never sins, nor consents to evil, but always resists errors and exhorts one toward the best things, as *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: *Mercurius Trismegistus*</note> describes more at length in the first book of the *Poimandres* <note>original: *Pimand.*; the opening treatise of the *Corpus Hermeticum*</note>. And consequently, by the power of the mind, such a spirit is eventually transferred to God because of its obedience, according to that saying of *Proclus*: *The soul, through acquired knowledge, becomes similar to the mind or the intellect itself.*

But on the other hand, if that spirit joins with the <term>animal soul</term> <note>original: *animæ animali*; the part of the soul shared with animals, focused on survival and instinct</note>, or clings to the lower part, it is depraved, polluted, and submerged and detained in darkness, until from a <term>good Daemon</term> <note>original: *bono Dæmone*; here meaning a guiding or guardian spirit, not an evil entity</note> it becomes an evil one. For that lower portion—namely, the animal soul—is always submerged in evil, sin, and lust, and as *Saint Paul* <note>original: *Divo Paulo*</note> testifies, it drags one toward the worst things. His words are these:

> I see another law in my members, taking me captive in the law of sin. <note>original: *Video aliam legem in membris meis, captivantem me in lege peccati*; quoting Romans 7:23</note>

From this also arose this divine discourse of *Saint Bernard*:

> O soul, decorated and made beautiful through the image and likeness of God, betrothed to the spirit through faith, helped by angels, a companion of bliss, an heir to salvation, a participant in reason—what business do you have with the flesh?

Indeed, *Bernard* did not see everything: for very often the spirit, in a treacherous manner, drags the middle soul down to lower things by flattering it, and shuts it up in the opaque body. There, for the most part, the spirit leaves the soul alone and idle, and it accomplishes this by the charms of the sensitive soul, to which it is more inclined to cling than to the mind because of its moist and material disposition, which rejoices more in its own likeness. Yet, where the proportion of the soul’s middle nature is large (which is always found in the spirit), there it makes its spirit more obedient to the mind. This is because the middle soul, or the "act of the world" and the "radius of nature," is of the remote nature of the mind itself, or the "act of God"; hence it participates in its property. Therefore, matter naturally tends toward the works of darkness, but form tends toward the arrangement of light, just as we see in the flame of a burning fire.

Is this, O readers, a new and unheard-of doctrine? Is this, I say, the opinion of the <term>Platonists</term> <note>original: *Platonicorum*; followers of Plato, particularly the Neoplatonists who emphasized the soul's ascent</note> disagreeing in any way from the truth? Examine yourselves, I pray, and you will find that this matter cannot finally be otherwise. For example: perhaps a crime to be committed is proposed to one of you; that is, he decides within himself to commit either rape, adultery, theft, murder, treason against the Prince, or some similar wickedness. But reason, which is always the companion of the mind, will resist this purpose of his to the best of its ability. Nevertheless, it very often happens as it usually does: at the end of this struggle, the spiritual sense and the appetite of the flesh are fulfilled, the admonitions of the mind and reason are rejected, and thus that intended crime is perfected. Here, then, we see that this intermediate spirit has neglected the counsel of the mind and, by clinging to the sensitive soul, has immersed itself in darkness.

But conversely, if the spirit—struck by fear of the Creator and following the footsteps of reason—clings strongly to the mind and leaves the conceived crime unperformed, and, as if inflamed by hatred and repentance for that evil counsel and purpose, turns itself to a better life, it is an evident sign there that this intermediate spirit has constantly embraced the mind and has held the animal soul, or the <term>idol</term> <note>original: *idolum*; here referring to the lowest, most material "shadow" or "image" of the soul</note>, in contempt.

But what need is there for more words? Is it not clear to us that there are two extremes in the world: namely, light and darkness, virtue and vice, good and evil? It follows, therefore, as if by concession, that there is likewise a certain and determined medium between them, which is apt to participate in this or that extreme, according as the object of one or the other shall seem more pleasant and delightful to it. And without doubt the human soul, or the **internal man**, is fashioned from these parts, insofar as he is perfect and complete, and consequently is judged to consist of a perfect number—namely, of a beginning, a middle, and an end. That is, of the mind, the spirit, and the idol (or animal soul), or what is the same thing,

### C A P. III.

->*On the reason why the mind is enclosed in an opaque body, and concerning its command within the human body.*<-

It is a source of wonder to anyone who reflects upon it, by what harmony those two opposites—contrary both in the nature of their essence and their spatial position—namely the Mind and the body, can be joined into one. And yet we see with our intellectual eyes that this happens through the mediation of an interposed spirit. Similarly, it will seem strange that this most excellent image of God, or rather the very ray of God, should be moved so far from its natural seat and become so debased in its condition that, although it is the most splendid, effective, divine, immortal, and purest light, it is nevertheless cast into and enclosed in a prison so dark, misty, terrestrial, and subject to corruption, and even so foul and filthy. 

But we acknowledge that this was done by the divine providence of the Creator, so that the mind might both love the nature of particular things <note>i.e., individual physical objects</note> and yet be concerned with the multitude, while also looking toward the arrangement and unity of universals <note>higher, abstract truths</note>. Hence, says **Iamblichus** <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the soul's descent into matter</note>: *Souls and heroes are more concerned with the multitude; Gods and Daemons with unity.* For the further the light descends into the **material pyramid** <note>a common Renaissance metaphor where light (the tip) descends into the base (broad, heavy matter)</note> from its peak toward its base, the more it inclines toward the multitude, as was said above. For by this way, the Creator willed that a certain **terrestrial God**, yet a mortal one, should observe the multitude of particular things on earth, just as He, as the **immortal God**, looks upon unity and universal things in heaven. In such a way, the Creator God himself is said to dwell both in earth and in heaven, and to be present everywhere. 

**Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: *Mercurius Trismegistus*; the legendary sage to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed</note> seems to agree with our opinion in these words from *Asclepius 4*, when he observed that the <term>esunode</term> <note>original: *ἐσυνοδὴ*; meaning a union, assembly, or conjunction</note>—that is, the form of the divine likeness—could not be diligent in all things unless God covered it with a worldly garment; so He covered it in a corporeal house. He perceived that all such beings were composed of both natures, confounding and mixing them into one as much as was necessary. Therefore, He shaped man from both soul and body—that is, from eternal and mortal nature—so that an animal thus shaped could satisfy both of its origins: to wonder at and pray to celestial and eternal things, and to inhabit and govern terrestrial things, etc. 

The power of the mind in the human body is therefore infinite, since—as **Hermes Trismegistus** testifies in the *Poimandres, book 12*—it is born from the essence of God (if indeed He has an essence) and is by no means divided from His essence, but rather connected to it in the same way that light is to the body of the Sun. And it is for this reason that the mind rules over all things, and nothing belonging to **fate** is impossible for the mind. Thus it happens that the human soul is superior to fate. And yet, it does not neglect those things which are subject to fate; and for this reason, the wise man—that is, one endowed with the action of the mind—is said to **rule the stars** <note>original: *sapiens astris dominari*; a famous maxim suggesting that human reason can overcome astrological influences</note>. 

It is also for this reason that the same Philosopher seems to acknowledge that all corporeal motion in the body is produced by the mind. For the external man was not made a living animal until the God-like breath was blown into him. **Hermes Trismegistus** says in *Poimandres 10* *that the soul, if deprived of the presence of the mind, is able neither to do anything nor to say anything.* Therefore, we gather from the sacred writings of the holy Philosophers that the "mind" is understood in two ways: namely, either as the primary and superior mind, which is the act and ray emanating immediately from God; or as the inferior mind, which is the image or trace of that primary and superior mind...

...a certain vestige, following the exact determination of the first mind: which secondary mind is Nature itself, or the worldly act. Therefore, the first Mind, or the ray of God, proceeding immediately from the supersubstantial nature, enters into the empyrean <note>The highest, most "fiery" or spiritual level of heaven</note> or rational spirit, where it formed the divine creatures produced on the first day of creation and endowed with divine sharpness. The image of this first mind also shone back in the middle of the abyss on the second day of creation, and produced the ethereal heaven and the life-giving soul of the material or visible world: which image of the prior mind and secondary mind is not undeservedly called Nature itself, or the worldly ray. And this is granted to individual animals and the other visible creatures of the world. Therefore, *Hermes Trismegistus, in Pymander, book 12,* called this secondary mind the nature of brutes and vegetables. This opinion is supported by *Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a 4th-century Neo-Platonist philosopher and bishop</note> with these words in Hymn 3: The mind, having descended into matter <note>original: "hylen"</note>, an immortal mind, the offspring of divine parents, small indeed but the whole of them, this and one everywhere, infused as a whole into the whole, turns the vast cavity of the heavens, preserving this universe; distributed into diverse forms, it is present; part of it is the assembly of stars, part the assembly of angels, part also, having obtained an earthly form by a heavy bond, and separated from its parents, has drunk in dark oblivion, etc.* Similarly elsewhere, the same *Hermes Trismegistus* seems to confirm that very thing with these words: *Mind, he says, is GOD in humans, and therefore some among the number of humans are Gods, and their humanity is nearest to divinity: For the good Spirit <note>original: "Daemon" — in this context, a protective or guiding divine spirit rather than an evil entity</note> proclaims Gods to be immortal, but humans to be mortal Gods. But in irrational animals, that mind is nature. For wherever there is a soul, there is mind; just as wherever there is life, there also is the soul in living things, even without the discourse of reason.* But indeed the middle soul is in its nature void of the first mind, although it is itself as it were a secondary mind, which suffices for the life of any creature. Hence, says *Hermes Trismegistus in Pymander, book 10: The soul, destitute of the presence of the mind, is able neither to do anything nor to say anything: but often the mind goes out from the soul, at which time the soul neither hears nor sees, but is like an animal lacking reason:* So great, I say, is the power of the supreme mind, which leaves a soul of this kind entangled in the body and drawn by the same as if to the lower regions. For this eternal essence, to speak with *Hermes Trismegistus*, is very far from the ignorant, the wicked, the lazy, the envious, the unjust, the murderous, and suchlike, or at least it is absent from its lodging, permitting them to the judgment of the avenging spirit <note>original: "Dæmonis ultoris"</note>, who, striking with the sharp edge of fire, afflicts the senses, and arms the person more and more to commit crimes, so that as one guilty of a fouler fault, they may be subject to sharper punishment; and it inflames them without any intermission toward insatiable lusts, fights with them in the darkness, examines their sin, and in a wondrous manner stirs up and agitates the force of fire for their torment. But indeed, to souls whose spirit adheres to it, the mind will be present most kindly and very favorably; for it is accustomed to flow into the holy soul and to raise it to the light of wisdom; for it will be benevolent to good, pious, pure, religious, and holy humans; by its presence it brings them aid, so that they immediately know all things; it inclines them to give thanks and to bless piously; it makes them surely yield their body to its death, and to loathe the allurements of the senses, as those who clearly judge how lethal the enticements of the senses are; moreover, the mind itself, performing the duty of a gatekeeper, by no means permits those falling into the traps of the body to achieve their end; for it continually blocks the entrances through which foul flatteries are accustomed to flow, and extinguishes all the kindling of lusts. Hence *Hermes Trismegistus in Pymander, book 12: To whatever souls the mind presides, it illuminates them with its own brightness, resisting their evil habits, just as a learned Physician afflicts the body of a sick person with pains, by burning and cutting it for the sake of recovering health: in the same way the mind afflicts the voluptuous soul, so that it may pull out the roots of pleasure, and cleansing the body of evil, it procures the good of the soul in no other way than a Physician procures the health of the body.* Indeed, even a more wonderful [description] of this mind...

...divine efficacy in bodies in his fourth discourse of the *Pymander* <note>The *Pymander* (or *Poimandres*) is the first and most famous text in the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus</note>, where he speaks in these words: *Whoever is supported by this divine creation, based on the comparison of their works, are regarded as immortal rather than mortal; they embrace all things in their understanding—those on earth, in the sea, and whatever exists beyond them above the heavens. But because the actions of the blessed Mind are not granted to everyone—for though its essence is in the body together with the vital soul, yet if the soul with its spirit does not seek and love it, neglecting the sensory soul, the Mind will be absent and will refrain from divine actions—therefore, the method of reconciling this divine form so that it may work within the soul and not be idle must first be investigated. Hermes Trismegistus says in *Pymander* 4: *The lover of the body cannot be washed in the liquid of the Mind’s mixing-bowl* <note>original: "mentis crateris latice." The "Crater" or Mixing-Bowl is a Hermetic symbol for the gift of Mind/Reason offered by God to humanity</note>, *for unless a person hates their own body, they cannot love themselves. But as soon as they love not themselves but God himself, they will immediately obtain the Mind; and having finally attained this, they will obtain knowledge in its wake.* 

The sacred Scriptures seem to agree with this discourse of Hermes Trismegistus in many places. Hence Saint John says in his 1st Epistle, chapter 2: *One who loves the world does not have the love of the Father in them;* and in the same place, chapter 3: *The world does not know the children of God, because the children of God have not known the world; because the whole world is placed under the power of the evil one,* as in chapter 5. Similarly, in the 1st Epistle of Saint John, chapter 2: *Those affected by the concupiscence of the flesh do not have the love of the Father in them. And elsewhere: Concupiscence is everything that is in the world, which is not from the Father, but from the world.* From these things it is clear that the Mind is not present in those who are captured by the love of the body or worldly desire, because GOD does not "know" such people <note>In the sense of divine recognition or spiritual union</note>, but only the world knows them, insofar as their actions are occupied with worldly things.

# CHAPTER IV.
### *That the mind and reason of man are not subject to fate, and that the stars cannot impose necessity upon them.*

By "fate," the ancient Philosophers understood the operation of the seven Planets in the fixed stars. For whatever is ordained by divine providence from the Archetype <note>The original divine blueprint or "World of Ideas"</note> in the intellectual world, that thing is committed to execution by the fixed stars and the seven Planets in the visible world. This is also confirmed by Hermes Trismegistus in *Pymander* 1, calling *fate the disposition of the seven governors* <note>The "seven governors" refer to the seven classical planets: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>; *to which he asserts all animals,* <margin>* even,</margin> *except for man, are subject.* Yet he did not wish all men to be subject to fate; for those in whom the divine Mind is present are not subject to fate in the way others are. His words from *Pymander* 12 are these: *All men are subject to fate through generation and change; for the beginning and end of fate are these two: namely, birth and transformation. And men indeed suffer what fate has established; but rational men, to whom the Mind assists as a guide, do not suffer in the same way as the rest; for insofar as they stand apart from wickedness, they suffer no evil at all.* Whosoever therefore...

...*uses the rewards of the mind granted by God for what is proper, he differs in nothing from the immortals; indeed, released from the chains of the body, he is led by both to the chorus of the blessed, and at the same time to that of God.* The Platonists also put forward a discourse of this kind: *The Mind is above fate through providence; therefore it is neither affected by the influences of the heavenly bodies, nor by the qualities of natural things; religion alone, therefore, governs it.* <note>original: "Mens supra fatum est in providentia..." The author is citing the common Neoplatonic view that while the body is subject to the stars/astrology, the soul can rise above them through spiritual devotion.</note> But why shall we recite or cite the authorities of others further in this place, when the most evident reasons, drawn from the very core of pure philosophy, are at hand? These clearly demonstrate that the mind and reason of man dominate the stars and their influences, and that they are not subject to the actions of the visible heavens. Will it seem fair that a most eminent king should be governed by his subjects, or be subjected to their punishments and passions? It would indeed be unjust to be led by such an imagination: that the Creator could be forced by His creatures toward something against His will, or that the act and ray emanating immediately from Him—which is by no means separated from His divine essence but perpetually connected to it—should be subjected to creatures established and strengthened by that very Mind and Word.

What power, then, do the stars or creatures of the middle heaven <note>The "middle heaven" refers to the region of the planets and stars, situated between the Earth and the highest spiritual realm.</note> have to act upon the creatures of the higher heaven, and especially upon their Author and Creator? Doubtless, therefore, gifts are poured down from the Empyrean heaven <note>The Empyrean is the highest, most spiritual part of the universe, where God resides.</note> through the divine benevolence of the Creator, and are received in the desired manner; however, they are not thrown back upward by the creatures receiving them. For this would be to return ungratefully that which is freely received for oneself and for those below, and in the manner of the Prince of Darkness, to forget the Creator's benefit, to be carried on the wings of pride into the heights, and to foolishly seek the loftier kingdoms. Elsewhere, therefore, we have explained at great length that this matter is otherwise; where, in our *Mundane Music* <note>original: "Musica nostra mundana." This refers to Fludd's earlier work on the musical and harmonic proportions of the universe.</note>, we declared that the Sun, the commander of the middle heaven, received its gifts from the sublimity of the Empyrean heaven—God the Creator so willing—through the power of the Diapason <term>Diapason: the Greek term for an octave, signifying the most perfect harmonic resonance between two different levels of existence</term> harmony. In this way, out of its abundance, it might pour a portion of life every day, hour, and minute into the lower regions, likewise through the power of the Diapason harmony, into the earth. 

From this it is clear that the lower region of the world receives its measure of life from the middle region in the same way the middle receives from the superior. Now it would be considered absurd if anyone said that the Sun and the middle heaven receive their life and formal nourishment from the lower region, or the supreme from the middle—just as if one were to infer that the cause proceeds from its effect, or the beginning from its result. For the Holy Scriptures recognize the distinction of the works of the first three days of creation. 

Briefly, the matter stands thus: The human soul, which we have declared above to be the internal man, is composed of three portions derived from a threefold heaven, as we have said. It acquired the nobler portion of its composition from the Empyrean heaven—indeed, immediately from God Himself—carried in the Empyrean spirit; namely, the ray of the Mind sitting in the rational chariot. <note>The "rational chariot" is a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where the soul is compared to a charioteer controlling two horses.</note> Its middle portion, which gives life to the body, acquired its power from the ethereal heaven; this, with its own spirit, receives the spirit of reason along with its master. Furthermore, we have previously explained clearly enough that the lowest portion of the soul, composed of the subtle essence of the elements, is the disposition of the animal and sensitive soul. 

Now indeed, it is manifest from what has been said that the nature of the middle heaven is ruled by the nature of the highest heaven, and that in turn by the essence of God: no differently than how the lowest and elemental nature is governed by the higher ones joined together. From this it follows that if the middle portion of the soul adheres to its lower member, the divine Mind itself will refuse to have communication with it. Whence it follows that the influences and operations of the stars will have the fullest dominance over such a soul and its entire body; since that portion of the soul will be devoid of the higher essences of the stars, and the soul will not be found present in its operations. For when the middle soul enters into a kind of covenant in this way with the ethereal spirit or the elemental soul, it consists of the true substance and form of the middle heaven, with its spirit...

...will be rejected with force. For what else does that divine Philosopher <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, mentioned on the previous page.</note> seem to mean, other than that those twelve Avengers—or impieties and authors of crime, which he recognizes as the effects of the signs of the Zodiac—are expelled from man by the presence of the Mind? This Mind draws down with it the properties of the nine virtues of the empyrean heaven, or the nine orders of intelligences (which we said above compose the number ten). 

In this way, the choir of Angels drove back and defeated Lucifer with his rebellious crowd. Thus:
*   The **Seraphim** bring the knowledge of God, by whose assistance Ignorance is driven out.
*   The **Cherubim** bring an abundance of the sciences and the gift of God’s wisdom and charity, by which Sorrow is compelled to go into exile, as is Inconstancy; for the fullness of science and wisdom, and the gift of charity (which is the gift of faith), give birth to constancy, and are said to lure men away from worldly desire toward the super-celestial.
*   The **Thrones** possess the gift of true and right judgment, whence all Injustice is removed by their presence.
*   The **Dominations** cause men to excel in spiritual power and to carry themselves bravely in spiritual battle; by their virtue, the soul fights spiritually against the temptations of the flesh, luxury, and deceptions.
*   The order of **Powers** follows these, denoting character, reverence, and humility; by the virtue of humility, Envy is removed.
*   The **Angelic** orders of **Virtues** give illumination and purification; by their virtue, frauds and illusions are removed, and the presence of their properties uproots fallacies; similarly, they purge the soul of all affections of anger.

*Dionysius* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose "Celestial Hierarchy" defined the nine orders of angels.</note> also relates that the **Archangels**, who hold the eighth order, have the duty and office of driving away the malignant Demons who take pleasure in humans, hindering them so they may no longer agitate men. For no affection is found in man more vehement in its recklessness than that which is stirred up by the Devil. Indeed, he tried Job—that chosen man—by these ways and means, striving to move and irritate him with recklessness so that, finally blinded by it, he might strike God with blasphemies. 

Finally, the **Angels**, who constitute the ninth and last order of God’s messengers, perform such a duty as to restrain the malice of the world. By the virtue of divine love, with which they are full, they uproot the malice of men and assist the pious against the malice of their enemies, as is found in *Genesis 32, 2 Maccabees, and Tobit, etc.* Indeed, these are said to remove not only the malice of men, but also their diseases.

From these things, therefore, the intention of the Philosopher can be discerned: namely, that by the virtue of the mind, with its nine ministers, the malice of the Zodiac is most easily driven back. This happens by the virtue of the ten powers, by whose presence the regeneration of the internal man occurs—a thing which he seems to explain elsewhere in express words: *“You have understood,”* he says, *“my son, the manner of this regeneration; the intellectual regeneration is composed of the present number ten, which rejects the number twelve.”* <note>original: "Intellexisti, inquiens, fili mi, regenerationis ipsius modum, denario præsenti numero intellectualis regeneratio composita est, quæ duodenarium numerum rejicit." This refers to the ten divine virtues overcoming the twelve zodiacal vices.</note> 

Moreover, he left us the way and method by which he recognized this mystery in these words: *“And that,”* he says, *“we have contemplated from generation itself. For whoever, on account of the goodness of generation which is according to God, loses corporeal sense—that is, whose intermediate spirit adheres more to the mind and not to the sensitive soul—knows himself to be composed of divine things; and having now been made wise, he rejoices with his whole mind in divine power.”* <note>original: "Idá, inquit ille, ex ipsa generatione speculati sumus..." This describes a mystical state where the soul detaches from physical senses to realize its divine nature.</note>

Oh, how great is the act of the Mind which is exercised through the innermost powers! For it is in heaven, on earth, in water, in air, in animals, and in trees; but in men it is indeed more immense. And finally, before the body, after the body, and wherever it is truly worshipped and sincerely apprehended, there it always acts, revealing all vices and the illusions of the Devil (*by producing the truth*) and driving them away once revealed. 

Nor should it seem strange to you, O readers, that I, along with *Mercurius Trismegistus*, have called the Zodiac a "dwelling-place" of the aforementioned horrible Avengers. For it is also read in the Holy Scriptures that the Devil is the prince of the visible and material world, who desires to possess the summit of his visible kingdom no less than the Creator of things is believed to sit constantly at the peak of the universal periphery.

### CHAPTER V.

->That the mind and the soul adhering to the mind are not subject<-

Since the mind is a true act of God arising from the very essence of God (to use the words of <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note>) and in no way divided from the divine nature, as was declared above; similarly, since it is the prince and, as it were, the center of all things, and (if it is permitted to say so) according to the opinion of Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pimander*, book 12, and <term>Synesius</term><note>A 4th-century philosopher and bishop known for blending Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> in his 3rd *Hymn*, the very soul of the Creator itself, so that it can effect whatever it wishes; for it rules over all, indeed even over law itself: it follows from this that it alone acts upon all things, and that all things suffer its actions (while the mind itself remains inviolable according to the nature of God). It is immobile and yet the "first mover" of things, and subject to the actions of none. For since it alone is the <term>actuality</term><note>The original Latin *actus* refers to "activity" or "reality" as opposed to "potentiality."</note> of things, other things cannot act unless they have the power of acting from the mind itself. Therefore, it is necessary either that the mind acts upon itself and consequently tolerates its own actions, or that it suffers in no other way. But truly, since every action occurs in a subject or a "patient" <note>The "patient" is the entity that receives an action, from the Latin *pati* meaning "to suffer" or "to undergo."</note> fit to receive the impressions of an act, and which is in some way contrary to the agent; therefore, the mind cannot act upon itself as a subject capable of <term>passion</term><note>In this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force, rather than just an emotion.</note>. First, because its entire entity is identity and formal, and it has nothing of matter within itself, nothing subject to passion, and nothing resisting its own nature, but rather its parts are homogeneous, and it is unity itself; for this reason, no contrariety is observed to exist within it. Hence it is that the Philosophers held that no pure element acts within its own sphere; rather, they said its actions are impressed upon a sphere contrary to it by nature. Much more so, then, do we affirm that the mind neither acts upon nor suffers within itself; insofar as it is the purest and God-like form proceeding immediately from God without any admixture of material spirit, which effects all things in this world and never suffers anything. Regarding this portion of the soul, <term>Iamblichus</term><note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul and theurgy.</note> speaks thus:

> *The soul in bodies is pure, and is not touched by disturbances, since it is a supernatural, unbegotten life; nor is it touched by any dissolving pain, since it is outside of every body.* <note>original: "Anima in corporibus pura est..."</note>

And in another place:

> *Since the soul is an individual and uniform essence, remaining incorporeal in itself and communicating nothing with the body, it surely does not admit the passions of division or alteration or any mutation.* <note>original: "Cum anima sit individua..."</note>

<term>Proclus</term><note>One of the last major Greek classical philosophers, who headed the Platonic Academy in Athens.</note> also seems to affirm that the middle soul itself does not suffer, but that all passions proceed from the body and are in no way present in the soul: *The passions of the body*, he says, *do not pass through into the soul, hence even though death belongs to the body, it is not an evil for the soul.* I can never sufficiently praise or admire his opinion, which is certainly full of divinity, since it draws an argument from the "greater" passion to prove that "lesser" ones harm the soul even less—as if he had said: "not the lesser, because not even the greater." For if the passion of death, which is the greatest of all and dissolves the very chains of the body, effects nothing toward the disturbance of the soul, but rather leads to its liberation from prison, the soul will be disturbed much less by the lighter afflictions of the body. But to respond to his argument, which was crafted with a marvelous sharpness of wit, by proving that the matter does not stand absolutely as he thought: we say that this liberty of the middle soul is not of itself, but because of its connection with the divine mind. Hence, if its spirit adheres to the mind and embraces the rays of divine light, it feels the evils of the body in no way; but rather delights in its disturbances, so that when the body is finally dissolved, the soul may be freed all the sooner from its chains. Hence <term>Porphyry</term><note>A student of Plotinus and a major figure in Neoplatonism.</note> says that *the soul, though always awake by itself, nevertheless sleeps, as it were, in the body.* And Proclus relates that *souls in bodies grow sick and, as it were, become delirious.* But, if indeed that intermediate spirit, the [middle] soul...

And then its <term>lucid soul</term><note>Latin: *anima lucida*; the higher, light-filled part of the soul's nature.</note> or <term>ray of nature</term><note>Latin: *radius naturae*; the spark of divinity within a human being.</note>—following its ethereal course by adhering to this disobedient, intermediary spirit—will perceive many deceptions and illusions of darkness as if looking into a mirror, and it will be troubled by the sight of them. ## CHAPTER VI.

->*(Why the human mind and reason inhabit the upper region of the Microcosm, the Empyrean heaven?)*<-

In our little book on the external man, it was shown that he is divided into three regions according to the arrangement of the <term>Macrocosm</term><note>The "Great World" or the universe at large.</note>, the upper of which we have—not without the most evident reason—compared to the <term>Empyrean heaven</term><note>The highest, most spiritual part of the heavens, often associated with pure light and fire.</note>. For just as in the Empyrean heaven of the Macrocosm there exists the natural seat and home of the Divine Mind and the rational spirit, according to the opinions of the most learned philosophers and theologians, so too is it observed by the more learned philosophers and physicians that the place and dwelling-room of reason and intellect is located in the head, or the upper region of the <term>Microcosm</term><note>The "Little World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. Indeed, even if we look at common experiments: a sphere fashioned from hollow glass, no matter how one tries to forcibly submerge it in water, will always be found to rise back up to its natural place; for the nature of its contents (namely, air) is to float upon the water. We perceive this same thing in wood, because of its airy and fiery disposition. This, therefore, is the reason why the mind, since it is the supreme of all things, possesses the upper part of the place in which it resides.

For although the rational or Empyrean spirit is its vehicle, and the <term>World Soul</term><note>Latin: *anima mundana*; the spiritual essence that animates the entire universe.</note> with its ethereal spirit is in turn the chariot of the intellectual spirit, and for all these the air is like a wagon in which the mind is introduced into the body with the others—nevertheless, the human mind possesses the peak of the entire animal semi-diameter. Like a most divine king or emperor, it always occupies the higher seat, both in the part of the internal man and the external. It seems to claim for itself the office of a pilot, cutting the corporeal ship through the fluctuating disturbances of the world and the tempestuous and stormy waves of this life, directing it safely to the land and the harbor of happiness—provided that its other ministers (namely, reason, life, the natural spirit, and the senses) are made obedient to it. 

But if they are rebellious and do not listen to the pilot's commands, they will undoubtedly cause an inevitable and fatal shipwreck for themselves, in which they will be swallowed up in the abyss of the world-sea with their bodily ship or skiff, and be gulped down by the living gap of darkness. Meanwhile, however, the pilot or governor—seeking the heights on immortal wings—will return to his blessed fatherland with his rational spirit; for that spirit, as long as it is not subjected to fate, is usually obedient to him. 

Hence, just as the pilot of a ship sits in the upper part of the stern and directs the lower sailors in their business so that they may make their journey prosperously and favorably—and the sailors themselves move partly in the lower part of the stern and partly in the upper, as occasion demands—so also the mind inhabits the upper region of the human body. To its command, the other ministers (namely the vital soul and the natural and sensitive souls) are present and ready to carry out and expedite all its mandates with diligence. 

And truly, what more evident argument can be sought for the fact that the mind inhabits this upper region of man than that we see him standing more upright and <term>orthogonal</term><note>Standing at a right angle; perfectly vertical.</note> than all other animals? From this it is most manifest that in his summit and peak there exists a most eminent force and action that raises and lifts the senses themselves toward heaven—not unlike how very heavy bodies are perceived to be raised on high by the power of artificial fire. Indeed, so effective is this divine fire (which <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>Latin: *Merc. Trismeg.* A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note> asserts *is accustomed to put on a fiery garment as soon as it is separated from the body*) that not only the bodies of men...

## CHAPTER VII.

### *That the light throughout the entire world-sphere is the same, and likewise the Spirit is the same; and how light tends toward the purification and elevation of spirits on high.*

In many places previously cited in our <term>macrocosmic</term><note>The "Great World," referring to Fludd's earlier volume on the universe/cosmos.</note> book, we have abundantly and clearly revealed the brief and very close relationship of the light of each heaven. For we explained that the light of the supreme region of the world, created on the first day, is the icon or image of the divine mind; and that the secondary light, which informed the middle heaven on the second day, is like a ray or likeness of the former and superior one; and finally, the third is the idol and image of the second. Similarly, by the power of the superior light, the <term>rational or empyrean spirit</term><note>The highest form of spirit, associated with the intellect and the highest heaven.</note> was created and called the ray of the mind (which is the ray of God). Likewise, the middle spirit was made vital or ethereal (or the <term>quintessence</term><note>The "fifth element," a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>) by the power of the middle light, and is called the ray of the world, the <term>Soul of the World</term><note>original: "Anima mundi"; the animating principle of the entire universe.</note>, and active nature itself. Furthermore, by the act of the lowest light in the lowest spirit, the four elements were produced and distinguished on the third day, and it is called the ray of the elements, and as it were, the element of fire, or a thin portion of light leaping downward into those parts. Therefore, all these alterations come from the actions of divine light, whose entire effort is to purify the impure and refine the coarse. And by this action, the spirit of the universal world—which, according to the witness of <term>St. Peter</term><note>original: "Divo Petro"; referring to 2 Peter 3, where the apostle discusses the role of water and fire in the creation and destruction of the world.</note>, is nothing other than <term>Water</term>—is distinguished into regions differing in purity and impurity, thinness and thickness, and into the disposition of the four elements.

From these things, it is clear that the universal light of the world is unique, and of the same action and nature derived from the eternal source, and that the differences in its operations exist not in itself, but in the diversity of the resisting matter. For that which resists more strongly requires a stronger act, and that which is weaker in its opposition needs less impression; and yet the ratio of the action is always the same. Similarly, the reason for the "passion" <note>The state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> proceeds from the diversity of the matter, differing in thickness and thinness. For that which is dense and compact grants a place to the impressions of the agent with more difficulty. Hence it happens that celestial light, because of the minimal resistance of its opposing spirit, seems to warm us imperceptibly, even though it nonetheless excels in its luminous office. Thus also we see that the same light, because of the narrowing of its rays in a thick spirit, becomes and turns out to be a destructive fire, intolerable to the sense of touch. Indeed, we are taught that the more it penetrates toward the center of the earth, the more vehement its burning and destroying faculty becomes; for as its rays tend further downward, they gradually find thicker matter and are thus finally compressed in an ineffable manner. From this it follows that it burns with the greatest torment and produces common fire. Thus also, nothing makes the flame of fire visible other than the contraction of the rarer inflamed parts of the air, or the gathering into one of the rays of light that were hidden and dilated in the air. In this very way we also see that humid air, invisible in its thin nature, is condensed by contraction into a visible and palpable cloud,

From these facts, therefore, it is clear that the parts of the universal light do not differ from each other, but are of the same nature; accordingly, the cause of their difference regarding us is the diversity of their operation. Similarly, the entire matter of the world is the same, namely water; which, however, is known to differ according to the greater or lesser proportion of light found with it and in it. 

Hence, we teach that the inferior light acts upon its <term>aëreal spirit</term><note>The "spirit" or subtle substance found in the lowest, elementary region of the world.</note> according to its proportion, just as the middle light acts upon its own; and again, that the middle light acts upon its <term>ethereal spirit</term><note>The subtle substance of the middle heaven, where the stars and planets reside.</note> no differently than the light of the higher heaven acts upon its own. Therefore, the entire difference consists in this: the inferior light is more resisted because of its meager proportion and the multitude of matter; however, the middle light is resisted less because of its equality with the ethereal spirit (the nature of which we showed above through the balanced fitting of the <term>formal and material pyramids</term><note>A core concept in Fludd’s philosophy where a pyramid of Light/Form descends from God and a pyramid of Matter/Darkness ascends from the earth; where they meet in equal proportion is the middle heaven.</note>), since it finds the spirit obedient to it in the same proportion. Furthermore, the superior light, being excellently abundant, acts with still less or the least struggle upon the <term>empyrean spirit</term><note>The highest, most refined spirit of the third heaven, the dwelling place of God and angels.</note>, because that spirit is very sparse, and for that reason is called incorporeal and plainly metaphysical—that is, placed beyond the boundaries of nature.

And this is that most evident reason by which men, illuminated by divine mystery—and for whom, consequently, God is not demonstrated <term>a priori</term><note>Reasoning from cause to effect; from the nature of God down to the world.</note>—ascend as if by a ladder <term>a posteriori</term><note>Reasoning from effects back to their cause; from the physical world up to God.</note> to reach the knowledge of God. For through the hidden operations of water with fire, which we observe here on earth, we can divine the effects of the middle light in its spirit; and thus also, from the manifest actions of the Sun in the air, it will not be impossible to judge the power of the primary light in the secondary spirit. Finally, once the rationale for the action of the middle light with its spirit is discovered, the diligent inquirer will not be entirely denied the ability to effectively behold the actions of the higher heaven and their effects to some extent. 

And so, at last, it will be perceived that the light, which has gone forth from the divine source, tends toward the purification, cleansing, and thinning of matter, and consequently toward its elevation and exaltation from a gross thing to a subtle one, and from a place subject to corruption to a seat most full of formal light, which satisfies its every desire. For the disposition of the divine essence is kind and inclined to always work toward the preservation, salvation, and redemption of things, and their promotion from darkness into the regions of light; thus, it is always engaged in the reformation of deformed things, eager to lead the arrangements of ugly things back into beauty, to reveal the deceptions of darkness and strife to the world, to confer and distribute the gifts of its kindness to each one, and finally to seal all things with the characters of its divine love.

Similarly, the whole **matter of the world** is the same, namely **water**; <note>In Fludd’s cosmology, "water" refers to the primal, unformed matter of the universe mentioned in Genesis, which is later shaped by light.</note> which, however, is known to differ according to the greater or lesser proportion of light found with it and within it. 

Hence, therefore, we teach that the **inferior light** acts upon its **aerial spirit** in the same proportion as the **middle light** acts upon its own; and again, that the middle light acts upon its **ethereal spirit** no differently than the light of the **superior heaven** acts upon its own. Consequently, the entire difference consists in this: that the inferior light is more resisted because of its meager proportion and the multitude of matter; however, the middle light is resisted less because of its equality with the ethereal spirit (the nature of which we showed above through the consistent adaptation of the formal and material pyramids), seeing as it finds a spirit obedient to it in the same proportion. For through the hidden operations of water with fire, which we observe here on earth, we can divine the effects of the middle light in its spirit; and thus also from the manifest actions of the Sun in the air, it will not be impossible to judge the power of the primary light in the secondary spirit. Finally, once the reason for the action of the middle light with its spirit is found, the diligent inquirer will not be entirely denied the ability to effectively behold, to some extent, the actions of the superior heaven and their effects. 

In this way, it will at last be perceived that the light which has gone forth from the divine source tends toward the purification, cleansing, and thinning of matter, and consequently toward its elevation and exaltation from the coarse to the subtle, and from a place subject to corruption to a seat most full of formal light, which may satisfy its every appetite. For the disposition of the divine essence is kind and inclined to always work toward the preservation, salvation, and redemption of things, and their promotion from darkness into the regions of light. Thus, it is always occupied in the reformation of deformed things, longing to lead the dispositions of base things back into beauty, to reveal the delusions of darkness and strife to the world, to bestow and distribute the gifts of its kindness to each one, and finally to seal all things with the characters of its own divine love. 

Do we not, therefore, observe in this elementary region that the flame of fire, by natural instinct, disregarding things superior and sublime, seeks the lower things with all its effort? Nor indeed can we turn it from this inclination without its sensible extinction. ## CHAPTER VIII.

->*On the unequal proportion of the body and the radiant soul, and that light labors*<-
->*only toward the elevation of the body toward heaven and the purging*<-
->*of its impurity here on earth.*<-

The matter of the body stands in proportion to its radiant soul just as the spirit of the lowest region of the world relates to its own light; which we stated earlier is found in a <term>sesquialterate proportion</term><note>original: "proportione sesquialtera"; traditionally a 3:2 ratio in music and mathematics, though the author here applies it to the structural imbalance between spiritual light and material substance.</note>: namely, that in that region, one part of light and three parts of <term>material Spirit</term><note>The subtle, vaporous substance that serves as the bridge between the physical body and the soul.</note> are found. From this it follows that the body is said to weigh down the soul and hinder it in its actions; so much so, indeed, that it does not allow the soul to accomplish what it desires, and it strives with all its might against the soul's actions, which aim to lift the body on high. 

That the soul is weaker in the body by many degrees than matter is shown by experiment. For if someone descends from a mountain, this motion is very suitable for the body, since every heavy thing, by a certain natural instinct, tends downward; indeed, the <term>external man</term><note>The physical, sensory body, which Fludd distinguishes from the "internal man" or the spiritual intellect.</note> rejoices because the descent seems easy to him. Yet this motion is against the nature and disposition of the soul, as was shown in the example of fire and the <term>spindle</term><note>original: "fuso"; likely referring to a physical demonstration mentioned in a previous chapter where a spinning or burning object illustrates the natural upward movement of light and fire.</note>. 

But in the ascent of a mountain, the external man is worn out, and the life-giving soul (which, however, is merely like a spark) acts vehemently and with all its strength to elevate that heavy weight, making its own <term>dwelling-place</term><note>A metaphorical term for the physical body which houses the soul.</note> labor toward this end. From this it is manifest that the mass of the body exceeds the measure of its radiant soul by many proportions; for the whole man seems to take pleasure in descent, which happens according to the appetite of matter, but is weighed down by ascent, which is according to the desire of light. 

Truly, if the power of the radiant soul were more abundant than the mass of the body, then conversely, man would be burdened by descent and would rejoice in his ascent; for the radiant soul, with every effort of nature, tends upward—indeed, even the Spirit itself vehemently desires to ascend upward with the spark of its light, which is always ready for such a task, as was said regarding the elevation of the <term>lit spindle</term><note>original: "fusi accensi"; likely a reference to a laboratory experiment or a philosophical model involving a burning wick or rotating device that moves upward.</note>. And indeed, this very point is demonstrated by the following experiment.

From these examples, it is clear that not only light but also its vehicle <note>The "vehicle" refers to the subtle matter or spirit that carries the divine light into the physical world.</note> tends toward the exaltation <note>In Fludd’s terminology, "exaltation" means both physical lifting and spiritual refinement or upward motion.</note> of bodies. Indeed, this is true to such an extent that even when this force cannot fully complete its work due to its own smallness, it nonetheless moves bodies and animals—which are supported by columns or feet—from side to side (to the right and left), forward and backward, or up and down, in the manner already described. But leaving aside these artificial devices, we also observe the same arrangement in plants; for in them, portions of light rising from the earth lift themselves upward toward their natural place along with their entire physical mass, aided by the rays of the Sun.

*And to now persist in our investigation of animals: I heard from a certain maidservant that once, because of its remarkable greed, she caught an older and larger cat <note>original: "cattam seu felem."</note> in the very act of gluttony. Finding herself without any other weapon but unwilling to let the opportunity slip through her hands, she attempted to crush and suffocate it by trampling it harshly with her feet. But when she stood upright with one foot placed on the cat’s throat and the other pressed firmly over its heart—tormenting and afflicting the wretched little creature without any pity in a deadly war against its voracious gullet—she perceived such great force in its body, and such vigor and efficacy in that tiny portion and spark of light or "act" <term>actus</term><note>In the philosophy of this era, "act" or "actuality" refers to the active, formal principle that gives life and motion to matter, as opposed to "potency" or passive matter.</note> enclosed within it, that she was struck with a kind of wonder. She continually feared that, despite her great weight, she might be lifted high and thrown down; she felt the immense vigor of the enclosed Spirit driving upward and lifting the mass of her own body.*

From these things, therefore, it is most evident that the **vital Spirit**, along with its active light, possesses the greatest power. This is true not only in man-made things—where **saltpeter** <term>sal nitri</term><note>Niter or saltpeter was viewed by alchemists as "congealed air" or a physical form of the universal life-force found in the atmosphere; its explosive nature in gunpowder was seen as proof of its hidden power.</note> takes the place of the aerial spirits (since it is nothing other than frozen air) and the nature of **sulfur** serves the role of light, whose luminous nature, when brought into action, is moved by the power of that Spirit—but also in vegetable...

TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VII.

## CHAPTER IX.
### *On the communication of human souls.*

From the preceding points, it may seem difficult to some—at least to those who look only with their physical eyes—to believe that the soul of one person, through the power of its spiritual radiance, could communicate and hold intimacy with the soul of another person even at a great distance, just as one person is accustomed to converse with another while still veiled and obscured by the "shadow of the flesh" <note>This refers to the physical body acting as a barrier to spiritual perception.</note>. Indeed, even the light of the sun, from which the "middle soul" <term>middle soul [anima media]: in Fludd's philosophy, the soul is the mediating layer between the divine mind and the physical body</term> of a creature is derived, can be hidden and obscured by an obstacle of thin, dark substance—much less impenetrable than the human body—as we see during rainy weather. How much more so, then, is the soul of man, which has descended from heaven, obscured? Following the sayings of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg." Referring to the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the *Hermetica*.</note>: *The soul, stripped of its higher natures and conscious of the Good, but deprived of eyes, entangles itself in bodily passions*, etc. It is clear that the soul, covered by the bulk of the body, is as if destitute of eyes, so that it cannot see things that are outside itself or in the darkness.

To these doubts we respond: this is indeed how things stand if we consider the soul only insofar as it regards "life" <note>i.e., the basic biological life-force</note>, which is merely the middle portion in the composition of the human soul. However, insofar as the soul is united with its mistress, the Mind <term>Mind [Mens]: the highest, divine part of the human being that directly reflects God's light</term>—without which a human soul cannot truly exist—the walls of the body can no more compress and restrain its rays than the water of a crystal-clear stream can prevent solar rays from penetrating to the very bottom. For Hermes Trismegistus says *that the Mind can be raised by its own sharp edge to the things above.* And elsewhere he assigns the reason, namely in *Pimander 12*: *Because the Mind is in no way divided from the essence of God, but is instead connected to it in the same way that light is connected to the body of the sun.* Therefore, he called the Mind "God in men," and says *that the humanity of men is closest to divinity*; hence he called men "His good spirits" <note>original: "Daemones ejus bonos"</note> and "mortal Gods."

From these points it is manifest that the "sharp edge" of the human mind and the rays of its light are so subtle and penetrating that the pores of the body, or its dark mass, can in no way hinder them from penetrating the very throne of the Creator and being present everywhere throughout the world. Hence it happens, as that same philosopher testifies, *that by the presence of the Mind, which he calls the nature of God, man encompasses with his intelligence everything that is on the earth and in the sea, and whatever exists beyond those things which are above the heaven; and he even raises himself up so that he may gaze upon the Good itself.*

The middle soul, therefore, is raised up by this supreme and God-like gift; with the Mind acting as a guide and opening the dark pores, the soul pours out its rays invisibly here and there toward external things. This is not at all surprising, since that Mind is an "act" <note>In the Aristotelian sense of *actus*, an active, perfecting force.</note> proceeding immediately from God, to whom (to speak with the Royal Psalmist <note>Referring to King David and Psalm 139.</note>) *darkness is not dark, but the night is as clear to Him as the day itself.* And this ray of God is like a spark of His divine wisdom, without which it is impossible for the human soul to judge the manifest things before its eyes, much less those things which are in heaven. 

The truth of this matter can be seen clearly from the following discourse of the Wise Man <note>Referring to the Book of Wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon.</note> in *Wisdom 9:15*: *The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things; and we find it difficult to judge the things that are on earth, and we find with labor those things that are in our sight: but who shall search out the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your mind, unless you have given wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from the highest*, etc. It is necessary, therefore, that the spark of the divine ray enclosed within man be refreshed from on high; by its abundance, a regeneration occurs, creating a perfect union between the augmented Mind and the mediating Spirit. From this comes prophecy and the foretelling of events occurring in remote places—which is why the Prophets were commonly called "Seers." From this also comes the truth of dreams and the correct explanation of things through visions; because by the power of that spiritual and invisible splendor, united to the rays of the two lower portions, the whole of the soul...

<summary>Fludd argues that while the physical body can obscure the "vital" soul, the higher "Mind" is a divine spark that can penetrate any physical barrier to communicate across distances and access heavenly wisdom. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the spiritual mechanics of the human soul, moving from the soul's internal state to its ability to project its power outward and communicate with other souls across vast distances, similar to how light or planetary influences travel.</meta>

->ON THE INTERNAL MICROCOSM IN THE EXTERNAL WORLD<-

The power of the human soul is emitted from the human body in no other way than the visible light and rays of the Sun are emitted from the solar body. Thus, a person staying in *England* can send a ray of their soul—like a messenger—to *Rome*, or to *the Indies*, or elsewhere, even in this very instant, without any obstacle. This occurs so that, with the will leading the way, one is able to see and meditate upon those things in distant parts through the "eyes of contemplation" (which are truly spiritual) just as we gaze at things in our immediate vicinity with our physical eyes. 

Indeed, what is more, the soul of one person can and often does speak to the soul of another through its radiations and "aspects" <note>original: "aspectus," a term referring here both to a spiritual gaze and the astrological concept of how celestial bodies "look" at each other</note> via a spiritual mouth. This is no different than how the light of one candle can be brought together and joined with the rays of light from another. But because of the density <note>original: "stupiditatem," implying a lack of sensitivity or a "dullness" of the physical senses</note> of our bodily composition, we cannot discern or perceive these mysteries. Hence it happens that, looking upon these things with a dull and blunted sense, we pronounce them frivolous and impossible, calling them sheer folly and vanity. 

And yet, we perceive with our open eyes a flame leaping out from a piece of dark, burning wood, illuminating everything in the black night with its light; we see it move the intervening spirit or air by its presence. We see a lit candle, in its proper proportion, cause images drawn on paper to move about <note>Likely a reference to early optical devices like a magic lantern or shadow puppets</note>. Without a doubt, the candle has a certain "whisper" within the moist medium or vehicle of its light, just as we can gather from the crackling sound a flame makes when it mixes with the air. But because it is denied to our coarse ears to hear such things—or at least to understand what is heard—we foolishly reject them. This is despite the testimony of *Solomon*, the wisest of all men, in the place cited above: 

> *The soul cannot perceive the secrets of the mind unless illumination from on high is present.* 

But we cannot persuade ourselves that any things truly exist unless we see them, and like *Thomas* <note>Referring to "Doubting Thomas" from the Gospel of John, who required physical touch to believe in the Resurrection</note>, we do not believe what we have not touched. 

Are we not taught by daily experience that wonderful effects are poured into these lower realms from the "applications" of the rays of the Planets and stars—namely from the sextile, square, or trine aspect, and similarly from opposition and conjunction? It is as if there were a certain consultation of light with light concerning things that have happened on earth, or are happening presently. Yet fools are most accustomed to cry out in derision: "What have we to do with the sky and the stars?" These are ungrateful men who reject the knowledge and recognition of their own "parents" <note>Fludd views the celestial bodies as the macrocosmic parents of the human microcosm</note> and impudently cast them aside; they are rebels against God their Creator, thinking that the most excellent ornament of His "machine" <note>The universe</note> is of no use and entirely empty. 

What, finally, is your physical speech but a proportional discourse of the mind? It is expressed through a physical instrument by means of sensible sound and tone so that the bodies of others (mediated by their souls) can understand the intention of the speaker's mind. For the body receiving such sounds cannot distinguish them without its own rational soul. Do you wish, therefore, for the intent of this speech to come from the soul as the "mover," or from the instrument? 

Therefore, anyone who denies the communication of souls should be judged most unworthy of reason. For these "lights" are far more subtle, excellent, and rational than the lights or fires that are observed to act so vividly upon these lower things. Indeed, the actions of the lights and rays of the stars (which create such admirable and pregnant aspects) are surpassed by many degrees by the "lights" of the soul, insofar as they produce the mind. In this, the human soul is to be equated even with the Angels; no philosopher or theologian will deny their communication and "intuitive discourse" with one another, as this same thing is found in the prophecy of *Daniel* and elsewhere. 

When these things are examined exactly, it will appear clearly that human souls have a communication and irradiation (or similar "aspect") among themselves—some with others—by virtue of the divine ray. This is a connection that even some of the lights of the celestial stars do not have with other stars. It is recognized that souls share a spiritual whisper or intuitive discourse among themselves, no less than the Angels who speak to one another in their own manner. From this also arises the wonderful power of the human soul in the matter of Geomancy <term>Geomancy: a traditional method of divination using patterns of points often associated with the element of Earth</term>, namely in the detection of theft—

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VII.

...demonstration of the state of life or death of someone living far away. *As for myself, while I was living in Oxford, I was once asked by a certain friend of mine, Mr. Cox, about his brother who was then a soldier following the wars in Ireland. With my mind calm, undisturbed, and entirely focused on the task, I watched my hand be guided in such a way that, once the points were cast and the Geomantic figure <note>original: "figura Geomantica." Geomancy was a popular Renaissance method of divination that involved making marks in the earth or on paper and interpreting the resulting patterns.</note> was constructed, I could indicate through the information provided to my soul that his brother had been killed in the war, having been pierced by wounds from behind. This occurred exactly as I predicted, as the event later proved; for he had been wounded by a weapon driven through his back, and eventually died from it.* But because we shall treat the wonderful operation of this science in its proper place elsewhere—where we shall declare it to be a most true science of the soul—we will omit those details here. Furthermore, it also happens sometimes, when this spiritual "vision" is somewhat hindered—either by too great a distance or by a defect and weakness of divine illumination—that the souls themselves leave their bodies for a short time, as if dead, and fly out until they encounter the radiation of the soul of the absent person whose health or business is in question. 

*This is a frequent occurrence among those in Biarmia <note>original: "Biarmia." A region mentioned in Northern sagas, usually identified with the shores of the White Sea in modern-day Russia, often associated with magic and shamanism in early modern literature.</note>, of whom Olaus Magnus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish writer and ecclesiastic famous for his descriptions of Northern European customs and folklore.</note> makes mention in his History. He notes that when someone approaches them to consult about the state of a far-distant friend, two men of this sort and caliber usually enter a certain chamber. There, with the doors closed, one of them handles a bronze serpent with one hand while holding a small hammer in the other; he strikes the serpent with his hammer while mixing in magical incantations. When this is done, the other man suddenly falls to the ground as if deprived of his soul. Then, after a significant interval of time, as the soul returns to his body, he rises, returning to the former health and integrity of his life, and truly recounts the state and health of the person living in those most remote places.*

*In the French Chronicles, we also find that a certain King, named Gontran <note>original: "Gontranus." Likely Guntram the Rich or Guntram of Burgundy (c. 532–592), a Merovingian king.</note>, while hunting, happened by chance to wander away from his company of hunters. Accompanied by only a single friend, he lay down exhausted under a great tree and eventually fell peacefully asleep with his head resting in the lap of that companion. During the time the king was sleeping, his companion noticed a very small creature—exceedingly thin and composed of barely visible air—exiting the King’s mouth. Closely observing its movement and path, he saw it hurrying toward a small stream, anxiously seeking a way to cross at some safe fording place. The companion then rose, drew his sword, and laid it across both banks, thus spreading a kind of bridge. The creature immediately hurried across to the other side of the water and entered a hole at the foot of a mountain. Staying there only a short time, it returned by the same path and re-entered the King’s body. It then happened that Gontran woke up of his own accord and told his companion that everything he had seen in his dream was exactly what the royal companion had seen happen to the small creature (or the "idea" <note>original: "idea," used here in the Platonic sense of a spiritual form or essence.</note> of the animal). Specifically, he reported that in his dream he had been greatly troubled by crossing a river, but finally, having found an iron bridge, he crossed the ford safely; he then entered a cave under an immense mountain and found an incomparable treasure there. Hearing his companion’s account of the little creature, the King entered the mountain through the cave and discovered a massive treasure there.* 

But truly, as the Supreme Spirit powerfully pours His divine impressions into the human soul, even greater things than these are accomplished; and indeed, these occur not by the powers of the soul leaving the body, but while they remain entirely within it. Thus Saint Paul confesses that he was "caught up to the third heaven"; thus the holy Prophets were accustomed to perceive the secrets of others, even in far distant places, and to see with the eyes of the mind—or rather, by the rays of the divine soul—as if by a certain holy splendor and love, as is demonstrated most abundantly in many places of the Holy Scriptures.

# CHAPTER X.

->*That the illumination of the mind, resulting from the inflow of the divine Spirit’s breath, is the cause of prophecy.*<-

---

Prophecy or Divination, according to the opinions of the ancient Philosophers, *is* that by which people of a holier order and way of life, being moved, both draw out the causes of present things and foresee the outcomes of future events. These Sages maintained that this oracular power descends into humans either from the Gods or from Daemons <note>original: "Dæmonibus." In this Neoplatonic context, "daemons" refers to intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not necessarily evil "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, for they taught that this divine spirit was breathed and infused by them. Indeed, their opinion seems to differ very little from the words of the Holy Scriptures. For in Deuteronomy 13:1, these words are written: *If there arises among you a Prophet, or one who says he has seen a dream, and predicts a sign or a wonder, etc., you shall not listen to the words of that Prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you.* Similarly: *But the prophet who shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die.* Deuteronomy 18:22. From this it is clear that the Pagan Philosophers understood by "Gods" the same thing that the Holy Bible understands by *Jehovah*—whether referring to the persons in the Trinity, or the one, only, and true God—and by "Daemons" the same thing the Holy Scriptures mean by *foreign gods*. And yet we also see that those intelligences cannot produce such wonders except by divine permission, since all divine spirit flows from God as from the highest source, and from nowhere else. Hence Jehovah said: *You shall not listen to the words of that dreamer or Prophet, for your God is testing you*; as if He had said: He has stirred up his ministers to test you. For Satan himself can do nothing against the permission of God, as is declared in the history of Job, and by these words of the Prophet Micaiah in 1 Kings 22 <note>original: "3. Reg. 22." In the Latin Vulgate Bible used by the author, 1 and 2 Kings are referred to as 3 and 4 Kings.</note>: *I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left. And Jehovah said: Who shall deceive Ahab King of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead? And one said one thing, and another said another. Then there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said: I will deceive him, etc. I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And Jehovah said: Thou shalt go forth, and also prevail, etc.* From this it is rendered manifest that no prophecies can occur without God's permission, and that the spirit of Prophecy proceeds either immediately from God himself, or mediately from one of his intelligences or spirits; these likewise act either with a lying spirit for the punishment of sins, or sometimes with a spirit producing true wonders and signs for the purpose of testing. But all prophecies proceeding immediately from God are always true and infallible, because *none of the words of God can fall fruitlessly to the earth.* Hence in 1 Samuel 3:19, a faithful Prophet is identified when none of his words fall to the ground. And in Deuteronomy 18:22: If a Prophet predicts in the name of Jehovah, and it does not happen, the Lord has not spoken this. But leaving these matters, let us return to our purpose. 

This act of divining happens, according to the *Platonists*, because of the descent or influence of higher minds into ours, which they call "illapses" <note>original: "illapsiones," meaning a gentle flowing-in or spiritual descent.</note>. And *Hermes Trismegistus* calls it *the sense of Daemons and the minds of Daemons*, whom the ancients called *Eurideas* and *Pythons*, who were accustomed to enter the bodies of men and use their voices and tongues for the prediction of future things. Of this kind were those *Pythonesses* <note>original: "fœminæ illæ Pythona." This refers to the Pythia, the priestess at the Oracle of Delphi.</note>, who, moved by the divine Spirit and as if snatched out of themselves, standing upon the tripod of the oracle located near the cave, brought forth the oracles of Apollo in a prophetic manner with a bold voice, just as one reads in *Diodorus Siculus* and others. Authors testify that those ten *Sibyls* were possessed by a spirit of this kind, who are said to have left behind many poems written concerning the God Christ. And that *Merlin, the eternal glory of England*, whose like...
