# TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VII.

...[Merlin], whom Europe has never produced in any other age, expressed many wonders by the power of this divine spirit and prophesied in a miraculous manner about the future affairs of England—not by the help and power of the Devil, as fools claim, but by the true Spirit. Indeed, he was endowed with the truest proof of a Prophet designated above: namely, that almost none of his words fell to the ground. For the words of true Prophets are arranged by God; indeed, the Spirit of God, entering into the Prophets, uses their tongues and voices as instruments or organs to make his future will known to mankind. And from this it follows that a Prophet cannot go beyond the command of Jehovah, doing either a good thing or a bad thing, as is held in *Numbers 24:13.* *For the Prophet does that which Jehovah has declared to him, and nothing besides. Numbers 22:2 and 20.*

As for what the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who believed in a hierarchy of spirits connecting the human and divine.</note> said—that prophecy occurs through the inflows and descent of spirits or minds into our own minds—this also seems to be confirmed by Holy Scripture in many places. For it is said of Balaam: *The spirit of Jehovah was present with him, that is, the man with open eyes, who saw the vision of the Almighty while falling down, but with his eyes uncovered,* that is, gifted with the light of the divine spirit. *And falling down,* this means being snatched outside of oneself <term>rapture: a state of being "carried away" or "caught up" by divine power</term>, with the faculties of the senses falling away: which is the method of seeing the visions of God.

It must therefore be known that, according to the Philosophers, there are three kinds of divination, distinguished by a threefold diverse action of the divine Spirit in man: namely, *Fury* <note>original: "Furor." In this context, it refers to a "divine madness" or inspired frenzy rather than anger.</note>, *Rapture* or *Ecstasy*; under which vision and *dream* are included. And we gather this same thing from the sacred book of *Numbers 12*, where it is declared *that Jehovah makes himself known to Prophets either through a vision or by speaking to them in a dream*; just as this is also proven by infinite examples from the Holy Scriptures. Likewise, that spirit drives those Prophets in a manner that is insane and furious to us. For it is read in *1 Samuel 19:24* concerning Saul: *But stripping off his clothes, he acted in a prophetic manner; and so he lay down naked before Samuel all that day and all that night.* <note>Fludd interprets Saul's nakedness and "insane" behavior as signs of being completely possessed by the Holy Spirit, causing him to ignore physical decorum.</note> Similarly, for a fuller proof of the inflow of the Spirit of God, Samuel said to Saul in *1 Samuel 10:5*: *And the Spirit of Jehovah will rush upon you, so that you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man.*

We could also point out many other passages from the sacred writings here concerning the descent and infusion of the Holy Spirit into men of pious life, but since these are hidden from no one well-versed in the scriptures, we think they should be bypassed here, so that we may hasten to our main purpose. We have therefore laid those things which have already been said as the foundation of our discourse, so that we may better explain, according to our intent, the power of the divine mind in men and its immense familiarity with the Spirit of Jehovah, and thus finally produce the reasoning behind prophecy and the true prediction of future events.

But we are taught in *Numbers 11:25* that true prophecy occurs and proceeds solely by the benefit of the divine Spirit. We also gather from *Numbers 12:7* that they [the prophets] explained God to us through prophecies by means of riddles and likenesses. However, we will briefly explain how these things happen according to the capacity of our intellect. *Hermes* <note>original: "Mercurius." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of the Hermetic tradition.</note> says that *the mind is the very essence of God, or at least not divided from the essence of God, but rather connected to it in the same way that light is connected to the body of the Sun.* Indeed, he says that this mind in humans is God himself, and for that reason some among the number of men are "Gods," and their humanity exists as close as possible to divinity; in this, he does not differ much from the opinion of the Prophet Isaiah, whose words are of this sort: *Declare to us the things that are to come, and we will say that you are Gods.* <note>Isaiah 41:23.</note> Saint Paul also, agreeing with the philosopher Xystus <note>Likely referring to the "Sentences of Sextus," a collection of Pythagorean-Christian moral maxims attributed to "Xystus."</note>, calls the soul the temple of God. And the Platonists said that the spirits or minds of the Gods descend into the minds of men; as if they had said that the divine ray, or the mind, or the most holy Spirit (which *Hermes* called the *God of fire and the power of spirit*; and elsewhere, the *intellectual spirit*; and elsewhere, the *fiery spirit, by whose breath he asserts the first movable of the world is carried and led around*) descends into the human soul and joins itself with the mind derived from that same root. By this connection and union with higher things, the soul is so illuminated by the flash—

# ON THE INTERNAL MICROCOSM WITHIN THE EXTERNAL

...by divine power, so that it might, as if snatched from itself, make the man different than he was before, according to those words of *Samuel* cited earlier: *And you shall be changed into another man.* <note>1 Samuel 10:6. This refers to the transformation of Saul when the Spirit of God came upon him.</note> We see indeed by common experiment that the sun’s power can lift an eggshell filled with spirit or "May dew" <note>original: "spiritu seu rore Majali". Alchemists and natural philosophers believed dew collected in May contained a celestial "spirit" or life-force that could be drawn upward by the sun's heat.</note> upward. How much more, then, can this splendor illuminating the human spirit—enclosed within the shell of the skull—lift it on high with its spiritual rays? For the power of this divine presence is so great that it opens the eyes of man (which were closed by the fall of Adam) and makes them fit and suitable to see the vision of the Almighty. By expanding his spiritual ears, it makes him capable of receiving the Word, so that he may hear and understand the speeches of the mighty God and know the knowledge of the Most High, as in *Numbers 24:15-16.*

For such a soul, according to the discourse of *Hermes* in the *Pimander, Book 11*, is full of Mind and God; the *Platonists* truly called such a soul "standing and not falling." <note>A philosophical term for a soul that has achieved a stable, unchanging state of divine contemplation, no longer "falling" into the distractions of the material world.</note> But there are very few, says *Hermes Trismegistus*, who have attained such a Mind overflowing with light. For when such a Mind flows into a holy soul, it raises it to the light of true wisdom, as he himself testifies in *Pimander, Book 10.* And elsewhere he says: *Whoever is supported by this divine nature is considered immortal compared to mortals, for by their intelligence they embrace all things on earth, in the sea, and whatever exists beyond the heavens; thus they raise themselves so high that they behold the Good itself. Pimander, Book 4.*

What is more, in this "divine mirror," by the power of the illuminating light, we see the past, the future, and present things far distant from us. Hence *Balaam* said in *Numbers 24:17:* *I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near,* etc. Furthermore, through this divine presence, many miracles are performed by the Prophets. From this, *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on theurgy and how the divine interacts with the human soul.</note> suggests that those who are divinely inspired do not live a purely animal or natural life, but that their entire action belongs to God, depending simply upon God, and performed by God within the mind or soul as if in instruments devoid of any movement of their own. He asserts this is the reason why many Prophets are not burned when fire is applied to them; clearly, God, breathing within them, repels the fire. His words are confirmed in the Holy Scriptures in the story of *Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego* in *Daniel 3.* Some even, though they are burned, feel nothing, nor do they perceive stings, gnawings, or any torments.

Furthermore, he concludes that the actions of Prophets are not human, because they travel through impassable places. Thus *Peter* passed through the closed gate of the prison. *Christ* walked upon the waves of the sea. *Moses* was carried into the presence of God through fire, and *Elijah* was raised to heaven in a fiery chariot. *Moses* crossed the Red Sea, and *Joshua and Elijah* crossed the Jordan River miraculously. *Iamblichus* tells of a priest in *Cataballa* <note>An ancient city where priests were said to walk over hot coals without injury.</note> doing all these things. By these examples, he seems to argue that Prophets, during the time they are inspired, live neither a human nor an animal life (which uses senses and impulse), but a divine one; he claims their soul is "idle" because God is there in place of the soul, moving them as a more excellent soul.

But we cannot entirely agree or adhere to these reasons of *Iamblichus*. Rather, we think the human soul in an inspired man behaves and is moved by a motion similar to how the Planets are said to move naturally from east to west. For just as the <term>Primum Mobile: "First Mover," the outermost sphere in ancient astronomy that carries all other heavens with it</term>, as *Hermes Trismegistus* testifies, is carried rapidly from east to west by the breath of the divine Spirit, and yet the natural motion of the stars from west to east is not removed or extinguished; so it is in the <term>Microcosm: "Little World," a philosophical name for Man as a reflection of the universe</term> when stirred by the breath of the divine power. For without doubt, the divine Spirit, joined to the mind as if to the First Mover, rotates the human mass with a certain "snatched" motion; so much so that the whole Microcosm seems to be moved, led around, and agitated by this motion, just as the entire <term>Macrocosm: The universe or "Great World"</term> is rotated by the motion of the First Mover. Yet, in the meantime, the planetary spheres in the Macrocosm, and the "middle soul" in the Microcosm (which is of a stellar nature), are known to move by their own proper motion, although because of the violence...

### TREATISE I, SECTION I, BOOK VII

...contrary thoughts are not perceived to move within us. Therefore, the Mind or the internal divine Spirit, when joined with the external and divinely infused Spirit, moves the intellectual sphere of man against the motion of the animal sphere, which is guided by the **middle soul**. <note>The "middle soul" (*anima media*) was viewed by Renaissance philosophers as the bridge between the eternal, intellectual Mind and the physical, sensory body.</note> In this way, although the soul may seem to be at rest, it is nonetheless moved by its own proper motion. But the Spirit, holding Dominion with the mind over both the soul and the body, snatches the whole living man toward the contemplation of divine vision. It unites the soul to itself, causes it to leave its human state for a time, and connects it to divinity, according to that saying of *Samuel* cited above:

> *And you shall be changed into another man than you were before, etc.* <note>original: "Et mutaberis in alium virum, quàm fuisti antea." This refers to 1 Samuel 10:6, where Saul is transformed by the Spirit of God.</note>

We also see that a lit candle, when exposed to the rays of the sun, seems to lose its own power because of the glorious brightness of the Sun. Indeed, its light—as if submerged in the glory and clarity of the Sun—does not appear to human eyes; yet in reality, the light is the same as it was before. Its action and power are not diminished, but rather its heat and activity are exalted by the power of the Sun. The same holds true for the inspired soul. For if, according to the opinion of *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that in states of divine possession, the human element becomes entirely passive.</note>, the human soul and mind were entirely vacant of action or even rested completely within the body, it would necessarily follow that when that divinely infused spirit departed again, the body would remain inanimate or totally deprived of the power of action. This is because it is the property of light and "primary act" <term>Actus Primus: A technical term in Scholastic philosophy referring to the fundamental state of being or "doing" that gives a thing its essence.</term> to either always act or, where it does not act, to cease to exist. On the contrary, it follows that the soul acts with greater activity and splendor through the presence and illumination of a greater light, and even more promptly, since "united force is stronger." Therefore, against these arguments of *Iamblichus*, it must be that the action of the inspired Prophet proceeds not only from God or the divine Spirit extraordinarily infused into him, but also that the soul itself along with the mind—as if snatched up by the presence of the divine Spirit—is stirred by a motion unknown to nature and unusual to the body. Thus, no reason for this motion is perceived by the soul or the senses; the powers of the soul, carried upward, forget lower things and, snatched by their intellectual sense, contemplate the superior mysteries of God. The pious soul thus draws the Mind toward itself, and the Mind, embracing its pious vehicle <note>original: "vehiculum". Neoplatonists believed the soul traveled in a "chariot" or "vehicle" of light or spirit.</note> and nourishing it with divine splendor, attracts divine rays—full of the divine Spirit—to itself through the magnetic virtue of its divinity. This rewards the soul according to its merit with beauty and gifts, leading it from the earthly path to the celestial one, according to that saying of *Hermes Trismegistus* in the *Pimander, Book 10*:

> *A good soul, when it has fulfilled all the commands of virtue and piety, certainly becomes either God or Mind.* <note>The *Pimander* (or *Poimandres*) is a foundational text of Hermeticism, a tradition of spiritual philosophy.</note>

Here, therefore, we must carefully observe that the miraculous works of the Prophets are not done by any power of the stars, nor by that portion of the human soul derived from them, nor by the body itself, but by the pure and free power of God. *But if anyone should perhaps say that the middle soul could be the immediate cause of this power or divine gift, we shall demonstrate* by an unbreakable argument that the matter is otherwise. For since this portion of the middle soul is contained within a single man and overshadowed by a decaying body, it is impossible for it to have a power or virtue effective enough for a divine work. From this it is clear that if anyone is divinely inspired, it follows that they possess a divine benefit through a holy illumination flowing from above, through which they are seen to participate in the action of God. For if divine works were from the soul, it would follow that the soul is, by its own nature and power, the master of wisdom and divinity; and consequently, every other soul would have the same property of divinity. Yet every soul is known to be far from such power. For even the soul that seems perfect is still imperfect in respect to divine things.

> *Therefore, it is not the soul (let me now use the words of Iamblichus) as the prime mover, but divinity that is the cause urging one toward divine works.*

Indeed, were it not so, religion would be in vain, since without the worship of God we would be masters of divine...

### CHAPTER XI.

->*How men, by the power of the illuminated mind, or by divine inspiration, may not only perceive things done in distant and remote places, but even understand the secret whispers of men far absent, and perform wonderful and ineffable deeds?*<-

By the power of the mind divinely inspired, or by the divine spirit sent from on high and united to the human mind, it is possible to perform and carry out all miracles whatsoever that the human heart can conceive or imagine by any reason, since all virtues or powers found in the world and its creatures are contained within the Holy Spirit and remain in it. From this, therefore, come those miraculous operations of the <term>Vates</term><note>A Latin term for a divinely inspired prophet or poet.</note> or Prophets, in respect of whom they are called in the Holy Scriptures *men with open and revealed eyes. Num. 24.* And they were commonly called *Seers, 1 Samuel 9:9: "Let us go to the Seer."* and in the same place: *"Is the Seer there?"* Similarly, men of this kind, breathed upon by God or the divine Spirit, are called *Seers, 1 Chronicles 29:29 and 2 Chronicles 12:15, etc.* Nor is it a wonder, since they not only foresee future things (whence Balaam says in *Num. 24: "I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near"*) but even present things, which are being done in the most remote and far-distant places. Thus <term>Jahaziel</term><note>A Levite mentioned in the Bible who prophesied victory for King Jehoshaphat.</note> clearly saw from afar that the Ammonites and Moabites had placed their camps at the height of the brook, which is opposite the wilderness of Jeruel, and he warned King Jehoshaphat and all Judea to go up and fight against them. *2 Chronicles 20.* Similarly, <term>Elisha</term><note>original: "Elizæus"</note> uncovered the secrets of the King of Syria who was fighting against Israel; indeed, he saw their actions and knew their plans, just as is read in *4 Kings 6*<note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 6.</note>. And all these and infinite other miracles they performed by the power and assistance of the divine Spirit, in whose splendor—directing their eyes—they beheld events in distant places; and by means of that most pure and refined Spirit, they even heard and understood the voices, speeches, and plans of men living in places remote from them, no differently than if they were nearby. Truly, these things cannot seem impossible to those who correctly know themselves. For whoever rightly considers the power of the internal man—as being constituted from the middle soul as the subject and the Mind as the divine form—will perceive that by the power of the Mind even more difficult things can be brought to a desired end. For its power is so widely expanded that even the Spirit cannot encompass it, but it is present everywhere and in every place; and yet it is incomprehensible, insofar as it is of the essence of God. Hence, <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term><note>A legendary figure representing a synthesis of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, regarded as the source of all ancient wisdom.</note> says: *“Man, supported by this nature of God, embraces with his intelligence all things that are on the earth and in the sea, and whatever else is above the heaven, and thus raises himself up so that he may even gaze upon the Good itself.”*

For we see in common experience that if we turn the keenness of our mind’s eye toward Rome, immediately—even while we remain most certainly in England as far as the <term>external man</term><note>The "external man" refers to the physical body and the sensory self, as opposed to the "internal man" or the spiritual soul.</note> is concerned—the person, the place, or the event previously conducted there before us presents itself to us, so that suddenly, and as if in the blink of an eye, we behold it, and so forth. And this happens even with the most remote places, such as Judea, etc. Indeed, we may even lift a simple ray of the human mind toward God Himself through serious contemplation. What, then, might this admirable essence achieve if it were illuminated by the Divine Spirit, from which, as a ray of God, it first flowed forth? 

112. But truly, the human body is so lethal and deceptive to the influx of this divine grace of the soul that those things which seem real to the soul are not, and those which truly exist are not seen by it. From this it happens that the whole man, if not illuminated by such a Spirit, is carried away by fallacies. Indeed, every external sense is deceived regarding its own objects; how much more, then, is the internal sense, which is covered on all sides by the shadow of the flesh. <term>Proclus</term><note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the material world is a mere shadow of higher spiritual realities.</note> seems to confirm this with these words: *Matter,* he says, *seems to possess all things, when in reality it possesses nothing.* From this it follows that carnal men are so distrustful and incredulous that they utterly deny those things which are not subject to the senses, mocking the truth of philosophy when it describes the internal nature of man, and mocking those who search into mystical and spiritual nature. For they are unwilling to admit by any reason what they have not seen or, like <term>Saint Thomas</term><note>A reference to "Doubting Thomas" from the Gospel of John, who refused to believe in the Resurrection until he could physically touch Christ's wounds.</note>, touched with their hands. For just as men illuminated by the presence of the Divine Spirit look only upon spiritual things—scorning all corporal things by holding them to be false and trifling—so also, conversely, worldly men who are occupied only with the senses tend to regard spiritual things as <term>chimeras</term><note>Fanciful illusions or impossible monsters from mythology.</note> and deceptions, while holding corporal and sensible things to be infallible; and thus they are deceived. Surely <term>Solomon</term> clearly declares the reason for this matter in the Book of Wisdom, Chapter 9, with these words:

> *The thoughts of mortals are timid and our foresight is uncertain. For the body, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind that muses on many things. We find it difficult to judge the things that are on earth, and we find the things that are before our eyes only with great labor. But who shall investigate the things that are in the heavens? And who shall know your mind, unless you have given wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from the highest, etc.*

From these words, it is clear that the external man cannot become internal unless he is illustrated by divine illumination. Hence, from what is said in the First Epistle of <term>John</term>, we perceive that one is a child of the world and another is a child of God, and that the child of God ought not to perceive the world or its dark acts, since the world does not know the children of God or His acts. 

113. But now we shall bring forward the reason why those inspired by the power and presence of the Divine Spirit—and by its conjunction and union with the mind of the internal man—are able to draw out and perceive the voices and secret whispers of men who are not present. The Holy Spirit of discipline, although it expands itself everywhere throughout the entire world and grants power, motion, action, sound, and even the voice itself to all things, does not assist everyone powerfully with its help. Rather, it assists only those to whom God, out of His mercy, grants it abundantly. For in some, it is present simply for the functions of life; in others, in a double proportion; and in some, triple, etc. From this arise the various gifts of that Spirit recounted by <term>Saint Paul</term>. 

114. This most Holy Spirit, I say, when inspired abundantly by God into certain people, makes the man into whom it is poured out hear and understand any voices of animals at will, because the Spirit itself is the cause of the production of vocal sounds. Hence, when it fell upon the Apostles in the form of fire, it rendered them skilled in every language. And <term>Philostratus</term> relates that <term>Apollonius of Tyana</term><note>Philostratus was a Greek writer; Apollonius of Tyana was a famous first-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> understood the chirping and speech of birds, or the meaning of those voices, by a certain divine power. Indeed, this Divine Spirit, governing the universal spirit and expanded through its universal members, tells the man in whom it dwells—and as it were, resonates to him—those same voices and tones which are heard in more remote places. Nor indeed will this seem impossible to the wise man, since the <term>Apostle</term>...

# TREATISE THE FIRST,
## SECTION I.
### BOOK VIII.
#### On the action of the middle soul of the Microcosm within the body.

---

### CHAPTER I.

> *On the properties of the vital soul and its ethereal spirit in the human body.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring stylized vines and leaves within a square border.</image-desc>

What this worldly portion is, which constitutes the middle part of the human soul, we have clearly and brilliantly explained in the first book of this work; namely, that considered in itself, it is like a spark of light from the World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi". In Fludd’s philosophy, this is the universal spirit that gives life to the entire universe.</note> descending from the sphere of equality. We have called this World Soul the "worldly ray," the "nature of things," the "second act," the "quintessence," <term>quintessence (quinta essentia)</term><note>The 'fifth element' or 'ether', which was thought to be the pure substance of the heavens, distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note> and the origin of the life of all living things. And this is so, insofar as it is considered by itself in its own nature, and without the admixture of the mind or the sensitive soul.

But indeed, insofar as it is the middle portion in itself, both in the composition of the universal world and of the human soul, it is rightly defined by Hermes Trismegistus in the *Pymander*, book 12, <note>Referring to the "Corpus Hermeticum," a collection of foundational texts for Western esotericism attributed to the mythical sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note> as "life void of mind." According to its being, it is divided into matter—which is pure spirit—and form—which is the light carried in that Spirit as if in a vehicle, acting incessantly upon it as if upon its own proper passive subject.

Hence, that form or light is properly called the **innate heat** <note>original: "calidum animati innatum". A vital warmth thought by ancient doctors like Galen to be the fuel of life.</note> by the Philosophers, and this ethereal Spirit is called the **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture (humidum radicale)</term><note>The internal 'oil' or fluid that feeds the innate heat; the preservation of this moisture was equated with health and longevity.</note>. These two, essentially joined, constitute life, and therefore, as the philosopher Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote on the nature of the soul.</note> attests, they do not die. By their power and presence alone, the four elements are balanced in their composition with such justice, and are joined together in harmonious peace by the bonds of this fiery Spirit, and are organized for vital and symphonic motions, so that the life of the animal and the plant—indeed, even of the most compact mineral—is procreated from this source.

Therefore, the total violation of the bonds of this soul brings about death and dissolution; but a partial violation induces disease and sickness, which is nothing other than the relaxation of the bonds of celestial harmony, and the unbridled rebellion of one element against its partners that are naturally incompatible with it; regarding which we shall later...

<header>ON THE ACTION OF THE MIDDLE SOUL OF THE MICROCOSM IN THE BODY.</header>

...it. Truly, the Sages have demonstrated that the reason why this soul is infused into the human body by divine will is twofold. The first reason concerns the <term>Mind (Mens)</term><note>In this Hermetic context, 'Mind' refers to the highest, most divine part of the human intellect, a spark of the Divine itself, distinct from the soul.</note>, which is the superior portion of the soul. Hence, **Hermes Trismegistus** in the *Pimander*, book 10, says:
> Since the earthly dregs cannot receive such a divine mind, nor can such a great divinity sustain itself within a body made of parts, the Mind took up the soul as a garment; and even the soul, being divine, uses the vehicle of the spirit, and the spirit runs through the whole living being, etc.

And for this reason, this soul is not ineptly called the **temple of God** by **Paul** and **Sextus the Philosopher**, as was said before. Conversely, the Mind rewards the soul itself in infinite ways for its labor and its blessed duty, insofar as the soul finds its supreme good within the Mind. For this soul was full of the Mind and of God in man from the beginning, as **Hermes Trismegistus** testifies, agreeing with the Holy Scriptures in this. From this it happens that, just as the soul is the cause of life in itself, so also the Mind joined with it, and firmly adhering to it, is the cause of a pious, holy, honest, and blessed life, which is the beginning of eternal life. And thence **Hermes Trismegistus**, in *Pimander* 10, uses these words:
> The human soul—not every soul, but the pious and blessed one—is divine.

And elsewhere:
> The good soul, when it has undergone all the commands of virtue and piety, certainly becomes God or the Mind.

Furthermore, the soul acquires knowledge through the presence of the Mind; through acquired knowledge, it becomes similar to the Mind or the intellect itself, as **Proclus** testifies in his work *On the Soul*. It is for this reason, according to **Hermes Trismegistus**, that the soul united to the Mind is said to be "standing" and "not falling." And **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the mysteries and the soul's ascent.</note> also explains most excellently the impotence of the soul enclosed in a body in these words, where at the same time he seems to indicate and show that infinite utility resulting from the presence of the Mind to which the action of the soul is obedient:
> The human soul is confined within a single species, and is too much overshadowed by a fading body; therefore it has no effective power for divine work. If ever we seem to be able to do something of that sort in some way, we only do it through divine illustration flowing down from above; through which we also seem to be participants in divine action.

And elsewhere he makes mention of this thing repeatedly in these words:
> Since, he says, the soul, which appears perfect, is still imperfect regarding divine things. For it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works; otherwise religion would not be necessary for these things, but we would be masters of divine works without the worship of God, if these things were done by the power of the soul itself.

By these words, as it seems to me, he has most evidently demonstrated that the Mind is required first of all for the composition of the human soul, and then that the middle soul acquires its highest good from it. For otherwise, prayer to God for grace and illumination would be superfluous if the vital soul possessed that property of itself, and thus there would also be no difference between a human and a brute animal. Finally, that reward of the soul is the greatest which it receives from the Mind: for its power to rise again after death consists in the virtue of the Mind. For just as the soul with its spirit was the cause for the Mind to descend into the body, because of its Spirit's inclination toward material things; so also the Mind is that power by whose lifegiving wings the soul is exalted back into its natural seat. Hence, most wretched is that soul which, neglecting the Mind, clings to the corporal soul; for when the dissolution of such a soul and body occurs, the Mind flies upward on its own wings and leaves the soul obscured in the earthly mud or the <term>whirlpool of matter (hyle)</term><note>Hyle is a Greek term for the fundamental, unformed matter of the universe, often associated in this philosophy with darkness and the "dregs" of existence.</note>.

It is clear, therefore, what kind of wages or reward the middle soul receives from the divine Mind for its labor, by which it covered the Mind like a garment or some protection by means of the Spirit, and preserved it untouched by the wretched body. It remains now to inquire what benefit, or what kind of grace the inferior portion of the soul (the daughter of the elements, or the sensitive soul) is accustomed to pay back to this middle soul for its benevolence toward it—by which it not only descended with its Spirit and brought life and motion to it and its body, but also brought down that most excellent super-celestial gem...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "middle soul" and how it is affected by the lower, sensitive soul and the material body. It specifically addresses the fall of the soul into matter, using the allegory of Adam and Eve and citations from Hermetic and Neoplatonic philosophers.</meta>

...carried and introduced with himself into her <note>referring to the lower soul or the material nature</note>. Thus, although she is most opposite to him in disposition, her presence is nevertheless exalted all the more as she is able to entice the middle portion of the soul to herself, and consequently she is puffed up with all the greater pride, the more eminent the victory her prince (namely, the prince of darkness) obtains against the portion of divine light present there, which bears the image of the Prince of Light. From this it happens that the lowest portion of the human soul first attempts to tempt the intermediate spirit with worldly delights and pleasures, so that it might thereafter better and more easily deceive the soul, while this Spirit solicits it. Did not the serpent tempt **Eve**, the woman or the passive principle, in this way, so that he might afterwards circumvent **Adam**, the man or the active principle, to such an extent that they were both then bereaved and deprived of the presence of God? 

Truly, by this reasoning, the moist nature of the Spirit—or **Eve**—and the active light of heaven—or **Adam**—by consenting to the counsel of the animal or sensitive soul and adhering to it, lost the presence of the divine Mind. Hence their misfortune and loss, which could never have been repaired or restored except by that copious presence of the fleeing Mind, which we received from the Savior of the world and the infusion of the fruitful Mind, in which is the Word of God. 

From this, our enigmatic explanation of the described pleasure of Paradise is made clear, which we set forth in our *Theologico-Philosophical Treatise on Life, Death, and Resurrection*. For the soul of Adam, through the copious presence of the Mind, was inclined to contemplate only superior things; but when it chose to adhere to the blandishments of the sensitive soul and the false and malignant instigations of the Devil, then the portion of the Mind flew away, and death succeeded, as if in its place. And so likewise, through a renewed and copious infusion of the Mind into these lower regions, in which the Word exists, the regeneration of the internal man follows, along with the resurrection of both the internal and external man. 

But now we shall produce the authority of the Philosophers, who speak of the blandishments and enticements of the sensitive soul or <term>idol</term><note>original: "idoli"; in Neoplatonism, the 'idolon' is the lower shadow or image of the soul that inhabits the body.</note>, and who also speak of its lethal inconvenience and ineffable unhappiness. 

*Mercury Trismegistus says that the soul, conscious of the nature of things and of the good, when deprived of eyes, entangles itself in bodily passions, and that it is necessary for it to look about with the eyes of the Mind, lest it perish utterly.* 

And elsewhere he says, *that the impious soul, loving the body, remains in its own nature and torments itself excessively. And elsewhere: because of its disjunction from the Mind, he calls the soul "not standing, but falling"; thus also in his Pimander 10, he asserts that the soul, destitute of the presence of the Mind, is able neither to do nor say anything, and he says that this soul differs in no way from the soul of brutes.*

Such, therefore, is the hope of the carnal and worldly soul; such is the wage of the animal soul, which it returns to the vital or middle soul for its descent from the heavens; such is its reception; such is the end of carnal hospitality; these are its riches, the effects of which are nothing other than frauds, lies, deceptions, illusions, and nothing of certainty; since all truth flows solely from the rays and power of the Mind, and proceeds from nowhere else. 

And certainly, most unhappy was this lot of the soul, by which, descending into such a dark abyss of <term>hyle</term><note>original: "hylæ"; the Greek term for primordial matter.</note>, it migrated as if into an inn and a dark prison, utterly foreign to its dignity, and indeed against its will. This is also confessed by **Iamblichus** in these words: 

*The soul, which glides downward, meets [matter], dragging with it the signs of chains and punishments, and shows itself burdened by the composition of material spirits, and occupied by the dissimilar disturbances of matter.* 

The Sage seems to confirm this opinion of Iamblichus in *Wisdom 9*, in the passage cited above: *The body*, he says, *which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses upon the sense or the mind that muses upon many things, and hardly can we discern those things that are before us.* 

To this also, in my judgment, the opinion of **Plato** and **Proclus** is consonant, which holds that it is not natural for souls to lead a life with bodies and to be involved in generation, but on the contrary to be separated, and that an immaterial and incorporeal life is rather more agreeable to souls; and they say, that when

...that when souls are involved in the process of generation <note>the cycle of birth and physical life</note>, they are like people living in a pestilent region; whereas, when they live outside of generation, they are like those who dwell in green meadows. This, therefore, is the reason why **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his book *On the Forms of the Soul* affirmed that all souls are "sick" when in the body. For the same reason, **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus</note> also said that the soul, which in itself is always most vigilant, "sleeps" while in the body. Hence **Synesius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop</note> also said that the part of the world-soul allotted to form by a heavy bond, being separated from its parents, has drunk from the dark river of oblivion, admiring the unpleasant earth with blind anxieties. Since the enclosed soul is afflicted by all these disturbances of the body, there is no doubt that its descent into the corporeal "tabernacle" <note>a temporary shelter or tent</note> of man is against its nature; just as the disposition of fire, which by its own property always seeks the higher realms, is sometimes forced by violence to tend downwards.

From whence, then, comes this unnatural union between these two extremes? Certainly, it comes from the divine will, so that God might enrich the lower things as well as the higher with his living blessings; and especially so that man, made in the image of God, might look upon both the lower and the higher. For the universal Creator sent the middle soul into man for a twofold reason: First, to use the words of **Hermes Trismegistus**, <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg."</note> *neither could the earthly dross receive a mind so divine, nor could the partial body sustain such a great deity.* Therefore, the Mind <term>Mens; the highest, purely intellectual part of the human being</term> took up the soul as a cloak; because the soul, being divine, uses the vehicle of the spirit; and this Spirit runs through the whole animal body. Furthermore, **Hermes Trismegistus** provides a second reason in the *Pimander*, Book 3: *The human soul*, he says, *is veiled in the shadow of the flesh, in order to undertake the discourse of the celestial Gods, to observe the works of God and the progressions of nature, to see the signs of good things, and to gain knowledge of divine power: a certain portion was granted for the judgment of good and evil, and for discovering the various craftsmanship of good things, etc.* From these points, it is manifest that the soul in its own nature is good and most useful to the constitution of man. Indeed, it is that "middle nature" in the composition of the human soul without which its two extremes <note>the divine Mind and the material Body</note> could not be joined together. But through the inclination of the flesh toward worldly pleasures and the deceptive charms of the sensitive part, the soul is deceived; and so, through the excessive, dark overshadowing of the opaque body, separated from its parents, it drinks in the oblivion of truth, and being robbed of its eyes, it entangles itself in corporeal cares and passions. Hence **Hermes Trismegistus** says in *Pimander*, Book 10: *When the compacted body scatters and distracts the soul into its own mass, then the soul is subjected to oblivion, and is deprived of the vision of the beautiful and the good. Oblivion itself is wickedness, etc.* From this, the assistance of divine illumination is necessarily required for its salvation, since without it, the soul can produce nothing good or holy in this life. Blessed, therefore, is he whose soul firmly adheres to the divine Mind. Blessed is the soul which, avoiding the voracious barking of Hyle <note>original: "hylæ"; the Greek term for primordial matter, often personified as a chaotic beast</note> and emerging from the earth, directed by the wings of the mind, guides its steps toward God with a light leap. Blessed is the Spirit which, after the fate and dissolution of the body, after hard labors and bitter earthly cares, having entered the ways of the mind, sees the peak and height of happiness shining with divine light. Blessed, therefore, is the Spirit with the soul, and thrice blessed is he who remains most faithful and constant to the Mind until the end, for such a one shall taste the cup of happiness and the eternal fruit of immortality. Therefore, O my soul, do not look upon the deceptive flatteries of the flesh and the world, but joyfully raise yourself toward higher things according to your own disposition; be nobler than common fire, whose nature is always to tend upward, and to despise and turn away from lower things by natural instinct. For since you are decorated and made beautiful in the image and likeness of God, betrothed to the Spirit through faith, bought and redeemed by the blood of Christ, helped by Angels, a companion of bliss, an heir of salvation, and a participant in reason, what have you to do with the flesh, with the senses, and with the world? ## CHAPTER II.

->*How the middle soul is infused into the body along with its mistress, the Mind,*<-

**Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus and a foundational teacher of alchemy and philosophy</note> asserted that the Word passes into the mind, the mind into reason, reason into the soul, and the soul into the spirit; this spirit then enters the air, and finally, all these things, slipping downward through the "aerial sea," are transferred into the body with and within that air, as if it were their final vehicle. We would also prove this same point in a certain way, were it not that we consider the Mind itself to be a ray of the **Word of God** <note>original: "Verbum Dei"; the Logos or divine creative principle</note>. For as Saint John testifies in his first chapter: *In the Word itself was life, and that life was the light of men,* etc. Therefore, when **Jehovah** <note>The Hebrew name for God used throughout this text</note> brought forth that word: *Let man be made,* the mud, which had been prepared by the hands of God, transformed into a living being; and by the power of the breath <note>original: "spiraculi"</note> which went out from His mouth along with the Word, all human virtues were produced. And so Adam was made a **rational animal** <note>In the philosophical sense: a living being capable of logic and discourse</note>, possessing the power of reason and life simultaneously. For we must not believe the fictions of those skilled in the art of painting, who—not blushing to limit Him to a single place—depict God in the form of an external man and imagine that He literally applied His mouth to the muddy face of Adam. Indeed, the "mouth" and "limbs" of God are found everywhere according to His divine pleasure; they are present everywhere, yet are never confined by space. For God Himself is seen by the **intellectual eyes** <note>the faculty of spiritual or philosophical insight</note> to be expanded throughout the entire universe, filling all things with His presence, so that according to the teaching of the Holy Scriptures, the earth is His footstool and heaven is to Him like a throne. Thus, whatever He speaks in the heavens is fulfilled immediately and in the blink of an eye upon the earth. Sitting in heaven, He said: *Let the earth be made,* and by the power of the Word the earth was established, and that indeed happened instantly. He also said: *Let man be made,* speaking thus from the holy heavens, and suddenly and in an instant, that which He commanded was done; for the impression of the Word infused the breath of life through his nostrils, and so on.

Now, just as the world is called the "image of God," and the threefold distinction of its regions is related to the threefold property of the persons of the Trinity (which is why they held the first place in creation, as was said in our **Microcosmic Treatise** <note>Referring to the author's previous work on man as a "little world" or Microcosm</note>); so also man, who is the image of the world and consequently the image of God, received this divine and God-like breath. Thus, for his very existence, man immediately obtained the power of the Word and the Spirit of the Creator. Consequently, he is a partaker of the divine essence, no less than the world itself is a partaker of the **Spirit of the Lord** which was moved over the waters. He also received a portion from the visible throne of Jehovah the Creator—namely, from heaven—from which he obtained his life-giving soul. From the elements, in whose region the footstool of Jehovah is placed, he received a "formal purity" from which his **image** <note>original: "idolum"; here referring to the sensory or astral part of the soul that mirrors the physical world</note> or sensitive part is made. And finally, from the earth, or the center of the entire machine, he claimed for himself the muddy, external, and opaque substance that serves as the lodging for his internal self. Thus, Jehovah breathed the breath of life into the **Microcosm** <note>Man</note> on the sixth day of creation (the day he was founded) in the same way He did for the **Macrocosm** <note>The Universe</note> on the first day. It is therefore evident that the Word, emitted like a true **supersubstantial ray** <note>a ray existing above the nature of physical matter</note> from God speaking at the creation of the divine human animal, and attended by the Holy Spirit, tended downward through the spirit of the intell-

...[the intelle]ctual expansion snatched up a portion of it to serve as its vehicle. That portion was subsequently received in the mid-heaven by its light and Spirit; from there, it leaped forward with them into the air of the elementary region, and finally entered into the nostrils of **Adam**. Thus, penetrating even to the center, it introduced a portion of every worldly region into the corresponding regions of the human body—arranged according to its lightness or heaviness—and disposed them within him in a marvelous manner. 

Indeed, we are taught by the experiment described below that it is necessary for the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"</note> with its vehicle to occupy the highest region of the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: "Little world"; the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe</term>, since its place in the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: "Great world"; the universe or totality of the cosmos</term> is the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, fiery level of heaven in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God and pure light</note>. 

In the same way, the formal part—namely the **middle soul** with the ethereal Spirit—enjoys the middle region of man, which is the chest <note>original: "thorax"</note>. This follows the example of the Sun, which claims the middle region of the world for itself along with its Spirit. Finally, the sensitive part, being adjacent to the fiery sphere, occupies the lowest belly of the Microcosm, just as the elements occupy the lower place of the world. 

The experiment is as follows: 

Fill a glass one-quarter full with water. Upon this, skillfully pour red wine so that it floats on the water (this can be achieved by pouring it over a crust of bread). Thus, the wine occupies the second quarter of the glass. Then, gently and skillfully pour the finest **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritum vini"; high-proof distilled alcohol or brandy</note> upon it, so that it likewise floats upon the previous wine and fills the third quarter of the glass. Once this is done, let that spirit be lit so that it burns. 

By this experiment, it will be demonstrated how the **ethereal nature** floats above the **elementary** or airy nature (just as wine floats on water); and then, how the **Empyrean nature** floats above the ethereal, and finally how the **fiery Spirit** floats above the Empyrean, as shown in the following demonstration.

From these things, therefore, it must be gathered how these natures behave within man: namely, the **Empyrean spirit** is in the cerebellum, while the **fiery and intellectual spirit** (or the Mind) is in the apex of the brain near the **pia mater** <note>The delicate, innermost membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord</note>, where the ethereal spirit is found in the smallest quantity, as was said regarding the cone of the material pyramid. Wine, in its nature, is compared to the ethereal spirit and light, because it floats above water or the worldly air. ...the thinner part is the **Spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritus vini"; in alchemy, this refers to highly rectified alcohol or ethanol, seen as the "purest" essence of the liquid</note>, constituting the empyrean region, while the thicker part is the phlegm or watery substance, equated to the air and water—or the sphere of moisture—in the lowest heaven. From these examples it appears most evidently that the Spirit of the ethereal heaven participates in the nature of both the lower and upper heaven, both in the world and in man. 

And this is that infallible reasoning by which we are exactly taught: that the nature of the empyrean heaven is joined by contiguity and a kind of continuity with the nature of the ethereal heaven (in respect to the Spirit) just as air is joined with water; and that by such a bond, ether is connected to air as water is to earth. Furthermore, the empyrean Spirit relates to the rays of the mind as air relates to fire, and the mind relates to the Spirit as fire to air, or ether to fire. 

Hence it is clearly established what the position of the parts constituting the **inner man** is within his external body: 
- namely, that the **mind** with **reason** dwells in the head, as if in the empyrean heaven or its natural seat, with the rays of the mind claiming the superior place there. 
- Next, that the **soul** <term>Soul: here refers to the "middle soul" or vital soul associated with life force</term> with the **ethereal Spirit** inhabits the heart in the "middle belly" <note>The chest or thorax</note>, just as the sun inhabits its sphere. 
- And finally, that the **animal spirit** <term>Animal spirit: from the Latin "anima" (soul/breath); the spirit responsible for basic sensation and movement, not "animalistic" in a modern sense</term> with the **animal soul** chooses the lowest belly for its natural station, where it uses the liver as its inn or laboratory.

The **rational Spirit** gives action to the senses, diffusing its invisible powers through the network of the nerves into the whole body, so that with reason and judgment we are able to see, hear, touch, taste, and smell things. 

The soul of virtue <note>The vital power</note> with its Spirit, possessing the center of the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: The "little world," meaning the human being as a reflection of the universe</term>—no differently than the Sun possessing the center of the visible heaven—transmits the rays of life universally through the external man via the arteries, both upward and downward, so that by their virtue he is able to live and move. 

The **animal soul** (or the "idol," or the aerial power) is fashioned from the forms of the elements. It receives its power partly from the elements and partly by taking over the duties of the higher powers. It acts and works in the liver to transmute the nourishment of **chyle** <term>Chyle: A milky fluid of digested fats and lymph found in the intestines during digestion</term> into blood for its own use. It then pours and disperses this blood upward and downward through the veins into the entire corporeal machine to preserve the parts of the elementary composition in their healthy state.

Therefore, the mind is contiguous to reason; thus it governs all operations. The rational Spirit is contiguous to the ethereal Spirit, and therefore they act through the rays of both natures. For the arteries communicate with the nerves, and the nerves with the arteries. Furthermore, a small branch of the arteries covering the brain constitutes a **wonderful network** <note>original: "rete mirabile"; a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain which ancient physicians believed refined the vital spirits into animal spirits</note> there; the branches of the nerves are indeed wonderful, and they prove the true seat of the mind. 

For just as God, sitting in the height of heaven, is the root and unity of all things, pouring the rays of His action downward only into the world and granting reason, life, and sense to His creatures; so also the mind itself, placed at the summit of the Microcosm, is the root of all nerves. Their branches run downward only, so that they may refresh the lower parts with the moderation of reason and sense. Indeed, the fact that God in the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: The "great world" or the universe as a whole</term> and the ray of His essence in the Microcosm do not emit rays upward from their essence (as if from their root) proves that there are no things created by the Founder above His own existence—no more than a number can go backward beyond the number one.

Therefore, the lower Spirits are like subjects of the higher ones, of which the **Mind** is the King and Emperor. If the soul reigning in the middle is obedient and faithful to this Mind, this "Republic" <note>The body governed as a state</note> will be most happy; but if it is rebellious, it will be most unhappy, and that soul will pay the penalty for its disobedience. 

From this it happens that the rays of the mind, acting through the intellectual Spirit, are terrifying to a rebellious soul, but gracious and lovable to an obedient one. To a rebellious soul, they usually bring cares, sadness, fear, distrust, despair, anger, rage, hatred, gluttony, drunkenness, and other such vices. Conversely, they are observed to induce in the obedient soul joy, gladness, boldness in truth, faith, hope, patience, gentleness, spiritual love, temperance, and other virtues of that kind.

This is called the "active and principal motion," which encompasses imagination, reasoning, and memory. However, they divided involuntary action into the **Vital** and the **Natural**. Here it must be observed in passing that the superior region <note>the head</note> commands because of the presence of the mind and reason, and acts at will—that is, voluntarily—much like God.

But truly, we perceive that the action of the vital region as well as the natural region—which we called the animal soul and the "image" <note>original: "idolum"</note> above—is involuntary, and governed as if by a higher power or a more exalted divinity. From the aforementioned authors, we therefore gather that the involuntary **vital action** consists either in the expansion of the heart alone—from which come joy, hope, confidence, love, mercy, and kindness; or in the expansion and contraction of the heart together—from which the motion of the pulse proceeds, consisting of *systole* <term>systole: the contraction of the heart</term> and *diastole* <term>diastole: the expansion of the heart</term>; or in the contraction of the heart alone—from which proceed sadness, despair, fear, hatred, envy, anger, fury, shame, and other such things.

O Christian men, look, I pray, how closely these physicians, Pagans, and Philosophers approached the shadow of the truth! For what could they have depicted better or more correctly through these things than our own opinion and meaning regarding creation? For first, we perceive that the vital action, situated and rooted in the middle region of man, and likewise the natural action, located in the lowest belly, are involuntary—that is, they depend upon the ordaining and disposition of a higher power.

Next, in the middle region—since life consists in its heart or center—we clearly see the actions of the three regions of the world. Insofar as in the expansion of the heart, there is born joy, hope, love, confidence, mercy, kindness, and similar actions of the holy soul, which are recognized as the infallible gifts of the Mind and of God; and they further denote the obedience of the soul, and its partnership, communication, friendship, and faithfulness with the Mind. For how much joy and gladness, what sort of faith and confidence, and what ineffable love, mercy, and kindness God pours into holy and good souls, the Holy Scriptures declare in abundance, confirming the assertions of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with secret wisdom and alchemy.</note> in manifold ways. Hence, that expansion of the fortress of life is willing, ready, and prompt, so that it may receive with joy the blessings sent by God and His Mind. For it does not fear the actions of God, which it always finds to be healthful for itself, but it greedily desires them as its highest goods, and in desiring them, it receives them. For we are taught by experience that no disturbance or evil can happen to the soul where the aforementioned gifts of God and the Mind are found.

Such, then, was the action of **Adam**, while he was still living in Paradise. For his heart was filled with the gifts and benefits of the Mind, and was always open and expanded to receive divine and superior actions. Whence also the "doors" or "gates" <note>Anatomical reference to the heart valves.</note> are found in the highest part of the heart, signifying that the heart expects the benefit and joy of life from above. Yet Adam, after his disobedience, was excluded from this exquisite pleasure; indeed, he was deprived of the supreme joy of heaven, insofar as he participated in the knowledge of evil. Thus, he now derives his highest pleasure from the "middle heaven," as its nature is to participate in both extremes: namely, in the goodness of the highest region and the malice of the lowest region.

And through this involuntary action, the soul with its Spirit is affected—partly by gifts infused from above by the empyrean Spirit <note>The Empyrean is the highest, most spiritual part of heaven.</note> and the mind, and partly by the malignant vapors of darkness, carried upward on the wings of disturbance and strife. From this comes the inequality of human life: now joyful, now sad; now moved by hope, now afflicted by despair; at one moment seized by love, at another infected by envy; now merciful, and now immersed in cruelty and rage; now gentle, and then suddenly, in an instant, perturbed. Do we not also perceive that these same properties of the middle heaven, and these same effects, are infused into us from on high in a certain fated way? Indeed, we are very often taught through **Astrological** experience that **Jovial** <note>associated with Jupiter; joyful or benevolent</note>, **Venereal** <note>associated with Venus; relating to love and beauty</note>, and **Solar** influences are for the most part good for us, while **Saturnine** and **Martial** <note>associated with Saturn and Mars; often linked to melancholy or aggression</note> ones are generally sad, fierce, and unfortunate.

Finally, that involuntary vital action, which consists of the contraction of the heart, is miserable and unhappy for the soul dwelling in the middle region of the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" is the human being viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe.</note>. For through this very action, that soul—already fallen from the happiness of the supreme region <note>the head or the realm of pure intellect</note> to a mediocre state—is cast down even further into the lowest abyss of misfortune; for while it receives all hope and solace from the supreme region, it is submerged in a whirlpool of darkness. Since it looks more toward the sensitive soul <note>the part of the soul responsible for feeling and instinct</note> than the rational soul and the mind, it is therefore deserted by the mind and perfect reason. Hence it is oppressed by cares, doubts, sadness, despair, fear, hatred, anger, shame, and pain; it finds nothing except the "horrendous barking" of dark *hyle* <term>hyle: a Greek term for raw, unformed matter, often associated with chaos</term>, and everything seems terrifying to it because it is deprived of the eyes of true reason and lacks the illuminating light of the mind.

Yet the soul does not perceive these horrible things until it has slipped into the sensitive pleasures of the lower belly and lingered there for a long time, neglecting the mind and super-celestial things. At last, it returns to the memory of its place, its birth, and its origin, seeing that it has been caught as if in material snares, so that it cannot extricate itself from them without the wings and help of the divine mind. For it finally notices that through its own disobedience it has neglected the mind. From this comes grief; from this, tears; from this, constant suspicion and fear that its bulwark may soon be invaded and destroyed; hence its frequent contractions and its constant passions and disturbances that lack all reason.

But some, devoid of reason, will cry out: how is it possible for this to happen? And since all these things are in nature, they will say: show us the natural reason for this matter, so that we may better understand it to be so, and so we do not utterly reject these reasons of yours. To these unbelievers we respond: just as the Sun of the world, positioned in the center of the heaven, shoots its rays both upward and downward by means of the Spirit—and indeed its rays leaping forth from above are filled with divine grace, by which it infuses life into lower things (and truly this would not happen unless there were a certain magnetic force in the sun, granted to it from creation, to perform such things)—so also the matter holds true in that portion of the **soul of the world** <note>Latin: *anima mundi*</note> (which is of the sun) located in the chest or middle belly of man. For if it eagerly expects benefits from the superior mind, and attracts good to itself by the magnet of piety, its gifts will flow down very easily and without effort to the lower parts of the bottom belly. And while its arterial branches stretching upward will overflow with the Spirit of light—since the nature of the soul looks upward toward the supreme region with the nature of fire, and by its own motion catches at higher things through a certain divine appetite—then its lower branches will either be filled with dregs (that is, the thicker liquid of the vital Spirit), or they will remain mostly empty, since their more excellent part, rejoicing in the vision of the mind, is already [drawn] upward.

Thus, the impurer Spirits in the arterial branch—conspiring by reason of their gravity and position with evil and the lower region—will be raised upward in place of the true quintessence <note>the "fifth element" or the purest, most refined essence of a substance</note>. The rays of the mind flee from these because of their impurity. By this path, the darker rays of the soul, which otherwise naturally tend downward, are now raised upward and produce an eclipse between the sun of the mind and the moon of the soul that has fallen into the lower belly. 

This, then, is the chaos of the interior <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The human being viewed as a miniature version of the universe</note>, whose confusion of elements we can discern here with true eyes, and whose irregular arrangement is reduced to harmony only by divine illumination (to whose acts even Demons are forced to obey). From this come those infirmities and passions of the soul which we mentioned above: namely sadness, despair, fear, etc. Regarding this, Hermes Trismegistus speaks in the *Pimander*, book 10, when he says:
> *that the impious soul remains in its own nature and torments itself exceedingly:*

And elsewhere:
> *The soul fallen into a human body, if it persists in evil, shall not taste anything of immortality, nor shall it enjoy the good.*

From here, therefore, arise all the terrible effects of melancholy, from which reason is estranged; hence mania, <term>Lycanthropia</term> <note>a mental disorder where a person believes they have transformed into a wolf</note>, insanity, the "incubus" <note>nightmares or sleep paralysis often attributed to a malevolent spirit</note>, fear-inducing dreams, vain apparitions, and infinite things of that kind. All of these, through the union of the mind with the soul, are driven into darkness and vanish completely; they are found to be nothing other than the deceptions and illusions of the Devil, hidden under the veil of darkness, by which the most miserable soul, submerged in clouds of sadness, is tortured so that it may despair of the kindness of God and the mind. 

We have here, therefore, in the <term>Microcosm</term>, all the regions or "bellies" of the <term>Macrocosm</term> <note>the great universe</note>. And just as in the lowest region [of the world] the air is spread almost everywhere, and water is refined by the operation of heat and turned into air, and fire is drawn from the subtle air, so also we see that in the lowest belly of man, the chyle <note>the milky fluid of digested food</note> of the stomach—which we compared to the sea of the <term>Macrocosm</term>—by the power of the working liver, becomes blood and is converted into air; that is, into the bloody mass which contains the hidden nature of the other elements within itself. Its subtle or fiery nature is thrust into the gall bladder; but the fiercer part is poured downward, as if into the lowest place of springs or the abyss of the earth; and likewise, the thicker portion is committed to that part compared to the earth, namely the spleen. 

Similarly, we see that the vital Spirits in the heart—as if in their own home and the root in which they are prepared—elicit a food similar to their own nature from the external air. This is the ethereal nature, invisibly inherent in the air, by which silent breathing the vital Spirits are daily and every minute nourished and refreshed, as if by the food of life. They nourish those bonds of the body's members by which the elements are connected in harmonious peace, so that the elements, should they find freedom through a lack of these bonds, do not fall into discord with one another. Otherwise, the harmony of life would be interrupted by discord, from which either dangerous diseases or death and the total dissolution of the whole would follow. The **Mind**, however, remains perpetually immobile and constant in its own nature, like that supersubstantial essence from which it is derived. From this, it is evident that the natural faculty of the lowest heaven <note>In the "Microcosm" or human body, the "lowest heaven" corresponds to the abdominal region governing basic biological functions.</note> acts toward the nutrition of those parts of man similar to itself, namely the elementary and bodily parts. Hence it is established that the solid parts are nourished by it, and are sustained and preserved in the same state by the addition, union, and assimilation of blood. From the waves of this "red liquid," the heart attracts to its palace—through <term>diapedesis</term> <note>the passage of blood cells through the walls of the capillaries</note>—that ethereal essence which is its due.

Similarly, the **vital faculty**, governing the middle region <note>the chest/thorax</note>, is known to nourish the "innate heat" with "radical moisture"; by their increase, vital Spirits are more abundantly dispensed throughout the whole body, and the bonds of the elements are preserved inviolate. Finally, the **animal faculties** <note>In historical medicine, "animal" refers to the *anima* or soul, specifically the functions of the brain like sensation and movement.</note>, strengthened by their own particular nourishment, render the senses whole, the imagination prompt, the memory successful, and the movement and action of the muscles more effective through the instruments of the nerves.

The **Mind** in the upper region, however, always directs its gaze toward its homeland, and is perpetually engaged in meditations on super-celestial things; it entices man to contemplate sublime things, and snatches him entirely toward the knowledge, worship, reverence, and love of God—provided the soul shows itself obedient to it. Whence <note>original: "Proclus de anim."</note> Proclus says in *On the Soul* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a highly influential Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> that **the soul, through acquired knowledge, becomes similar to the mind or intellect itself**, etc. 

The **Rational Spirit** pours these ideas of the mind, by a certain remarkable harmony, into a well-disposed soul; it passes through the "sieve" or diaphragm of the first region into the second. The soul, inspired by these influences of reason, rejoices vehemently and, as if snatched up by the contemplation of higher things, does not look back at lower ones, except as its duty requires, to infuse the actions of life into them. 

The **natural soul**, or the lowest part of the internal man, being full of worldly cravings, first tempts the appetite of the ethereal Spirit with carnal flatteries, since that spirit is itself of the nature of elementary matter. That spirit, subsequently deceived by the allurements of the "idol" <note>likely referring to the false images of sensory pleasure</note>, further deceives the soul itself and drags her down with him to lower things, and thus both are most miserably deceived. Did not this very thing happen to **Eve and Adam**? <note>The author interprets the Fall of Man as an internal psychological process where the lower soul (Eve) seduces the rational spirit (Adam).</note> 

The allurements of this sensitive soul are the love of the body and the craving and pleasures of worldly things, which originate from the **liver**; the **gall bladder** <note>original: "cista fellis"</note> extols the praises of vengeance, wrath, ambition, strife, and arrogance; the **stomach** is irritated by the stings of gluttony and drunkenness; the **spleen** <note>original: "lien"</note> brings a disposition toward envy and a life full of cares and anxiety, inviting the soul to its melancholic lodging; the male organs draw the soul with the pleasure of the flesh and intercourse, etc. If the middle soul consents to these, and slips down into the theater of these iniquities, then the Spirit's reason—having been coerced and made deceitful, and wandering from the truth of the mind—uses false reasons for things as if they were true, and feigns that deceptive and illusory things are real; and thus the soul,

## CHAPTER III.

->*How the mediating soul is sometimes called immortal, and sometimes mortal, and by what reasoning it is said to be in a place.*<-

We have already spoken concerning the immortality of the soul in the final chapter of Book 4 of our *Treatise on the Microcosm* <note>original: "Tractatu nostro de Microcosmo"; referring to Robert Fludd's extensive work on the human being as a "little world" reflecting the universe.</note>. Here, however, we propose to deal with its mortality, alongside the reasoning for its immortality. Indeed, the soul is truly said never to die insofar as it is the image and likeness of the Creator; it is, in fact, a spark from the Creator’s own ray. Hence, it is impossible for it to be enclosed by the boundary of death, since, as an act of God, it can never lose its life or its being. 

Otherwise, according to a certain mobility of its own, by which it can become either better or worse, it is to be considered mortal. For it is thought to be subject to death when it loses the ability to live well; though even then it is called immortal insofar as it cannot lose the ability to live miserably. Hence, if the soul clings to the animal nature and the flesh and is subjected to the world, it is said to "die"—that is, to be thrust down from happiness into misery. But if it is fixed upon the Divine through constant contemplation, it is thought to live and to acquire the name of immortality, and to possess it happily. 

In a similar way, in respect to the incorporeal God, the soul is "corporeal," since nothing should be believed to be invisible and incorporeal by nature except God alone—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. God is called incorporeal and invisible because He is infinite and not at all circumscribed, simple, sufficient unto Himself and in all ways within Himself; and, since He is everywhere, He is recognized as being invisible and incorporeal within Himself. 

Every rational creature, however, is corporeal—that is, fashioned from Spirit as its matter and Light as its form. Thus we say that angels and all the **Virtues** <note>In this context, "Virtues" refers to one of the traditional nine orders of angels.</note> are corporeal, even though they do not consist of flesh. We affirm that intellectual natures are corporeal because they are circumscribed by "place"; just like the human soul, which is enclosed by flesh, and therefore can be said to be "in a place" and "local." It is "in a place" because it is present here and not elsewhere; it is "local" because that which is present to something is not entirely elsewhere. 

Nevertheless, the soul does not have physical dimensions, nor a physical boundary, since it lacks physical quantity. But because it is confined by its presence and operation, it is itself called local. Yet it is not like a body, to which a beginning, middle, and end are assigned according to its location. In respect to the incorporeal nature <note>Meaning the absolute nature of God.</note> which is unchangeable everywhere, the soul is called corporeal because it is not such a thing itself. However, it is not placed or moved through the space of a location such that its larger part occupies a larger place and its smaller part a smaller one, or that it is smaller in a part than in the whole. 

Indeed, it is present as a whole simultaneously through all the particles of the body; it is not smaller in smaller parts, nor larger in larger parts, but in some places more intense, in others more relaxed; it is whole in all parts, and whole in each individual part. For just as God is everywhere in the whole world and in every creature of His, so the soul is everywhere in its whole body, as if in its own world—namely, the **Microcosm**. Yet it is more intense in the brain—just as God is said to be more abundantly present in the **Empyrean heaven** <note>The highest part of the universe, traditionally the home of God and the angels.</note>—and there it acts rationally. Similarly, it is in the heart as if in the Sun of the ethereal world, where it operates effectively and vigorously, just as God is said to be in the heavens. In the other members of the whole body, as they are more or less noble, the soul is perceived to be more or less relaxed or effective. From these things, therefore, we see that as long as the soul keeps itself in the heavens...
