### CHAPTER IV.
->*That the breath of life was given not only to humans, but also to beasts, and concerning the difference between the two breaths, as well as the creation of souls.*<-

Since we gather from Holy Scripture that the breath of life <term>spiraculum vitæ; the divine animating breath mentioned in the Book of Genesis</term> was given not only to humans but also to other animals (for in *Genesis 7* it is read: *All men and all things in which there is the breath of life on the earth died.* And in the same book, *chapter 6: I will destroy all flesh in which there is the Spirit of life*), a significant doubt may therefore arise as to what the difference is between the breath of life of humans and that of beasts. For the solution of this doubt, it must be understood that the *breath of life* in creation is twofold: namely, the first was conferred upon the world to complete the constitution of its fabric, and was breathed by Jehovah on the first day into the primary matter <term>hylam; the formless, chaotic substance from which the universe was fashioned</term>, so that out of nothing—or rather, out of that which did not yet exist in an active state—He might produce something, or indeed all things, into action. For this reason, Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg."</note> called the world the *Son of God*, and all the Platonists called it the *Image of God*. From this divine breath, therefore, the world was immediately created and the waters were given form, from which, according to the teaching of *Genesis*, the world was made; *And the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters, etc.* And by the power of this vivifying and fiery Spirit that gives form to the world, all the world’s creatures received the breath of life indirectly <note>The author uses "mediately," meaning the life force flows from God through the world-soul to the creature.</note>, as if by a certain inhalation of the world flowing from God as its root; so that the Platonists did not speak foolishly, agreeing with Hermes Trismegistus, that *God is the Father of the world, but the world is the parent of all creatures.* That is, God first breathed His spirit of life into the world along with the Word, and by its presence, the world and all its creatures received their powers, both vivifying and otherwise, according to that saying of the Royal Psalmist: *By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their powers by the Spirit from his mouth.* From these things, it is clear that beasts, plants, and minerals received their lives directly from the Soul of the World <term>anima mundi; the "world-soul" believed by Renaissance philosophers to animate all of nature</term>, while the world itself drew its life and spirit from the breath of God. Consequently, it is manifested that the spirit of elementary life proceeded indirectly, and not directly, from God, and that this single breath of life, once breathed into the primary matter at the beginning for the existence of the world, is sufficient to continue the virtue of all creatures until the final "LET IT PERISH" <note>original: "PEREAT"; referring to the end of the material world.</note>. But indeed, man, the prince of all animals—and for that reason called the image and likeness of God no less than the world itself, whence he also obtained the name of the Microcosm <term>Microcosmus; "Little World," the idea that the human being is a miniature map of the entire universe</term>—attained this same grace from the Creator on the last day of creation, just as the world did on the first day. For in the same way that God breathed into the deformed and dark primary matter for the existence of the world on the first day of creation, in the same way, I say, Jehovah breathed that same breath into the obscu—

[...the framework] of man’s external mass; and this was done not immediately, in the way that the rest of the world’s creatures received their form from the world, but it was made immediately by the Creator himself. Hence man is as complete in his essence as the world itself: indeed, there is no nature in the world that is not likewise found in this most noble creature, man, as we have clearly explained above. From this, then, as it seems to me, no doubt or hesitation can be left regarding that opinion which asserts that the soul proceeds by traduction <term>traduce; the doctrine that the soul is transmitted from parents to children through natural generation rather than being newly created by God for each individual</term>. 

For if the first breath of life suffices for the perpetuity of the world and the continuation of its creatures—since, as the Psalmist says, *all the powers of the world and its creatures proceed from the Spirit of his mouth* <note>original: "à Spiritu oris ejus procedunt omnes virtutes mundi & creaturarum ejus"</note>—why should His second breath not likewise suffice, providing the same result without repetition and renewal in the succession of men, just as the first breath does in the continuation and preservation of species in other creatures? Therefore, the contrary opinion <note>Creationism, the view that God creates a new soul for every human being at conception</note> seems to detract from the power of God rather than add any honor to Him; insofar as it seems to argue that God was not as strong and powerful at the end of His creation as He was at the beginning. Otherwise, His Spirit would be believed to be as strong at the end as at the beginning, and consequently, it would perform the same function in the preservation of the Microcosmic species <note>the human race, viewed as a "Little World"</note> as it performs in the Macrocosm <note>the universe or "Great World"</note> and its creatures. 

Indeed, if a single breath of God can continue and preserve the succession of mortal men until the final "LET IT PERISH" <note>original: "PEREAT"; a reference to the end of the world</note>, what need will there be for more? For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts</note> testifies, *it is done in vain through many things when it can be done through fewer* <note>original: "frustrà fiat per plura, quòd potest fieri per pauciora"; a principle of parsimony similar to Ockham's Razor</note>. 

Having considered these things, we see, first of all, how great a difference there is between the breath of life in beasts and that which is in man: namely, that the former is immediately from the world, and thus lacks manifest reason; while the latter is immediately from God, and thus adorns the internal man with intellect and clear reason, joining him with his Creator by its nobility. Next, we see that the divine breath in man differs in no way from that which was communicated to the world. And yet, one and the same breath of the world suffices to perpetuate the species and power of the world and its creatures forever. Therefore, the breath of man will also be sufficient for the continuation of the human species, and consequently, there will be no need for the constant creation of souls. Concerning this argument, however, we shall say no more, since we have already discussed the reason for this doubt quite clearly above.

# TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII.

...[ef]fect, making a man sharper in intellect, weightier in reason, and far deeper than others in divine contemplation, since it emits its invisible and spiritual rays further and more powerfully. Whence it happens that it raises and extols the meditations of the soul higher toward the throne of God. Hence Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of the soul and its ascent to the divine.</note> says regarding the soul:

> *The soul's perfections are more ready for discovery: but its imperfections stand in greater need of external aids; for the former are more mobile of themselves and participate less in the lower nature; but the latter move themselves less, suffering more the bodily lot. These also, when they achieve perfection—namely, rising from the body and gathering themselves from matter—become more fruitful and inventive, immediately concerning those things in which they were previously sterile and ambiguous, due to the unfit sluggishness of life from touching matter, and the filthy torpor contracted from generation.* <note>Proclus refers here to the Neoplatonic idea that entering a physical body (generation) "numbs" the soul, and spiritual perfection requires "gathering" oneself away from material distractions.</note>

Through which Proclus seems to ascribe the greater or lesser effects of the rational soul not to its strength or weakness in its own essence, but rather to the good or bad disposition of the body or its opaque veil. Although the body does something to help or hinder, yet the power of the mind—presiding over the rational spirit—is so great in man that if it is effective and full in its action, the darkness and opacity of the body can in no way resist its influences, since the divine splendor illuminates the darkness within them; indeed, *darkness is not darkness to it, but the night is as clear to it as the day.* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 139:12.</note> Furthermore:

> *The word which, by the testimony of Mercury, is in the mind, is life itself and the light illuminating in the darkness; and the mind itself, which Mercurius Trismegistus calls the soul and essence of God in Pimander 12, rules over all things.* <note>Mercury refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus. The "Pimander" (or Poimandres) is the most famous text in this collection, dealing with creation and the nature of the Mind.</note>

By the copious breath and fullness of this Spirit, the truest and most divine prophets are made from simple men, the most courageous from the faint-hearted, and the most skilled from those ignorant of art or science—if only we give any faith to the Holy Scriptures. And consequently, it follows that the body is not an impediment to the actions of the mind, but rather that either the mind itself, unwilling to act in a wicked body, is said to be idle, or even that its Spirit has not been increased and multiplied by the Most High. Hence Mercury says:

> *The mind is not given to all; and elsewhere he says that it is given to all, but in some—namely in the wicked and impious—it does not act at all, or is idle. In others it acts indeed, but sparingly; but in the good, pious, and reborn, it works abundantly, and is multiplied in another by its inward flows.*

From this, therefore, we see the reason for the variety in the actions of the mind, and that the diversity of its operations is the cause of exaltation and dejection in man; since its more intense benevolence or full presence makes one wise, while its neglect and absence makes them ignorant and not much different from a beast. 

But the reason why one man is more agile and lively than another consists in the good disposition of the <term>middle soul; the anima media, or vital soul, which sits between the divine mind and the physical body</term>, which, since it is in irrational animals as well as rational ones, produces the same effects in any animal. From this comes the animal's lightness in jumping, speed in running, and ease in movement and life. And this disposition for the most part usually happens even to those animals whose body parts are not strong, but weak. Thus it is clear that this animal faculty arises from the source of the middle region—namely, from the heart, in which the middle soul (or the vital and ethereal soul) is cherished. 

Therefore, the cause for the greater or lesser action of the middle soul is provided by the multitude or scarcity of the mundane ray or secondary light, or the soul of the middle heaven, which is also called the <term>Soul of the World; Anima Mundi, the spirit that animates all of nature</term>. And here we recognize with Proclus that the body can do much to hinder the operations of this soul: since this is that portion of the human soul which is said to be weighed down by earthly dregs and burdened by the shadow of the flesh. But indeed, the flowing proportion of this soul produces its effects even against the body's will, as we shall clearly demonstrate by the experiments described below.

One animal of the same species also differs from another in the strength of body and limbs. For this man, or that horse, is stronger and sturdier in composition than another. This habit of the man or animal proceeds not from the middle soul, but from the natural or lowest faculty, or the nature of the <term>animal soul; anima animalis</term> or <term>idol; idolum, the lowest "image" of the soul that governs the physical form and growth</term>, whose...

Its duty is to preserve the members of the body in their strength and vigor, and to restore solid parts—consumed by weakness and wasting—to a valid and robust state. But a bad constitution generates bad, scarce, and poorly nourishing blood; and for this reason, it nourishes the limbs poorly and leaves them weak. For a greater quantity of substantial light produces a more vivacious effect; a lesser quantity, indeed, a lesser one; and this is seen in different individuals of the same species. For example, we see that a doubled portion of gunpowder <note>original: "pulveris bombardici"</note> multiplies the explosive force of a war engine <note>original: "tormenti bellici," referring to a cannon.</note>; and consequently, it is known to carry the weight of the iron or lead ball higher or further.

From this also arises the difference of all species in any genus of animals and plants. Thus the spirit of minerals, which comes from the darkness of the lowest heaven <note>The sublunary or terrestrial realm, closest to the center of the Earth.</note>, differs from the spirit of vegetables, which comes partly from the middle spirit and partly from the lowest. Hence, vegetables are related to minerals by origin and nature, but their spirits are diverse. TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII.

...and the light in man differs from the spirit and light of other animals no less than the inflamed and burning **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini"; refers to highly distilled alcohol, which was considered a "spiritual" and pure substance in 17th-century alchemy.</note> differs from the oil and liquid ignited in a lamp. For, just as the fire from the spirit of wine is composed of a spirit that is partly airy and partly ethereal (wherefore its thinner ignited part does not consume by burning), yet the fire of a lamp retains only an airy and more thick nature, so that it burns up flammable material; so also is the case in the difference between those two souls—namely, of man and of brute animals. For as the spirit of wine is far subtler than oil, and yet both are spirits; so too the spirits of both species are both indeed of a spiritual disposition, but they differ in rarity and purity as the spirit of wine differs from oil, or air from ether, or ether from the intellectual spirit.

## CHAPTER IV.
### That the human soul by its own nature embraces unity, but with respect to matter inclines toward multiplicity.

The human soul, by itself in its nature and origin, embraces unity; for its prince and summit is the **mind** <note>original: "mens"; in this context, the highest, most divine part of the soul that connects directly to God.</note> itself, or a ray of that unity, so connected and continuous with the supernatural unity or essence as a ray of the Sun is to its body. Through the mind, therefore, the middle portion of the soul is raised toward unity, just as we see in the nature of fire, which, in ascending upward, forms an acute angle visible to bodily eyes. By this very act, it signifies <note>brevigraph for "that"</note> that it vehemently attempts and desires to ascend with spiritual wings to the cone of the **material pyramid** <note>The author, likely Robert Fludd, used the concept of two intersecting pyramids—one of Light/Form and one of Matter—to explain the composition of the universe.</note>; for in the extreme point of the cone or angle, uniformity and unity alone are found. Furthermore, the middle soul, since it is a ray of the world, or a secondary light, is also called—as **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of wisdom texts (Hermetica) combining philosophy, alchemy, and magic.</note> testifies—the "second mind" or the "image of the first mind." From this, it is manifest that its unity is the origin from which its acts gush forth. It is clear, therefore, that the portions of the internal man, insofar as he is formal <note>Relating to "Form" or the spiritual blueprint of a thing, rather than its physical matter.</note> in his essence, look back toward the fountain of their existence by their own self and by a kind of natural instinct. But it has been so brought about by the divine will that—to speak with **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul's descent into the physical world.</note>—

> so that to the soul descending, there are born from the world multiform lives and various garments, drawing it indeed into a perishable composition.

Which **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Porphyry, known for his works on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine.</note> also confirms thus:

> The soul, he says, which glides downward, drawing with it the signs of bonds and punishments, and of material spirits, shows itself burdened and occupied by the dissimilar perturbations of matter. From which it is manifest that the substance of the soul has fallen away from the state of unity into the abyss of multiplicity—that is, from a simple purity into a foul and impure composition.

Hence **Proclus** says:

> The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from the divine souls, by whom it was filled with intelligence and power, simplicity, and purity. But it has joined itself to generation and nature, and to material things, by which it has been imbued with oblivion, error, and ignorance.

Now, what formal and divine unity is, and how it exists as constant in itself, immutable, indivisible, not to be multiplied, and how nothing is to be subtracted from it or added to it (since it is the whole and without it there is nothing), we have declared clearly enough in our **Treatise on Divine and Abstruse Numbers**. However, as matter descends further from the cone of its pyramid toward its base, it is thereafter more and more multiplied, because in tending downward it always turns out thicker; so that in the upper region its grades are increased by the number ten, in the middle by a hundred, and in the lowest by a thousand—as we have also delineated in its proper place earlier in that same Treatise, both by words and by a living demonstration. From this, therefore, it is manifest, according to the opinions of Proclus and Iamblichus expressed above, that the more the soul tends downward—that is, toward the base of the material pyramid—the more it is immersed in the multitude of matter.

This page explores the opposite pull: how matter fragments that unity into the "multiplicity" of the physical world, and how knowledge can lead the soul back to its source.</meta>

->ON THE MEDICINAL ACTION OF THE SOUL'S SPIRIT IN THE BODY<-

The abundance of matter, desiring to be given form, divides that universal soul—which revolves around unity—into infinite parts, giving these parts to each member of the multitude. From this comes the multitude of species and individuals; from this comes the ignorance of the uniform soul, now divided into parts, its forgetting of itself, and its errors; and from this comes its sorrow in such a captivity. For, according to *Proclus* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on how the soul descends into the physical world.</note>, souls are sick and delirious as if in a human body; or as *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a student of Plotinus, often used the metaphor of "slumber" to describe the soul's state when distracted by the senses.</note> suggests, they sleep perpetually in the body. For this reason, *Iamblichus* says that the property of souls is an inclination toward multiplicity and the motion of generation <note>original: "motum generationis"; refers to the process of being born and creating new physical life.</note>, even though by themselves and in their own nature they look toward the unity of the Deity, which is permanent in itself and yet the unmoving cause of all motions. 

For since it is the nature of the soul to always be in motion, insofar as it is a simple act, it produces multiplicity through its own motion by accident, by means of generation. Indeed, the bodies that enclose the souls and blind their eyes are accustomed to turn the motions of the souls toward their own appetites, which revolve around multiplicity. And thus it happens that the soul's motion in bodies produces the generations and growth of individuals of every species. This same thing even occurs in human bodies, which enclose the most noble form; it is their unique privilege, by virtue of divine splendor, to possess a soul more exalted than other creatures. Whence it happens that the soul, although bound in its prison by spiritual chains, sometimes remembers its homeland; and its vision, on the wings of divine rays, is sometimes raised on high, according to that saying of *Iamblichus*: *The soul heard a divine harmony in the intelligible world <note>original: "mundo intelligibili"; the realm of pure thought and divine forms, as opposed to the visible world.</note>, which it remembers here when it hears melodies that bear a divine trace; and remembering it, the soul is vehemently moved toward it.* 

Similarly, according to *Synesius* <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note>, there is also in those who have fallen down to this place *a certain power calling them back to heaven*, etc. Indeed, to holy men—and even in this life—the way is revealed by which the human soul, by leaving behind multiplicity, can return to unity, which *Mercurius* <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note> calls the way of regeneration: namely, the breathing-in and flowing-in of the divine spirit. And even *Proclus* seems to depict for us a certain way by which we can return from multiplicity to unity: namely, the acquisition of knowledge <note>original: "scientiae acquisitionem"; "scientia" in this context refers to true, certain knowledge of the cosmos and its laws.</note>. Whence he says *that the soul, through acquired knowledge, becomes like the mind; that is, the soul, by leaving behind multiplicity through the power and illumination of knowledge, approaches unity.* 

For all multiplicity is so diverse in itself that some things seem contrary to others in every respect. Therefore, if we wish to ascend to unity, where there is no contrariety, it will be necessary to apply ourselves to true knowledge, in which multiplicity has no opposition. For although passions are contrary to passions, and likewise senses to senses, thought to thoughts, and opinion to opinions, yet no knowledge is found to be contrary to another knowledge. Indeed, in knowledge we gather a multitude of propositions and notions into one; we also connect a number of sciences by a certain single bond. Thus, far from being contrary to each other, even notion serves notion, and the lower sciences serve the higher, and thus the latter have their beginnings from the former. 

So we see many notions of Geometry contribute to a single Theorem and its demonstration; thus we notice that points, lines, angles, and surfaces, with their respective notions, are referred to a body or to three dimensions. Thus we see numbering, addition, subtraction, and multiplication depend on one another and are necessary for division and the extraction of roots. So also the rules or propositions concerning sounds, tones, semitones, the Fourth, the Fifth, the Octave <note>original: "Diatessaron, Diapente, Diapason"; these are the fundamental musical intervals that Fludd believed mirrored the structure of the universe.</note> and the notions designating the proportions of temporal signs all lead to the truth of a single symphony. And although such notions exist in multiplicity, they nevertheless denote a single thing: namely, melody. Likewise, we perceive that Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Optics lead to the cognition of Astrological truth. There is, therefore, no contrariety in the multitude of sciences, since they lead to unity; but there is contrariety in the multitude of matter, which always distracts and wanders...

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII.

...and departs from unity. It is necessary, therefore, having understood the multitude of sciences, to hasten from those which propose only one specific thing toward the One itself. For this reason, let compositions, divisions, and complex discourses be set aside, and let a transition be made toward the intellectual life and simple contemplations. For, to use the words of *Proclus*, <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who described the soul's journey back to its divine source.</note> *science is not the highest peak of knowledge, but more eminent than it is the intellect and the illumination of the soul: for it is through the intellect alone that we may know the boundaries—namely, one of unity and the other of multitude.* Therefore, the multitude must be fled through the steps of knowledge preceding in their own order; but we shall also proceed hereafter in a similar way through the steps of knowable things to prove this same point. All sensible things <note>Things perceived through the physical senses.</note> must be avoided, since they are crowded together, divided, and utterly changeable. Let us, therefore, transfer ourselves from these to the incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has an external <note>original: "adventitiam," meaning something added from the outside rather than being essential to its nature.</note> unity, and is dispersed through itself and full of weakness. Because of this, its "good" is divisible, external, distant and discordant from itself, and residing in a foreign seat. But when we have ascended there, and have been situated within the body [of truth], we shall behold that soulful order moving above bodies by its own power, acting through itself, and possessing its own substance in and from itself. Let us then leave behind the multitude that is foreign to our souls, and by cutting through the ether and ascending even further upward, let us betake ourselves to the intellect and the intellectual realms, so that we may possess the unity of things and there become contemplators of that nature. We shall behold that nature remaining in eternity—a vigorous life, a vigilant intelligence that lacks nothing of life. Thus, when we find this, we will very easily observe how much more suitable and better it is for souls, and we will see whether any multitude is found in it, and whether it is uniform or multiform. Here, then, you will perceive that highest good which the human soul always desires to reach. Here is the source and origin of all created things. Here is the summit and peak of joy and gladness. Here is true and sole simplicity and that truth of which *Plato* and *Pythagoras* speak *when they admonish us so greatly to flee the multitude so that we may attain the simplest truth.* Indeed, so that we may do this, they prescribe a way and method for us that does not differ from the path of *Proclus*; namely, that we must avoid the varied multitude *first of the passions, then of the senses, thirdly of imaginations, and fourthly of the opinions depending on them.*

<margin>*</margin> And the judgments of these things do not seem to differ in any way from our intention. For, when the soul is enclosed in darkness, it uses the sense as if it were its leader. From this, its sharp focus is then turned toward so many subjects in the third [level], that they produce uncertainty and inconstancy in the soul; and thus the rays of the soul, distracted by so many and such great objects of the senses and the contemplation of them, allow their sharpness to be blunted, so that they cannot penetrate to the throne and seat of unity. In this way, the soul becomes doubtful as to whether it should turn itself toward finding the truth, insofar as it is no less deceived in matter than it is deceived by the illusions <term>præstigiis: tricks, sleights of hand, or deceptive appearances</term> of the matter surrounding it. Therefore, *Proclus* says not ineptly: *just as matter seems to have all things, though in truth it possesses nothing, so too the soul, suffering from a double ignorance, seems to itself to possess what it does not.* And this happens because of the manifold effect of the sense. For this reason, the multitude of the external senses must first be cast away. Finally, we must not conceive in our imagination the fictional, vain, and false things that are like phantoms conceived in the air; for these likewise distract us from that unity which is the sole truth. And furthermore, we do not think that the opinions of men—which contradict themselves and the truth—should be believed in any way. Thus, at last, by returning toward unity through the steps of the millenary scale <note>A symbolic ladder of 1,000 steps representing a high degree of spiritual ascent.</note>, we shall ascend to the middle heaven, where we will find greater certainty and perfection. ### CHAPTER VII.
### Why this middle soul has given only vegetative life to vegetables and plants, while it grants sense along with vegetation to all animals?

We have indeed spoken some words previously regarding the variety and difference between the soul of vegetables and animals. However, in this place, we will discuss more broadly the difference and distinction of the soul in these kinds of creatures. We declared elsewhere in the preceding sections that the souls of vegetables are from the clearer spirit of the "middle darkness" of the second day of creation, reverberated downward from the middle heaven of the world, with portions or sparks of the "second light" enclosed within it. And we demonstrated there that this same spirit is also the soul of all animals. But to some, it will perhaps seem absurd or hardly probable that the same light with such a spirit should be the origin of both creatures (since they are separated by such great difference); for they will argue that the same things cannot differ so much from themselves. To whom we answer, that the soul of a plant does not differ from the soul of an animal except according to "more and less" <note>A philosophical concept where two things share the same essence but differ in intensity or degree.</note>.

We will briefly declare here the reason why the plant has less of the "middle nature," while the animal has a more abundant portion of it. Sacred Scripture teaches us that plants and vegetables, rising from the pores of the earth, were created with the earth itself on the third day of creation; at which time, indeed, the celestial rays were not yet contracted into the Sun, but were diffused through the universal mundane spirit <note>The *spiritus mundanus* or World Spirit, a subtle substance that permeates the universe.</note> and especially dilated and dispersed around the celestial spirit. <margin>But as according to that old axiom of the Philosophers, *united force is stronger; so, when dissipated, it is weaker.*</margin> From this it came to pass that the soul of the plant was not as strong, luminous, clear, and effective in performing its functions as is the soul of animals, which arose from the celestial rays having been narrowed and simultaneously collected and united into the solar body. 

For on the third day of creation, before the creation of the Sun, light was equally dispersed around the earth and mixed and involved with dense and thick vapors of *hyle* <note>original: "hylæ," referring to primordial matter or the basic "stuff" of the universe before it is organized by light.</note>; whence it happened that it was obscure, and no more to be compared to the beauty of the Sun than the splendor of a shining cloud can be compared to the Sun, or illuminated air to fire. But after all the rays of heaven were gathered into the solar spirit, leaping upward from the earth with sparks of its light, the wonderful effects of the rays contracted together suddenly revealed themselves to the world. First fish, then birds, and finally animals were procreated. Thus, according to the increase of the Sun's dominion—or rather the operation of its predominance over the rebellious vapors of matter, which were elevating and exhaling themselves upward from the earth into the elementary region—the soul was produced day by day, gradually stronger and more powerful, and brought into the light through creation. 

Thus, the wonderful operation of the Sun in the production of more perfect creatures is clearly demonstrated, and consequently, the deficiency of vegetables is explained. For only dilated rays of light and coarser spirits concurred in their creation, so that no help from the Sun—that most noble and vivacious creature produced from rays contracted together with spirit—was present in the work of the vegetable. Having considered these things again and again, we shall perceive...

TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII.

...[we have shown] that the spirit of vegetables is coarser and thicker than the spirit of animals, since its rays were weaker; for the refinement and purification of spirits consists in the abundance and vigor of the rays of light. Thus, just as the power of the light is—namely, greater or lesser—so also is the rarity and purity of the spirit greater or lesser. But light, before the creation of the Sun, was more diffused: therefore, it was less powerful. It follows, then, that in plants, the portion of the soul is coarser in its spirit and scanter and thinner in its light than in animals. For this reason, it happens that the souls of these two types of living beings differ from one another. 

Indeed, we find another difference between the nature and essence of these mentioned souls, since the soul of animals, flowing from the Sun, claims for itself the property of a solar nature—which we said above was forged from the light and Spirit leaping out from the darkness of the <term>empyrean heaven</term> <note>The highest, most "fiery" heaven in ancient cosmology, believed to be the home of pure light and the divine.</note>; and therefore we demonstrated above that it is a participant in reason. However, the soul of vegetables, drawing its origin from the spirit and light of the darkness of the <term>ethereal or middle heaven</term>, possesses neither a spirit nor light capable of reason, nor can it be compared in the simplicity and purity of its form with the soul of animals. From this it follows that, while plants are slow in their movement and are fixed to the earth and remain immobile, we see that animals are light, subtle, agile, swift, and move here and there by a certain will. This, then, is the difference of lives in both of those types of living beings; this is the reason for dignity in one, and for depression and lowliness in the other, since one is richer in fire and celestial Spirit, while the other is more dejected by poverty and moisture.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*That the vital soul is composed of innate heat and radical moisture, and that it participates in the nature of the Sun; likewise concerning the pyramidal shape of the heart, and that it is the palace of the vital soul; and how this soul, by means of the Spirit, is dispensed through the whole body.*<-

Since both the ancient Philosophers and the princes of Medicine are accustomed to make frequent mention of **innate heat** and **radical moisture**—from the mixture of which they say life arises—it seems worthwhile for us to briefly declare what this heat and likewise this moisture are. Those more skilled in the secrets of nature are accustomed to say that heat is derived from motion, and motion from the act or the moving principle. Certainly, heat is nothing other than the effect of motion, just as motion is nothing other than the action or act of visible or invisible light. Hence it is manifest that where there is heat, motion is also present, and consequently, with motion, there is essential light acting as the mover. 

From this, it happens that heat is understood by some as the effect of motion, or as a mere quality, or sometimes as the mover itself. For in the works of <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC); the author is likely quoting from the treatise *On Flesh* (*De Carnibus*).</note>, we find it written: *That mortal substance <note>original: "Illud mortale." Note that many classical versions of this text read "immortale" (immortal). The author here treats it as "essential and endowed with immortality" despite the OCR reading "mortale."</note>, which we call heat, when all things were in turmoil, flew to the highest region, which the ancients called the **ether**.* Here, therefore, Hippocrates did not take heat for a mere quality or accident, but for an essential thing endowed with immortality; namely, for the universal substantial light, from whose nature that portion of living beings is derived which is called **innate heat**. Without the motion and heated effect of this heat, the lives of creatures could in no way have been brought forth, since its presence [governs] the rebellious dispositions of the compounded elements...

This Spirit is, as it were, the vehicle, the fuel, and that passive moisture through whose presence and intervention heat and light—by way of <note>original: 'metonymiam'; a figure of speech where the effect is named for the cause.</note> metonymy, taking the effect for the cause—are carried downward (because Spirit has a natural relation to Spirit) and act upon a well-disposed subject. And this spirit is called "radical" for this reason: because it was joined with the heat in the first creation. Or, it is like the root and tree of solar fruits; or it is the root and material origin of the creature, through whose limbs or members it runs. So also, that light or heat can be called "innate," insofar as it is the first boundary and point from which it moves toward generation. Or it is called "innate" as if "born-together" with that natural moisture which is the ethereal spirit, in which it lives and grants life to the creature in which it dwells.

When these things are properly considered, we will perceive that this <term>innate heat</term> <note>The internal heat believed by ancient physicians to be the source of life and digestion.</note> in its <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The fundamental life-fluid that acts as the 'oil' for the lamp of innate heat.</note> is nothing other than that **fifth essence** <note>original: 'quintam essentiam'; the purest, incorruptible element beyond the four earthly elements.</note>, through whose harmony in the **perfect fifth** <note>original: 'Diapente'; a musical interval of a fifth, used here to represent cosmic harmony.</note>, the dissonance of the **quaternary** <note>original: 'quaternarii'; the number four, representing the four potentially conflicting elements: earth, air, fire, and water.</note>—which is an even and imperfect number—is reduced to a peaceful concord. Therefore, the Philosophers, both the theoretical and those practiced in the work of Chemistry, have passed down wonders concerning the virtue and power of this fifth essence. For they seem to recognize that it is nothing other than the union of the ethereal Spirit with its own lucid soul. For this reason, they have asserted that the fifth essence of a thing is the same as that **vital soul** <note>original: 'anima illa vitalis'.</note>, which they affirmed emanates from the middle sphere of the ether (which they called the sphere of equality, and in which they placed the **world soul** <note>original: 'animam mundi'; the soul of the universe that connects all living things.</note>).

For even the common folk and those entirely ignorant of literature know and have discovered through experience that plants and trees turn green again every year and become young again, as it were, and possess a multiplication of visible light from its abundance, as if from a glorious fountain. Furthermore, it is also the opinion of the wiser Philosophers that "the Sun and man produce man." <note>A classic Aristotelian principle suggesting that human life is generated by both the biological parent and the celestial heat of the sun.</note> From these things, therefore, it is evident that the lives of creatures are of the essence of the Sun and are, as it were, its nurseries, sent down from its perennial fountain. Hence some have said that the heaven is like the male part of the entire world, while the earth and its elements are the female part; or rather, that the earth is the universal matrix, receiving into itself the golden seeds of the heaven and the Sun, which pass into innumerable creatures of every species through digestion in the womb of matter.

This mobile matter, upon the application of fire, suddenly liquefied and became like blood; but then, just as suddenly, it was reduced back to its former immobile shape, like a crystal decorated on all sides with golden rays. I also saw clearly enough that the garment and vehicle there was the Spirit. Whence I perceived with intellectual eyes that, by the same logic, the soul is the garment of the divine mind, just as the Spirit is the garment of the soul. ### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII.

...this soul is infused as a whole into the whole [body], and into every part of the body; we must ask what is the principal seat of this soul in the human body. For it is said that God’s throne is in heaven, even though His presence is at hand everywhere; or rather (lest we compare divine things to earthly ones) we see that the solar body is in the heart of the heavens, and yet its rays and presence are found through its action everywhere. 

We know, therefore, by diligent inquiry, that the principal seat of the vital soul is no less in the **heart**, which is situated in the middle of the middle Microcosmic region, than the Sun's seat is in the middle of the sky. If we rightly consider the figure and position of this palace of life, we will perceive that it was ordered and arranged from creation according to the image, likeness, and position of the <term>pyramid of the formal world</term> <note>In Fludd's philosophy, the "formal world" refers to the realm of divine light and ideas, often represented as a pyramid of light descending from God.</note>; for its base tends upward, while its cone points downward. By this it seems to be known that this bodily organ is an instrument chiefly occupied with the vital form: for indeed, the vital rays undoubtedly delineated its pyramidal shape for us, as their nature is to shoot their rays downward toward the earth.

Therefore, this life-giving Spirit exists with its royal light in the heart, as if in its own proper sphere. From there, it scatters its rays—which are its connected essences—through the entire body, no differently than the Sun is accustomed to emit and shoot its rays from its middle sphere in the sky to the lowest and most distantly situated parts of the world. It runs, therefore, through the veins into the mass or "bloody sea," and the airy waves of the body, and finally through the limbs and more solid parts, just as the rays of the Sun go through the elements into the airy and watery sea so that they may finally refresh the earth and its dense members. And it is from this that we are taught by Holy Scripture that <note>original: "sanguinem esse animarum quasi vestem"</note> **blood is, as it were, the garment and receptacle of souls.** 

How this happens is succinctly demonstrated by the divine Philosophers. The soul, carried downward through its medium, is first infused into the middle point of the heart, which is the center of the human body, and from there is diffused through all the body’s parts and limbs, when it joins its "chariot" to the natural heat, and through that heat to the Spirit arising from the heart. Through this Spirit it immerses itself in the humors, and through those humors it clings to the limbs; and it becomes equally close to all of these, even though it is transfused through one thing into another; just as the heat of a fire clings closely to air and water, even though it is carried through the air to reach the water. Thus it is clear that the ethereal vehicle of the immortal soul is enclosed by a thicker and mortal body. 

Similarly, <note>original: "Merc. Trismeg." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Hermeticism.</note> **Hermes Trismegistus** says: *The Spirit diffused into the veins and arteries and the blood moves the animal on all sides, and the soul in the spirit holds the mass of the body suspended and carries it about; reason is in the soul, and the mind is in the reason.* 

By these words he teaches us very well how all the internal parts of man are dispensed through the whole human body by means of the Spirit. However, we cannot agree with him in this one respect: that the mind, or reason, or vital soul are transferred into all the members of the body through the Spirit and are present everywhere in their actual essences in equal portions. Rather, we say that the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"</note> in the rational Spirit inhabits the upper region of the Microcosm <note>The head.</note> as a more worthy place; and the **Soul** possesses its middle region <note>The chest/heart.</note> as its natural seat. 

But we say these things exist there in their regions just as God is in the highest heaven and the Sun is in the middle. For God, sitting in heaven, sends the rays of His presence into all parts of the world, according to that saying of the Wise Man in <note>original: "Sap. 1." The Book of Wisdom.</note> Wisdom 1: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world.* And in Jeremiah: *He made heaven His throne and the earth His footstool.* 

So also the human mind, derived from divine stock, scatters the rays of its presence through the nerves (as if through mediums) everywhere into the lower parts of the body, yet it itself sits constantly at the summit of the Microcosm above the intellectual Spirit, as if carried on the "wings of the winds." Similarly, just as the Sun, possessing its position in the heart of the sky, communicates form to things below it by its rays, and is said to be diffused everywhere through the elements by its power, essential light, and influence; so also the essence of the soul, sitting constantly in the human heart, [scatters] its rays of life into all...

### ON THE ACTION OF THE MIDDLE MICROCOSMIC SOUL IN THE BODY

...is known to disperse throughout the parts of man, both solid and fluid, while yet remaining in the heart itself, no less than the essence of the Sun remains in the middle of the sky or the solar body; this is not unsuitably attributed to the heart. Therefore, the aerial spirit—which is most familiar to the body—flows and pours through all its limbs in the form of blood and humor, carrying with it the traces of the Ethereal Spirit. In the streams of this spirit, the rays of ethereal light (or rays of nature) are carried, in which the intellect and rational Spirit are emitted from on high like certain atoms, or rather <term>insensible habits</term> <note>Fludd means qualities or dispositions that cannot be perceived by the senses but reside within the spirit.</note>, upon which and in which the Spirit of the Lord and the finest rays of His mind are perceived to float immediately. 

Just as from a certain source—in which there is a mass of saffron, a collection of blood, or even a cloth recently dipped in ink—we see the entire stream exiting from it becomes colored, even though the coloring principle always rests within the source itself. Hence, every limb of the body is moved toward what is good or useful according to the determination of the mind, with reason showing the way. 

From this it also happens that any limb is moved by reason of the rays of the vital soul, both according to the direction of the rational Spirit (namely, by voluntary motion) and according to the faculties of life (by involuntary motion). For the middle soul moves the joints and limbs of man for life, and reason governs that movement so that it happens according to the mind's intentions—unless that soul, being subjected to the <term>natural soul</term> <note>The "natural soul" refers to the lower, vegetative functions shared with plants and animals, such as growth and digestion.</note>, moves in an irrational course like the beasts. Therefore, the middle light becomes the first mover in an animated being, and its Spirit (or vehicle) is that which is moved first; finally, by its motion, the body is stirred and driven to perform its functions. 

For it will not be impossible to take a very evident demonstration of this from a lower, contracted light (or common fire) combined with air. By the presence of fire, we see the external air moved and led here and there according to the motion of that fire or life. From this we also perceive that images painted on paper are moved around together with the paper itself by the power of a lit candle (as we shall say below), where the light of the candle excites motion, the motion stirs the air, and the air, by its motion and agitation, carries around the bodily dimension of the paper and images. <note>This likely refers to a "lanterna magica" or a heat-driven carousel where the rising heat from a candle causes a paper cylinder with figures to rotate.</note>

From this, it is manifest that the nature of motion is the same in the lowest fire as it is in the middle, and the same in the middle as in the highest. However, the action of the lower fire is more blunted due to the abundance of resisting matter than the celestial action; and again, the celestial action is more repressed for the same reason than the super-celestial. We conclude, therefore, that we are permitted through experiments in this lowest region—taken from the mutual actions of fire and air—to investigate the higher mysteries and, in a way, to perceive the mutual operations of the heavens.

### TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII. 

It is also proven that this lower fire is very close in affinity to the celestial fire, even by the single fact that, through its own power in the correct proportion, it is accustomed to hatch eggs and produce chicks just as successfully as the natural heat of a hen derived from the higher realms. For this experiment has been found and made manifest not only in parts of Africa, but even in Europe itself, and has been proven in these our own days; namely, that chicks were led out from their own shells or husks and brought into the light by the benefit of a moderately warm furnace, yet they lived according to the custom of nature. Similarly, in a heated <term>hypocaust</term> <note>original: "hypocausto"; an underfloor heating system or a room heated by one, used here like a greenhouse</note>, we perceive that flowers and shrubs not yet budding suddenly bloom by the power of fiery heat and push forth their inner parts.

But, to ascend now to the celestial fire, do we not say that *the Sun and man beget man*? <note>original: "Solem & hominem procreare hominem"; a common Aristotelian maxim in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> Here, by "the Sun," the entire fiery substance of heaven is understood, from whose spark—combined with the specific form of man—a human is generated. Do we not also see that the worms of the earth receive their bodies from the earth, but receive the form or soul by which they live from the ethereal region? Whence the Philosophers maintain that they are generated through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The historical theory that living organisms could arise from decaying organic matter</note>. This was also the Poet's <note>Likely referring to Ovid</note> opinion regarding the generation of the serpent *Python* from the rays of the Sun and the mud of the earth, mixed with a small amount of watery moisture after the deluge. 

We ourselves have been taught by similar experience; for the entire substance of a dead raven, hung in a place exposed to the Sun or in a sunny spot, was turned into innumerable worms within the space of a few days by the Sun’s life-giving power. We also read in several authors that bees emerged in great numbers from the head of an ox by the operation of celestial heat; these bees certainly did not receive their souls from a dead thing, but from the celestial rays. Furthermore, is that heat of horse manure much inferior to this fire? By its power, hairs are very often turned into worms and snakes; I have seen animals of this kind with my own eyes. 

And what should we think of that monster which, bearing the form of a Dragon, was found in a certain cave receiving putrid and foul waters, along with the blood of animals flowing down through a pipe from the kitchen of a certain English nobleman? It surely received its soul, without a doubt, from the light full of heat within the decay, but the substance of its body from the putrid and, as it were, <term>menstrual</term> <note>In early modern science, this referred to a "prime matter" or a generative fluid that provides the material for a body</note> matter, after the example of that *Python*. *Diodorus Siculus* also narrates that after the flooding of the Nile, when the water had almost dried up and the earth—having taken the form of mud—was made drier by the Sun, many beasts were created as if anew; among these, he records that some were found created only halfway, while others were found with a completed form. 

By all these examples, it is manifest that the vital souls suited to living bodies are nothing other than celestial rays and sparks, as it were, derived from the luminous fountain of the universe, which we have named above as the "acts of nature." Since, therefore, the matter stands thus in these two lower heavens, why should reason and intellect not also proceed from that universal fountain of super-celestial light, of which they are rays, since they are the acts of that Creator? Not only have the Philosophers called these rays "super-celestial and divine," but also those more skilled in Theology. 

At this point, however, a certain doubt comes to our memory which is not unworthy of resolution, namely: *Whether the soul is nourished by some food or not?* It is certain that the soul requires its own proper food for its presence no less than other things in nature have need of their nourishment; this can surely be demonstrated by many arguments. For we see that the action of any body whatsoever proceeds from the soul. Yet its entire operation is occupied with nourishment: namely, in the appetite for food, its preparation, its attraction to the stomach, its retention, its conversion into blood, and other similar tasks. Therefore, it seems the vital soul requires nourishment for the preservation of itself as much as for its "machine" <note>the body</note>. ...the light of the soul may be extinguished and die. We also observe that fire requires the presence of air, as if it were the food for its life. For if a burning fire is enclosed in a place surrounded by walls so that air cannot enter, it will suddenly be extinguished and, as it were, killed. From this it is certain that the food of the lower fire is air, and that the nourishment of the ethereal fire is the Ethereal Spirit. 

But what of this? Shall the vital soul therefore die? Certainly, as far as we are concerned, it dies, and as far as we are concerned, it requires nourishment; yet, if we consider the nature of light with our intellectual eyes, it is clear that it requires neither food, nor does it die. For although the soul, as well as light and fire, seems to desire an aerial <term>fuel</term> <note>original: "fomitem"; literally touchwood or kindling, used here to mean the material that sustains a flame</note> for itself, it does not do so out of a necessity for food, as if it could not live without it; but rather so that it might obtain a passive medium upon which it may act, as if upon a well-disposed subject. 

For it is impossible for light, which is pure action, to exist unless it acts upon some subject; for it always acts, and never ceases to act upon some subject, whether to a greater or lesser degree. However, the effects of its action do not aim to nourish itself, but rather to first heat the passive subject, and through its heat to thin and refine it, and finally to exalt that refined thing, transforming it from a corporeal matter into a spiritual one. Hence we see that when the soul cannot find other sufficient food to act upon, it consumes its own "tabernacle" <note>A metaphor for the physical body</note>; just as we see in those suffering from <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "tabidis"; refers to wasting diseases where the body appears to be eaten away from within</note>. From this it is certain that the soul does not work for its own sake, but for the sake of the matter—both spiritual and material—with which it dwells. 

But indeed, that <term>innate moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum illud innatum"; in Renaissance medicine, this was the vital fluid thought to be the "oil" for the lamp of life, preventing the body's heat from burning itself out</note> born within it is suited to it and lasts forever with it; it is like <term>Psyche</term> <note>The Greek personification of the Soul</note> joined with <term>Cupid</term> <note>The god of Desire/Love</note> in perfect love. And although fire, when the wood is burned or the air excluded, seems to be suddenly suffocated, it does not die; rather, because of the lack of a continuous supply of thicker air, it is dissipated through the air (whether enclosed or open), and thus becomes invisible again, just as it was before. For the entire air is filled with invisible fire, which is invisible precisely because it is dispersed and thinned throughout the medium. 

Fire therefore seems to be extinguished and deprived of life when it returns to its invisible nature; for indeed, those things we see in the body and in matter behave in a different and contrary way within the soul. For the more the body ages, the more it is weakened, while conversely, the longer the soul lives in the body, the more it grows young again, and grows rich in knowledge, counsel, and wisdom. Likewise, the weight of the body lies in heaviness, but the soul's weight lies in lightness and subtlety, for its perfection consists in degrees of these qualities. And so it is with other things. # OF THE FIRST TRACTATE, SECTION I.
## BOOK IX.
### On the action of the sensitive soul in the body.

### CHAPTER I.
#### *On the properties of the sensitive or animal soul, or the lower portion of the internal man, in the human body.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' set within a square frame featuring a central floral motif and scrolling leafy borders.</image-desc>Although the <term>middle soul</term> <note>original: "anima media"; in Fludd’s philosophy, this is the mediating spirit between the divine Mind (mens) and the physical body</note> is by its own nature of the freest condition, and of infinite dignity, knowledge, beauty, and perfection; nevertheless, insofar as it is understood as one with the mind which it carries within itself, and is overshadowed too much by the decaying body, it is to that extent weighed down. Against its true nature, it is made prone to contemplating lower things, as if it were deprived of its spiritual eyes. And hence it is that it is led by the senses against its nature, and by looking downward against that nature of hers, she is rendered inclined to contemplating and admiring vile and abject things; for her natural disposition, when she is free from the body, urges her—according to the nature of a fiery flame—to strive upward and look upon higher things. Therefore, the middle soul enclosed in the body has two guides: the higher and more noble of which allures her to the good and exhorts her to occupy herself with celestial meditations. The lower guide, however, solicits her to embrace evil and vile things and the effects of darkness. Thus, this soul seems to be placed in the middle between two extremes that differ in condition and disposition, according to that saying of <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonic philosopher who organized the works of Plotinus.</note> **Porphyry** in *Occasions*: *The middle soul is between the indivisible essence, which is the intellect, and the essence that is divisible among true bodies. However, qualities and material forms are divisible according to bodies.* <note>original: "Anima media est inter essentiam individuam, quæ est intellectus, & essentiam in vera corpora divisibilem. Qualitates autem, materialesque formæ secundùm corpora sunt divisibiles."</note> **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers, influential in shaping medieval theology.</note> also describes the miserable conjunction of this lowest portion of the internal man with the middle soul in this way: *The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from the divine souls, by which it was filled with intelligence, power, and purity; but it has joined it to generation and nature, to material things, by which it is imbued with error, forgetfulness, and ignorance. For to the descending soul are born multiform lives from the world, and various garments, drawing it indeed into a decaying composition, but obstructing the contemplation of separated things.* <note>original: "Animæ in corpus descensus sejunxit quidem illam à divinis animis... conjunxit verò generationi & naturæ materialibus rebus... Nam animæ descendenti adnatæ sunt ex mundo multiformes vitæ, vestesq́; variæ..."</note> **Iamblichus** <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist known for his work on theurgy and Egyptian mysteries.</note> also seems to assert this same thing in *The Mysteries*: *The human soul,* he says, *from the*

<header>ON THE ACTION OF THE SENSITIVE SOUL IN THE BODY.</header>

...is encompassed and overshadowed by the decaying body; for which reason it has no effective power toward divine works. If ever we truly seem to be capable of such a thing in some way, we act only by a divine illustration flowing down from above, through which we also seem to be participants in divine action. Similarly, elsewhere: *The soul, which falls downward, dragging with it the signs of its bonds and punishments, shows itself weighed down by the burden of material spirits, and occupied by the discordant disturbances of matter.* From these assertions of the Philosophers, therefore, it is evident that the human body and its connatural spirit—which we named above the <term>idol of the soul</term> <note>original: "animæ idolum"; a term used in Neoplatonism to describe the lower reflection or "shadow" of the soul that governs the body</note>, the natural soul, the elementary power of the elements, the directress of the body, and the origin of the senses—is the cause of error, sin, and lust in the <term>middle soul</term>. It is through this spirit that the soul unfolds its powers of feeling in this body, perceives bodily things through the body, moves the body through space, rules it in its place, and nourishes the body within the body. This is what we call the sensitive soul and, with St. Paul, the <term>animal man</term> <note>original: "hominem animalem"; referring to the "natural man" driven by instincts rather than spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14)</note>. It is this that is submerged in darkness and ignorance. For this portion of the internal man leads the human being toward the worst things: speaking of which, St. Paul says, *I see another law in my members, captivating me in the law of sin.* <note>Romans 7:23</note> Therefore, Plotinus says that if the soul, by neglecting the mind, adheres to this "idol," it is depraved and loses its merit until it is made into an evil Demon. Since we have spoken sufficiently in the preceding sections about this lowest portion of the internal man and its disposition and nature, we shall deal with it only briefly in this place, and as if in passing.

### CHAPTER II.

->*By what means the middle soul is allured to lower things, so that it is accustomed to neglect higher things.*<-

Since the human soul is in itself rational, concupiscible <note>the faculty of desire or "wanting"</note>, and irascible <note>the faculty of anger or "spiritedness"</note>, it is subject through its concupiscible quality to the affections of desiring or loving something. And therefore it must be known that, just as there are many objects of appetite and love, so too are those objects found not in only one region of the world, but in all of them. Consequently, some of them allure more toward God, others toward the world, and others toward the Devil: for the objects of pleasures and appetites in the coarse and terrestrial region call the soul away from God and turn it toward vices. Therefore, sensual love is to fulfill the appetite of the flesh and to subject oneself to the nature of the external man. For just as a man consists of two substances—namely, soul with reason, and flesh with its senses, which is to say, soul and body—so also is there one love particular to the body or flesh, and another proper and peculiar to the rational soul. Wherefore, if the soul is dragged downward by the pleasure of the senses, which are of the flesh, it is submerged in darkness. But on the other hand, if it is raised upward by the power of illuminated reason, it is clarified by immortal light. Therefore, the chief force of "elementary" <note>pertaining to the four physical elements</note> love is found in the lowest region of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>the human body viewed as a "little world" mirroring the universe</note>, namely in the <term>seminal vessels</term> <note>original: "vases seminariis"; the reproductive organs</note>, with a lustful impulse or the pleasure of intercourse, by which the souls of men are carried headlong in the manner of brutes. And truly, in respect to this appetite and its object, what difference is there, I pray, between a man and a beast, since the force of the appetite in both is directed toward the seminal vessels, in which the pleasure of carnal love is stored? Hence it happens that the location of this object is placed at the base of the lowest region, so that it may be known to us that love of this kind is nothing other than terrestrial, brutal lust, and the seductress of the celestial soul toward earthly things. And certainly, there are very few men who know any love other than this one, whose companions are gluttony, laziness, and other such things. But truly, the soul itself, when free from the shadow of the flesh, knows a more excellent love in the "middle heaven," both chaste and virginal, where the effects of its desires [are] more...

# TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK IX.

...they are more clear and simple, weighed in the just scales of Astraea <note>original: "Astrææ"; the Greek goddess of Justice and purity</note>, since here she is joined in a simple marriage with the most chaste Psyche <note>original: "castissima Psyche"; the personification of the Soul</note>, and is occupied with the chaste and pure life of the world. Thus, even in the fertile region of man, she generates joy, gladness, hope, mercy, and other such pious and chaste offspring. Indeed, when the reason of the <term>desiring faculty</term> <note>original: "concupiscibilis"; the part of the soul responsible for appetites and desires</note> in the soul is established with prudence, fortitude, and justice, it then receives the gift of illumination from the Spirit. From this effect, it rises into four most chaste daughters, born of the super-celestial fatherland, which are called the Cardinal Virtues: namely, **prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice**; which are, as it were, the origins and hinges <note>A play on the Latin "cardo," meaning hinge, from which "Cardinal" is derived</note> of all virtues.

Nor does the desiring faculty of the soul achieve this alone (namely, love by itself); but rather when joined with the <term>spirited faculty</term> <note>original: "irascibili"; the part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and rejection</note>, which is hatred. For through hatred of the world and of the self, one makes progress in the love of God and neighbor; through contempt for temporal and low things, the desire for eternal and heavenly things grows. Therefore, in the object of lower desire, there is no path leading to the higher things, but rather it acts as an obstacle. Truly, carnal children are nothing other than worldly and plainly illegitimate in respect to those celestial ones which men ought to produce so that they may pass toward God. Of these children—both the base or illegitimate ones, as well as those born of chaste generation—excellent mention was made in *Wisdom, chapter 3.* Whence also, regarding carnal generation, it is said there, *that happy is the barren and undefiled woman, who has not known the bed in sin; she shall have fruit in the visitation of holy souls* <note>original: "in respectione animarum sanctarum"</note>, *that is, she shall enjoy spiritual children. And the eunuch who has not wrought iniquity with his hands, etc. For unto him shall be given the chosen gift of faith, and a most acceptable portion in the temple of God.*

Similarly, in *Wisdom, chapter 4: O how beautiful is the chaste generation with charity; for the memory thereof is immortal, because it is known both with God and with men.* For this reason, holy men of past ages, so that they might live chastely and without carnal appetite, led an austere life, so that they might diminish the attraction of the feminine object and dominate worldly desire. They observed that by the luxurious act and the impulse of intercourse, their chaste thoughts were defiled, and the operations of the soul occupied with God were called away from heaven to lower things by the sensible enticements of the flesh. Indeed, the **Apostle Paul** himself complained of the depraved effect of this appetite, saying: *I see another law in my members, taking me captive in the law of sin.* Therefore, the desiring property of the lower region of the Microcosm <note>The "Little World," referring to the human body and spirit as a reflection of the Great World/Universe</note> leads man to the worst things. For thus it is read in *1 John 2: He who loves the world has not the love of the Father in him, because all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and pride.* And *in the same, chapter 3: For this reason the world does not know the sons of God, because the sons of God have not known the world.*

And I certainly believe it would come to pass that a man would deserve the name of a saint and be able to perform miraculous works if, by constantly overcoming carnal temptations, he kept his <term>seed</term> <note>original: "semen"; here used in an alchemical and physiological sense as the carrier of vital light or "spirit"</note> untouched in its own vessels. For every year his light would be multiplied; which, indeed, without its own emission, would grow into such an abundance of light that it would illuminate the entire dark tabernacle <note>The physical body</note> of that man and, as if transfiguring it, would lift the mass of the body upward on fiery wings. 

But a double obstacle resists this virtue: one is the pollution or defilement of the seed, contracted by infinite mixtures, which the divine light does not love insofar as it is concerned with unity. And the other is that immense dominion which the flesh, together with the senses, holds in the human composition, soliciting the soul day and night to the fulfillment of its appetite. Thus, I think there is almost no one born of a mother who has so preserved his seed untouched for himself that he has not handed over a portion of it to others. But if such a person were found, he surely, as I believe, would be able to perform wonders both in prophecy and in the curing of diseases, and in the prolongation of his life, for many reasons which it would perhaps be tedious to recite in this place. etc.

# ON THE CONTEMPLATION OF THE PYRAMID OF KNOWLEDGE

Therefore, the **formal pyramid** is the presence of the divine Word. By the wisdom, action, justice, and power of this Word, **moist nature** <note>original: "natura humida"; in this context, it refers to the primal, fluid substance of the universe before it is fully formed</note> is led from the potentiality of <term>hyle</term> <note>original: "hylæ"; from the Greek word for "wood" or "matter," used by philosophers to mean the raw, unformed material of the universe</note> into the actuality of the waters, and is shaped into a spherical figure. This mass of waters is called the **universal spirit**, or the **second Pan** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, Pan represented the "All" or the totality of nature; the "second Pan" refers to the created physical world</note>, the son of *hyle* produced by <term>Demogorgon</term> <note>A primordial creator god often associated with the deep abyss or the soul of the world</note> after the "dispute"—that is, the prince of darkness. This is nothing other than the universal moist nature expanded through the entire world-machine.

This is, therefore, that **spiritual or moist pyramid** and universal water, which we have called the **physical pyramid** in many places throughout our *Macrocosmic* and *Microcosmic* Treatises. This is shaped into the form of a material pyramid because its upper part is more subtle <note>In early science, "subtle" means refined, thin, or spirit-like, as opposed to "gross" or dense</note> due to the infinite presence of light, while its lower part is thicker due to the greater or lesser absence of light.

It must be understood, moreover, that the reason the physical or material pyramid has its base positioned opposite to the base of the formal pyramid seems to be this: namely, because moist nature in its origin is entirely contrary to the disposition of **lucid nature** <note>Light-filled or divine nature</note> in its *nature, substance, operation, and location*.

Indeed, by looking at the *nature* of both, we see that **coldness** is the natural companion of moist nature, while **heat** is the hearth-fire of light. Next, they differ regarding their *origin*, since moist nature was produced from the womb of *hyle* or chaos (pregnant a second time) from potentiality into a specific existence. But lucid nature was always "in act" <note>An Aristotelian term meaning fully realized or active, rather than just a possibility</note>, and was always reserved in that very supersubstantial essence until the creation of the world; in this essence it shall remain eternally, like a son in a father, and yet in a wondrous way, it will always be present to mundane matter.

They also differ in *substance*, because the material spirit is, in some way, more or less corporeal, and consequently physical; but the substance of light is incorporeal, and as it were, supersubstantial in itself. They are also entirely diverse in *operation*, since light always acts by itself, while moist or spiritual nature always suffers <note>In the sense of being passive or receiving action</note>. Finally, they differ in *location*, since the source of light is from the summit and apex of the heavens, while the matrix of the spirit is established by the earth itself.

Therefore, just as lucid nature—by always tending downward from the lucid source—is found to be increasingly thinner, scarcer, and more rare (as demonstrated above), so conversely, moist nature—springing and rising up from its thick material source or matrix—is thicker, denser, and more corporeal at the bottom (which is why we fixed the base of its pyramid on the earth). But by rising upward little by little and step by step, it becomes increasingly slender and thin, until it forms the point <note>original: "conum"; the cone or apex</note> of its pyramid exactly where the pyramid of light has its base. Thus, we have described the parallelogram of moist nature, and likewise its pyramid, by joining together the two upper extremities of the parallel lines.
